column23: Crane operator was lifting a decompression chamber located on the south side +14ft level with the north side crane's auxiliary line.  When the decompression chamber was being lowered down onto the drill deck the crane operator observed a broken wire rope strand on the cranes auxilary line.

Contract operator was using the crane to move diesel tote tanks. During the process of lowering the boom into the cradle, the main winch cable jumped out of the main winch spool. The operator completed lowering the boom into the cradle and placed the crane out of service. New cable has been ordered to complete repair.

UPDATE: Per investigation, there was no deficiency found with the crane beyond the damaged cable. It appears that the cable "stacked" in the spool while rolling up the winch. This lead to the cable jumping out of the winch spool. The damage to the cable occurred when the operator noticed and attempted to reseat the cable by running the winch. Corrective action: the cable is to be replaced in it's entirety. 

During investigation it was found that there were two policy violations, subsequent to the incident. 1) it was learned that the crane pre-use was performed but not properly recorded on the pre-use inspection form. 2) it was learned that neither the crane operator nor the PIC immediately take action to place the crane OOS according to FWE policy. The PIC and crane operator have both been formally reprimanded. Additionally, they have been tasked with specific re-training and responsibility for holding area-wide crew change safety meetings to teach others the lessons learned from this incident.

Upon returning from hurricane evacuation, the generator was visually inspected with no issues observed.  Unit was started and about an hour after being returned to service production operations staff noticed the lights flicker while working in the office.  A production operator went towards the generator and opened an access door.  Upon opening the door, the operator noticed small fire and smoke.  He announced fire while shutting down the unit.  The other two operators on board met him at the unit with a fire extinguisher.  They opened the door again, at this time they saw a small flame near the generator windings.  They partially discharged the extinguisher at the flame.  When the chemical residue settled they saw another small flame.  They discharged more of the extinguisher towards the flame and monitored the unit for 30 minutes to ensure the flame was extinguished.  The fire was extinguished in less than two minutes and only one handheld extinguisher was utilized.  There were no injuries associated with this event and the only damage was to the electrical end of the generator.  These are the preliminary findings.  The event remains under investigation by Company.

A Company employee was tied off to a drain line while approximately 8 feet above the deck. While repositioning, the drain line failed and he fell to the deck. He was flown in by the field helicopter to Hospital where they diagnosed him with a dislocated shoulder. They were able to put the shoulder back into place but he is in a sling and has a follow up appointment tomorrow. We will be flying offshore to perform an investigation on the incident tomorrow morning.
NOTE: The contractor's job title is "Fitter".
REQUESTED INFORMATION: The job scope was to repair drain lines below the deck.
REQUESTED INFORMATION #2: 
(1) Has the IP gone back to work? 
RESPONSE: The injured person has not returned to work. He was given a light duty release and chose not to accept light duty so he was terminated. He now has an attorney.
(2) Is it normal protocol by Company2 to tie off of drain lines that are above 6' without knowing the loads that they can maintain and a person's body weight that ties off to them? 
RESPONSE: It is not normal protocol to tie-off to drain lines. The following information was sent to all manned platforms following the incident: 
.	Consultant or PIC did not properly evaluate the elevated work hazards, qualify the level of risk of the job, and establish the required safeguards.
.	Stop Work Authority was not used by anyone on the crew.
.	The initial anchor point could not support 5000 pounds.
.	The Consultant or PIC did not perform a proper Hazard Analysis which would have identified the possibility or potential for a fall.  The following methods should have been considered:
o	Fall Elimination
o	Fall Prevention - Fall prevention may be accomplished by the use of manlifts, scaffolds, or temporary access ways with standard hand-rails, midrails, and toe boards.
(3) Was tying off to a drain line part of a safe procedure in the JSA that was written at the time? 
RESPONSE: Neither of the 2 JSAs written for this task identify tying off to a drain line as a step.
(4) In the final report, we also would like to know what is/are the lesson(s) learned from this incident and how to prevent it from happening again. 
RESPONSE: Findings:				
.	The daily work scope changed without the proper job planning.
.	Crew had access to the necessary equipment (scaffolding) to complete the job safely but did not take the time to retrieve it.
.	Discussion from production personnel was perceived by the consultant and crew that they were to quickly perform the newly identified work. So they felt rushed.
.	Personnel recognized the potential hazards and agreed there was a safer way to perform the job task but no one spoke up. 

Company Policies Failed
.	Consultant or PIC did not properly evaluate the elevated work hazards and establish safeguards.
.	Stop Work Authority was not used by anyone on the crew.
.	The initial anchor point could not support 5000 lbs.

Corrective Actions and Reminders  
.	Review Safety Alert with all personnel.
.	When the work scope changes, take the necessary time to complete the pre-job planning.
.	A Hazard assessment must be performed by a qualified individual for each job task.
.	Be aware that how a message is delivered will determine how it is perceived by others.
.	If the message you receive gives the wrong perception, then questions need to be asked and more discussion needs to occur (possibly including your FWE Supervisor).

IP was on South boat landing assisting with hooking up water line to take on potable water for the platform. M/V Candy machine tied up on the back side of the boat landing which put the boat tie off rope laying across the entire deck of the boat landing. IP was assisting with hooking up hose from the boat to the hose connection at the bottom of the staircase, with his back to the boat landing deck. Then the boat drifted North with the rope moving across the boat landing deck with rope tightening against the hand railing. The hand railing then broke at the bottom base striking IP in the back causing him to fall forward into the grating steps of the stairwell. IP injuries to his lower right back, laceration to his right knee, and left ankle pain.

After investigation on site, it was determined that the particular hazard of the tie off rope sweeping across the boat landing and contacting the base of the handrail was not anticipated by platform crewmembers or the vessel captain. The Job Safety Analysis (JSA) did not highlight this hazard. The prevailing sea state caused the vessel to move causing the tie off rope to quickly became taut and to sweep across the landing in the direction of the seas which caused the tie off rope to contact the base of the handrail. Remedial measures will include recognition of the tie off rope position with regards to seas to ensure that the sea state does not permit the tie off rope to lie on or sweep across the landing. The downed section of handrail will not be re-installed. 

The injured party, a Company employee, sustained a broken left ankle and a laceration to his right knee requiring stitches.

At 1:45 pm a BSL alarm tripped on the preheater, causing the fuel gas valve to shut down. The isolation valve to the pilot gas and main burner were closed. Flames were noticed in the burner section. As a precaution, the fire alarm was sounded and personnel mustered to their station.

Flow was diverted from the preheater system to the heater treater.  A 20 # PK fire extinguisher was discharged into the burner to extinguish the flames.

Once the unit was cool to the touch, the flame arrestor was removed to try and identify the source of the fire. A Glycol leak was found by a weld inside the fire tube.  The preheater system has been placed out of service.

No equipment damage occurred.  The failed weld has to be repaired.

Estimated Preheater Repair is $21,500, this cost includes labor, material, NDE (Non Destructive Exam),trucking and boat transportation.

At approximately 11:30 am today (11/7/2017), a welding machine in a safe work area over heated. Coolant fluid from the welding unit activated the pressure relief valve and heated coolant escaped the unit. The heated coolant came in contact with the TSE loop. The poly line on the TSE loop melted from the heated coolant, which initiated the alarm system. The emergency response and muster plan were initiated and the facility was shut in. Fire response team responded to area. No fire was detected but steam from the heated coolant and TSE loop was observed. A hand held dry chemical extinguisher was discharged to the area as a precaution. The area was reviewed and designated as safe and personnel de-mustered. All coolant was contained within the skid. Welding unit has been taken out of service. Facility production will be re-initiated.

At 10:15 PM the night Operator was in the control room when he heard a loud squealing noise outside.  He then stepped outside to investigate and when he looked down through the grating below, he noticed some flames coming from inside the #2 sea water lift pump's (cooling water) electric motor fan guard. He alerted the platform PIC via the Gaitronics system and immediately proceeded downstairs, turned off the pump and extinguished the fire utilizing a 30lb Purple-K hand held extinguisher. Once the PIC arrived on scene additional seawater was applied to completely extinguish the fire and cool the motor.  This fire was contained within the motor only and was extinguished in less than 5 minutes after it was discovered.

It appears that the #2 sea water lift pump (cooling water) experienced a bearing failure which caused excessive heat buildup. The heat caused the upper seal to fail allowing some oil to become overheated and ignite.

FINAL - On December 4th between 3:19 and 3:22 PM Company had an automatic activation of the FEES (fire explosion evacuation strategy) system which activated the ESD, blowdown, and sounded the muster alarm.  The activation was caused by a detection of two gas detectors in the enclosure of the High-pressure compressor.  The unit was not running at the time as we were in the process of removing the LOTO and returning valves to the normal operating position following an annual maintenance exercise. The gas reading on the enclosure was monitored in the control room and gradually dropped to zero.  After the levels were at zero, the enclosure was opened to verify the gas was dissipated. UPDATE 1/5/18
Photos of the fire damage have been attached and answers provided for the questions listed below:  
#1) Where is the thruster #4 siplink/cabinet located? In the forward section of the Starboard Aft Machinery Space, Second Deck.
#2) Was a hot work being performed? No
#3) Elaborate on how this cabinet operates: This cabinet is a 11kV variable frequency drive for the thruster.  A siplink takes 11kV AC power, converts it to separate DC positive and DC negative busses by use of power stacks, and then converts the DC positive and negative back to AC through a different set of power stacks.  This process sends clean power to the end consumer, in this case, the thruster motors. 
#4) What equipment was involved? Fire started in Convert#4 in the cabinet.  This cabinet is required to run the thruster, Thruster #4 is unavailable due to the damage. 
#5) Did an explosion occur inside the cabinet? Neither an explosion nor indications of an explosion were observed during or after the event.
#6) Did an arc flash occur inside the cabinet? Yes

There was a fire on the gas compressor that developed between the exhaust system and insulation blanket. The investigation is underway to determine the root cause. This eWell will be updated after the investigation is complete.

**Update - January 18, 2018**
Our office was closed due to the weather conditions on January 17, 2017 so we were not able to submit an eWell update on the follow-up due date. The investigation is still ongoing so there is nothing to report at this time. 

**Update - February 9, 2018**
The findings of the investigation are as follows:

IMMEDIATE CAUSES: 
  * A problematic Kenco Oil Regulator / Level Safety Low (LSL) malfunctioned, exacerbated by increased oil viscosity due to excessively cold temperatures.  In response to the low level alarm, operations manually added oil to the running engine to clear the alarm, exceeding the OEM maximum recommended level.  Residual oil migrated thru the engine, breached the exhaust system and ignited.

SYSTEMIC CAUSES:
  * Communication
     ** Lack of recognizing and reporting chronic issues to maintenance organization.
  * Training / Knowledge transfer
     ** Knowledge transfer not effective
        *** Hazard Identification - Overfill
        *** Crankcase Oil Level Checking

ACTIONS-
 * Issue a memorandum to communicate the "Consequences of Overfilling Oil Levels and proper way of checking crankcase oil levels." 1Q2018- Maintenance Superintendent
  * Review with operations during annual safety meeting  2Q2018- Maintenance Superintendent

AREA OF IMPROVEMENT-
  * Verify current operations / maintenance are in line with OEM / Industry accepted practice. 1Q2018 - Maintenance Superintendent
  * Mount Kenco Oil Regulator/ Sensor directly to the engine.  This will ensure a directly level measurement and increased temperature. 1Q2018- Production Operations

**UPDATED April 17, 2018**
In response to the BSEE's comments about changing the incident root cause:
We initially thought the root cause of the incident was due to the missing o-ring and higher than normal oil viscosity due to unusually low temperature. The investigation team took a deeper dive by contacting the engine manufacture and further investigation determined that the missing o-ring and high oil viscosity was only a contributing factor to the incident and in fact the root cause was determined to be overfilling the engine sump with oil. The reason why this changed the root cause was because if the engine had not been overfilled, the oil would not have carried over through the crank case breather and into the engine's air intake system resulting in a fire.

  * A Safety Bulletin and Maintenance Memorandum was sent to field personnel notifying everyone of the investigation findings, root cause and addressed corrective actions.

Please accept this report as the final report.

Shell considers this incident to fall in a "gray area" of the incident reporting regulations for the following reasons:

Contractor Supervisor: 

SBM Release on Blackhawk - While back flushing the Coriolis Meter, synthetic based drilling mud was discharge overboard. The mud dissipated quickly with no sightings on the surrounding sea. The release has been secured. The NRC was notified at 01:51 on 1/23/2018 (NRC #1202602). 

01/31/2018 - The investigation has not been finalized at this time. Preliminary findings, corrective actions, and additional details have been collected. 

On the night of 22-Jan, the mud logger called the driller asking to backflush the Coriolis meter.  The driller initially told the mud logger that they did not have the people available and would let him know when they could.  As another job on the drill floor closed out, the Aux side AD came into the driller's shack asking the forward plan.  The driller asked the AD to go line up so they could backflush the Coriolis.  The AD left the driller's shack and said they would call when they had it lined up.  After checking the alignment, the AD called the driller and told him they were ready.  The driller asked the AD to confirm the trip tank valves were closed before they would turn on the mixing pump.  The AD confirmed the trip tank valves were closed and the driller turned on the #2 mixing pump.  The AD went up to the gumbo box to check for returns.  The mud logger called the driller after 5 minutes of pumping letting him know there were still no returns to the active system (shorebase real-time monitoring called the mud logger to confirm the loss in the active system as well).  The driller called the derrickhand and AD to check the lineup.  After 11 minutes of total pumping, mud was seen flowing out of the auger from the cuttings dryer and the pump was shut down.  
 
The current root causes of the investigation are:
1.	Complacency with routine tasks
.	The AD assumed the shakers were on and the driller (who knew the shakers were off) assumed the AD knew to turn on the shakers as part of the lineup.
2.	Policy was not known or understood
.	GEMS policy (5.3.2.a) which covers Oil Based Mud does not cover this type of fluid movement but does say when circulating the shakers must be on and manned.
.	There was no procedure or JSA (not required) in place to cover this operation
3.	Hazard not identified
.	The hazard of large enough quantities of fluid getting down into the cuttings dryer to flood the auger and go overboard was not identified and therefore was not labeled as an environmentally critical discharge point
 
The proposed action items are:
1.	Review incident with all crews - a flash alert was sent fleet wide for this incident
2.	Develop a Site Specific Procedure for onboard fluid transfers
3.	Revise GEMS 5.3.2.a for clarity and modernization
4.	Evaluate barrier options to prevent liquid discharge through cuttings overboard line
5.	Hold Time Out for Safety focusing on crew complacency - these have already started
6.	Issue Safety Alert fleet wide to address environmentally critical discharge points
 
Per the Terms of Reference from the investigation, an interim investigation report is expected by 6-Feb and final release by 20-Feb.

Note:  In Helix CAR that manual monitoring/measurement is occurring for the MG #1 in service generator until all automated monitoring installation is complete. Information from attached Helix Corrective Action Request Form:
Description: The Motor Generators 1 & 2 supplying power to the Production Plant equipment have been identified with no remote monitoring of temperature for the drive end and non-drive end bearings since initial installation. No manual measurement of the temperature was found either.

Root cause: Defective/ malfunction of part (bearing) which created overheating that ignited its lubricating grease.

- Machinery item not covered under Class Machinery Items and not subject to inspections by Class surveyor. Machinery not essential for the main Power generation nor Propulsion power.

Employees were performing routine maintenance by replacing the gas pressure control valve on the cleanup separator. The valve is located on a vertical run approximately five feet from the ground. The employees bolted the top flange of the valve to the upper spool flange, and were in the process of seating the lower flange of the valve to the lower spool flange. The employees then determined that a chain fall device was necessary to complete the job. A chain fall device was attached to the upper spool to raise the upper spool and valve enough to slide the valve into position. At the time of using the chain fall, employee #1 was on a small platform above the valve operating the chain fall device while employee #2 was standing on a ladder near the valve awaiting the valve to line up so they could install the bolts between the lower flange of the valve and the lower spool flange. While the chain fall device was in use, the valve was at an angle to the side of the lower spool. When the chain fall raised the upper spool with attached valve to a height above the lower spool, the valve and upper spool which were at an angle from their normal position, kicked (released energy) back towards normal position. Employee #2’s right arm was in the path of the valve and when the energy released, employee #2 tried to stabilize himself by grabbing the lower spool with their left hand. Employee #2’s left hand middle finger was pinched in between the valve flange and lower spool flange when they reached out to brace himself.
Contributing Factors:
1. Body positioning - During the operation to line up the valve and spool, Employee #2 should not have been on a ladder near the potential release of energy.
2. JSA - Employees filled out the proper EIL and JSA during initial job planning. Once the job scope changed and a chain fall was needed, JSA should have been updated to include the new equipment and hazards associated with said equipment.
3. PPE – Employees at the time were wearing nitrile gloves while performing the job.
Corrective Action/s:
1. When a release of energy is to occur it should be controlled with the use of a come-along or similar device. At no time should an employee be near a potential release of energy.
2. When job tasks change, JSA’s need to be updated as per company policy.
3. Impact resistant gloves shall be issued to all field employees. Impact resistant gloves shall be worn whenever employees are working on a JSA which has pinch points as a hazard.

-Be advised that following internal investigations and completion of the required inspections as per API RP 2D, the subject crane has been returned to service today, 2/17/18. 

**UPDATE** 3/1/18

Initial, on-site investigation revealed that the Aux line's deadman had contacted the underside of a 4X4 cross-brace structural member above the racking tower. This observation suggested that at the onset of the booming-up motion, the aux line's deadman got obstructed on the structural member, leading to high tension on the Aux line and failure of the Aux winch. While the Aux winch remained firmly attached to the crane structure via the mounting bolts, the excessive force deformed one of the Aux winch side-plates, leading to the unspooling of the  Aux line, and the descent of the Aux ball, which fell onto the pipe-rack fingers below. Note that the operator raised the boom only 2 feet prior to Aux-winch failure, and reported no signs of engine power increase or noticeable resistance to boom-up during the incident. 
 
On February 20, 2018, a team inspected the failed components. The observed deformations and sheared side-plate bolts point to complete mechanical overload as the failure's driving force. The relative ease in which the boom-up action overloaded the Aux winch is attributed to the significantly larger load capacity of the boom winch relative to that of the Aux winch. The inspection lacked any observations pointing to design flaws, maintenance negligence, or crane operator error as contributing factors to this incident.

At approximately 11:05hrs while in the process of installing the gooseneck for the boost line, one of the maintenance baskets failed while in use, allowing the basket king pin to become disconnected from the slewing axle platform and fall over.  The operator's fall was arrested by their SRL and immediately recovered by the adjacent Work Basket Operator.  There were no injuries as a result of this incident. An investigation is ongoing.

03/14/2018 FINAL REPORT:
1. Water depth and distance from shore added.
2. The maintenance basket is located in the moon pool; it was the Port Forward moon pool basket.
3. More details on the load: the load was the weight of a single person; however, the roughneck was utilizing the basket to maneuver the boost line hose due to the difficulty of stabbing the hose. This was being done by using a 0.5in manila rope tied off to the top rail of the basket, causing a side load on the basket and the axle that secures it to the platform. The breaking strength of the rope is estimated to be ~2,385 lbs.
4. There were no injuries as a result of this incident.
5. The following equipment was damaged: axle, retaining nuts, and some hydraulic hoses.
6. Estimated repair cost is ~$5,000.

Key Learnings/Root Causes:
-It was found to be common practice to utilize the work basket(s) for pushing and pulling activities which is against the OEM's operating guidelines.  The practice of using the work basket for any push/pull activities has been ceased, as they are meant for man riding activities only.
-An HSE alert was issued in 2015 that addressed the risks of using the basket for pushing/pulling activities.  The alert was mistakenly put into the maintenance system, which did not circulate the alert to the operators of the work baskets.  Transocean has since made all crews aware of the alert, and has issued a 'Quick Share' throughout the TOI fleet making everyone aware of the dangers of utilizing the work baskets for pushing/pulling activities.

At 0506 two smoke detectors were activated.  Upon investigation it was determined that the port aft fire pump which had been running was the cause of the smoke.  No indications of flames present.  The upper bearing and mechanical seal on fire pump #3 will be repaired or replaced.  The port aft fire pump #3 will be out of service until repairs are complete.  There are two fully operational main fire pumps still available.  Notification has also been made to US Coast Guard.

UPDATE (3/15)
At present, the pump is operational, but will be out of service during inspections and/or while repairs are completed.
#1)Why was the fire pump running?  Pit cleaning operations were underway and extra pressure was requested. We used the opportunity to test run the fire pumps and get additional training on fire hose usage. 
#2) Was a muster required? Yes, full muster achieved in 10 minutes from activation of alarm - the following incident report was provided to the USCG (CG-2692):  
Two port aft machinery space smoke detectors were activated. The bridge team contacted the captain who activated the general alarm and made an associated announcement for crewmembers with assigned duties to report to their stations, and all other to muster on the bow. A muster of the crew was completed and fast response team reported to the scene. A common alarm was noticed on thruster 5, and suspecting that as the cause of the smoke, it was secured. The fire and gas system was placed into auto mode which allowed outputs including shutting down the port engine room to go through. Ventilation to the space as well as fire pump number 3 (Port Aft) which had been running in the space were also secured. Upon arrival on the scene the second mate indicated there was smoke but no other indications of fire. A damaged upper bearing on the fire pump was determined to be the most likely cause of the smoke.
Fast response team arrived on scene and completed a full sweep of the space to ensure there was no fire. The team then checked on the equipment that was suspected to have caused the smoke. It was determined to be fire pump number 3 which had been running in the space caused the smoke. Thruster 5 and the port engine room were restarted. The activated smoke alarms were reset and cleared. Personnel were dismissed from their muster station while the fast response team and maintenance personnel remained on fire watch.
#3) Was the smoke coming from the mechanical seal; if not where was it coming from? The upper bearing was the most likely source of the smoke, though by the time the fast response team arrived at the scene, the pump had been shut down, and there wasn't any smoke being produced.  There have been no indications that the smoke came from any other equipment within the space.
#4) Were the only damaged parts to the upper bearing and mechanical seal?  Though, initially the mechanical seal leaked, further testing did not produce any indications of what could have caused the smoke.  During inspection, the seal was found to be loose.  Engineers tightened the seal and are presently performing a function test of the pump.  At this point, we have not identified the need to change out the seal or conduct any repairs to the upper bearing.  We will continue to test run the pump for a period of time over the course of the next few days to ensure it is fully operational.
#5) Was anyone injured as a result of the incident? No
#6) Estimate the cost of the damaged equipment. The full extent of the damage will be better known during disassembly, but the total cost will likely be under 10k

At 03:30 one (1) bbl of 6.6 ppg synthetic chemical fluid base fluid was released to the Gulf of Mexico. This release occurred while tripping in the hole with the 16" RTTS at 2,742 feet. After tripping in hole through a reverse riser cap the drill string became unbalanced and approximately 21 bbls of base fluid U-tubed out of the drill pipe and onto the rig floor. 20 bbls were contained on the rig and a total of 1bbl was spilled to the water, creating a brown expression on the surface of the water. NRC notification was made (NRC #1207764).


Estimated length and width of the spill. 
Occurred at night and could not see the entire loss of SBM. The 1 bbl was determined from what was lost from the active system and what was recovered in cleanup and from the Haz Area drain tank.

Wind speed and direction. 
Wind speed: 5 KNTS    Wind direction: SE

How was the 21 bbls that was released on the rig floor contained? 
The 20 bbls that were captured was contained inside the rig floor kick plate, diverter housing, and rig drain lines.

How did the 1 bbl of fluid make it into the GOM? 
There were two routs of escape for the fluid. 
a)A hydraulic line penetration through the diverter housing allowed base fluid to be released to the moonpool
b)The haz-area drain system is designed to divert the three-way valve to discharge overboard in case of heavy rain, the automated system diverted the flow overboard which put SMB in the water on the stbd side of the rig.

Was the RTTS plugged at the bottom that created the underbalanced state? 
No, while tripping in the hole through a reverse riser cap of 6.6 ppg base fluid, the open-ended drill string became under-balanced. The following events occurred beginning on March 09, 2018 on the Doyon 15 Drilling Rig. The events described below aren’t necessarily related concerning cause and effect; rather, are a sequence of events describing two simultaneous incidents concerning mechanical issues related to the rig’s top drive and a well control event.

At approximately 0130 hours, the rig experienced problems while drilling, related to the top drive torque let-off procedures, which resulted in the unthreading of drillpipe downhole. The driller was able to reconnect the drillstring downhole. It was decided to pull the drillstring out of the hole to verify and torque all connections and inspect the bottom hole assembly.

Employees visually noticed signs of extreme heat in the top drive while tripping drillpipe out of the hole. Their observations included one of the top drive’s metal access panel covers brightly glowing orange in color. The cover was for access to motor number 3 (of 4 motors) and the drive system. Additionally, there was smoke emanating from the top drive. Their statements also indicated that there was no active fire visually seen coming from the top drive. When the access panel was opened there were signs consistent with extreme heat and/or fire to include: visible heat markings on paint and metal; the smell of burning material; drive belt materials that were melted and fused to various parts of the top drive; and, evidence of burnt and charred belt material.

It was found that the six (6) drive belts for motor 3 and one (1) adjacent drive belt were destroyed. It was also found that the bearing assembly for the drive shaft to motor number 3 appeared to be unserviceable. The drive belts’ debris was removed from the top drive, and, the the motor off-line was taken off. After, the drill crew continued well operations without the use of motor 3 to pull the drill pipe out of the hole.

The driller and tool pusher observed that approximately 6 barrels of drilling fluid per hour were being gained after pulling approximately 200’ of drillpipe out of the hole. The drilling fluid weight was increased from 10.5 ppg to 10.7 ppg at 0330 hrs. The weight of returns did not increase within the expected timeframe; this was attributed to an influx of water. The annular preventer on the Blowout Preventor Stack was closed at approximately 0720 hours. By 03/10/2018, the well was brought back under control through the application of safe drilling and well control practices. Once the well was secured, operational focus transitioned to repairing the top drive.

March 9, 2018:  While rigging up a return line on well A6, the IP was retrieving a 5 foot section of chicksan pipe from a storage pipe rack to be added to the return line. After putting the section of pipe across their left shoulder, the IP turned their body away from the storage rack to walk away.  In doing so, they failed to see a grounding spool for the E-line unit on the surface deck, stumbled on it and struck their left knee on the deck surface grating. On March 12, 2018 (crew change day to begin field-break), the IP notified their supervisor of the incident and requested to seek medical attention on shore.  IP stated at the time of incident they did not believe they sustained an injury, but noticed on the evening of March 11th, they began to feel discomfort in their left knee.  March 13, 2018, the IP was evaluated by a PA (Physician Assistant) and diagnosied with Lt.Knee Chondromalacia Patella. They were not given any prescriptions, but were given a "Restricted Work Release" with instructions to limit their walking and climbing.

April 9, 2018 Final update:  IP was medically re-evaluated and given a full-duty release to return to work on March 27, 2018.  Our investigation revealed IP simply did not see the grounding spool on the deck when they attempted to turn and walk away from the pipe rack. To prevent any future re-occurrence, Fieldwood has reiterated to all P&A operations the need to maintain good housekeeping and should a piece of equipment become a potential tripping hazard, it should be flagged for personal awareness.

On 3/17/2018 at approximately 8:00 am, production operators performed a routine once a week startup of the backup platform diesel air compressor.  Shortly after start up, the alternator grounded out through the ESD cable and a resulting 1" flame was witnessed from the melted cable insulation.  Within seconds, personnel quickly extinguished this flame with a portable 30# fire extinguisher.  The air compressor was shutdown, battery disconnected and unit marked out of service before being shipped in for a third party evaluation.

Initial Action:
* Generator was shutdown
* Extinguished flame with 30# portable dry chemical unit.  
* All stop issued, personnel mustered.  No injuries.
* Unit was marked OOS and sent in for evaluation.  

Investigative Findings:
* The air intake duct (measures 2.5") and the air ESD flapper assembly (measures 2.75") were incorrectly sized.
* The differential gap of .25" was made up with duct tape.  
* The air ESD flapper assembly was solely supported by the air intake duct system by way of hose clamps.

Lessons Learned:
* The air ESD flapper assembly parted from the air intake duct, causing the supporting bracket to make contact with the voltage output post of the alternator.
* The air ESD flapper assembly's support bracket was not adequately supported

ERT's corrective measures and actions to prevent recurrence:
1. The correct boot assembly will be utilized to make up the .25" difference between the two systems.
2. A support will be added to the ESD flapper assembly to prevent using hose clamps as sole support.    
3. Incident findings will be related to all GOM platforms.

Damages and parts that will be replaced:
* Air intake rubberized boot
* ESD flapper assembly
* ESD cable
* Unit will be repaired and shop tested by PELSTAR before sending back offshore

Initial Report 03/18/2018: 

No harm to people, no damage to equipment or the environment. On 03/18/2018 at approximately 00:48 hours, the smoke alarms (4) in the port pontoon area went into alarm and activated the vessel's General Alarm system. A rig wide announcement was made to muster at the forward lifeboats. The Fast Response team arrived on scene in the Port Aft pump room and observed an atomized cloud in the air throughout the pontoon forward & aft passageway with a strong smell of soap present. 
 
It was determined that in the process of cleaning the tank a leak developed in the pump. The pump was stopped to investigate, leak was secured and the pump was charged to continue work. As the pump was stopped while in use, the discharge head pressure resulted in a back flushing of the diaphragm pump which flooded the exhaust breather on the pump. When the pump was charged again to resume work, the fluid that had accumulated in the exhaust breather was discharged into the air as an atomized mist filling the passageway with a cloud which in turn activated the Fire and Gas general alarm.
 
The pump was tested and found no more fluid in the exhaust breather and the pump was then operating as designed. The crew was released from muster and normal work resumed at approximately 0105.

Description of incident:

On 3.25.2018 at ~ 5:30 PM while lifting a rental crane base beam off the MV Courage a shock load occurred.  Upon rig up to the beam to be lifted, the load line stinger hook dropped below the bottom flange of the beam as the MV took a wave roll and shock loaded the crane.  A SWA was immediately issued, the crane was laid in its rack and tagged out of service.  Talos contacted third party crane contractor Gulf Crane and arranged for a fly out to inspect the following morning.    

Initial Action:
* All Stop and SWA issued.  No injuries, no damage observed at the time.
* Crane was laid in its rack and tagged out of service.
* All Platform construction that was crane supporting was shut down until an inspection could be performed.

Casual Factors:
* Crane stinger with associated hook was not properly secured away from beam flanges
* Wave rolling of the vessel caused the stinger and hook to fall below the lower beam flange 

Corrective Action:
* D ring between stinger hook and load connected slings must be secured by rigging personnel away from the lift so as not to fall below or entangle same.
* Crane Operator to communicate to riggers load is not secure to begin lift 
* This incident will be communicated to all Talos platforms.

Attached is supporting documentation including the crane mechanic's inspection findings

While making normal rounds on the platform, an employee noticed smoke coming from the production deck and out of the exhaust tip of the #2 platform gas generator. They then also noticed some flames coming out of the exhaust tip in addition to the smoke. The employee went to the MCC building and shut the fuel block valve in an attempt to shut down the generator.  However, the generator failed to completely shut down and began sputtering and/or dieseling. The ESD was then utilized to shut in the platform and a fire water hose was used to cool down the generator. When the generator continued to diesel, the fire hose was used to spray water into the exhaust.

At this time it appears that some sort of internal mechanical failure (possibly a failed piston) is the cause of this generator failure. A Maintenance Foreman is going out to the platform today (4/17/18) to join the field mechanic to investigate and confirm the actual cause of this incident.

The Maintenance Foreman arrived on location at 10:17 AM on 4/17/2018 to investigate this incident of the reported flame coming from the #2 gas generator exhaust pipe. They debriefed the incident with the production operators & PIC on location and completed a JSA to troubleshoot the root cause of the engine exhaust flame. Upon evaluation of the worksite, they found manual block valves for engine fuel gas supply closed & verified LOTO. They then removed sparkplugs from engine to perform a compression test on the engine and found the #1 right bank sparkplug broken and unable to be removed from the cylinder head. Sparkplugs removed from the right bank of the engine were wet and fouled with lube oil and the left bank sparkplugs were light grey showing normal combustion. They removed the #1 right bank valve cover to inspect upper valve train and performed compression test on the engine. During compression test they found one of the exhaust valves on the #1 right bank not returning to the closed position when engine was rotated. Removed #1 right bank rocker arm assembly and found seized exhaust valve. Then disassembled engine to remove #1 right bank cylinder head. After removing the head they found the broken head of the exhaust valve and a hole in the piston exposing the oil cooling jet on the top of the connecting rod. The piston cooling jet is a machined orifice in the top of the connecting rod. This sprays engine lube oil on the bottom of the piston crown for cooling. After careful inspection, it appears that the engine continued to run after initial valve/piston failure. The exposed piston cooling jet sprayed engine oil at normal engine oil pressure into the #1 right bank cylinder. As the engine continued to run, atomized oil from the #1 right bank cylinder also entered the right bank intake manifold every time the intake valves opened, allowing oil into all the right bank cylinders, confirming the oil fouled right bank sparkplugs. This event would also confirm the excessive amount of heavy smoke reported. The broken exhaust valve allowed lube oil to flood into the engine exhaust manifold and muffler. The left bank cylinders still firing with a normal air/fuel mixture provided sufficient heat to ignite the accumulated lube oil in the muffler and exhaust pipe. After ESD was initiated and fuel gas was shut off, the excessive atomized oil still in the right bank intake and excessive heat generated by combusting raw lube oil would have created a "dieseling" effect which would confirm the reported event of the engine not shutting down at ESD. When water was introduced into the exhaust pipe it cooled the heat down to interrupt the dieseling effect.

They continued with repairs replacing the #1 right bank piston, liner, connecting rod and cylinder head. After repairs are complete, a full safety system check of all components will be conducted to confirm everything performs as designed and per the SAFE Chart before returning to it to service.

Attached is a follow-up report prepared by Helix, who owns, operates and maintains this equipment.  

The overheating of an internal component (capacitor) of the inverter board inside the UPS cabinet located in the bridge caused the small flame which was extinguished by itself immediately when the power supply to the UPS was manually switched off. It was not necessary to use a fire extinguisher. The smoke was not enough to activate smoke detector therefore no fire alarm triggered. 

It is estimated the flame lasted for less than ~10 seconds.  The supply power was immediately secured to the unit and a platform ESD was initiated at 14:09.  ERT notified BSEE and received approval to come back online once confirming DP system returned to 100% operational.

Platform personnel did not muster. The fire was out before there was chance to even sound the alarm. All of the incident commanders and on scene leaders were on the bridge when it occurred. There was not even enough smoke to set off the fire alarm on the Bridge.

At ~10:30 AM 5/17/2018 while performing a BSEE approved conductor drive operation at EW 305, a shackle pin fell ~ 10' to the platform work deck.  A stop work authorisation was implemented. No personnel were within 25' of the drop zone and no injuries resulted. 

The pin's nut had backed off when the securing cotter pin was lost.  Only the pin and nut fell as the shackle remained intact with the sling as there was no load on the rigging at the time.  

This rigging equipment is supplied, monitored for use and maintained by the third party contractor doing the conductor driving.  

Talos has classified incident as near miss. 

Responses to BSEE Return Comments:
LOCATION OF/AND WHAT EQUIPMENT WAS BEING USED? 
EW 305A.  The equipment used was a pneumatic conductor drive head to hammer a well conductor in place for possible future new well use.  

WHAT ARE THE DETAILS ABOUT THE LOAD AND/OR MATERIALS BEING USED? 
Picture #1 show they drive head being loaded onto the conductor pipe (no incident at this time)  
Picture #2 is drive head fully set upon conductor pipe.  This is the time of the incident where the cotter pin, nut and shackle pin fell to the deck ~ 10' (no personnel with 25' of landing area).  The shackle itself did not fall and remained within the wire rope sling loop.  There was no load on the shackle or sling at the time of indent (not relaxed wire position).  

WAS ANY EQUIPMENT OR STRUCTURE DAMAGED? 
Only replaced the entire shackle assembly including shackle pin, nut and cotter pin. 

WHAT IS THE ESTIMATED COST TO REPLACE THE DAMAGED EQUIPMENT?
Less than $200.

Planned Corrective action provided by the contractor:

The preferred way to dress four-part shackles when using them on hammer jobs (due to the energy involved) is to replace the nut with a nylock jam nut, tighten with a crescent wrench, and then to apply several wraps of duct tape around the nylock jam nut/cotter pin after they have been properly installed onto the shackle.  Unfortunately, this information may not be consistently followed throughout Hammer Operations globally.  Planned corrective action:
1. Confirmation from hammer operations personnel and management that this is, in fact, the preferred way.
2. Identify any other/additional operational issues that this might present and ways to mitigate them.
3. Based on feedback from items 1 and 2 above, propose a Service Bulletin/Operations Bulletin to the respective bulletin proposal committees.
4. Based on feedback from item 3 above, draft a Service Bulletin/Operations Bulletin and send to the respective bulletin review committees.
5. Release the Service Bulletin/Operations Bulletin to global personnel and management to raise awareness and to promote the above procedure to all Hammer Operations globally.
6. Identify and update "sustainable" documentation to give this information a permanent "home."

Started a jet pump for the first time.  Within 2 minutes, a fire started started under the exhaust insulation wrap.  Nearby personnel grabbed a fire extinguisher and immediately put out the fire.  Appeared oil was coming out of the exhaust.  All stop was called.  Jet pump was taken out of service.  No injuries or evacuations.

The fire was burning less than 5 minutes.  No ESD was initiated.  Muster was not called.  No damage greater than $25,000.

Fire cause and corrective action detailed in attached report.

The summary below of fire cause and preventative measures taken from the attached report for reference:

Problem Reported:
EXHAUST BLANKET FIRE ON 6X6 JET PUMP

Problem Found:
UPON RECEIPT OF THE 6X6 JET PUMP G&M PERSONNEL COMPLETED A THOROUGH INSPECTION 
OF THE UNIT.  THE EXHAUST INSULATION BLANKETS AND EXHAUST COMPONENTS HAD VISIBLE SOOT AND OIL RESIDUE PRESENT.  THE BLANKETS WERE REMOVED AND THE UNDERLYING COMPONENTS WERE INSPECTED AND FOUND TO HAVE AN OILY FILM. COMPONENTS AND BLANKETS WERE CLEANED.  THE UNIT WAS TEST RUN AND IMMEDIATELY COVERED THE AREA IN BLACK SMOKE.  THIS WAS DETERMINED TO BE FROM RESIDUAL OIL IN THE MUFFLERS.  AFTER 15 MINUTES OF RUNNING UNDER A LOAD THE SMOKE CLEARED OUT AND THE PUMP PERFORMED AS DESIGNED.  THE FIRE WAS IN OUR DETERMINATION A RESULT OF EXCESSIVE OIL IN THE EXHAUST SYSTEM LEAKING DOWN THE OUTLET AND SATURATING THE EXHAUST BLANKETS AND COMPONENTS. THIS IS DUE TO LONG TERM IDLING OF THE ENGINE UNDER A NO LOAD CONDITION.

Solution or Preventative Measures to Prevent This Problem From Occurring Again:
ON OUR PREVENTATIVE MAINTENANCE SIDE WE HAVE DETERMINED THAT THE EXHAUST SYSTEM SHALL BE INSPECTED WITHOUT BLANKETS DURING THE NORMAL MAINTENANCE CYCLE (IE OIL CHANGE SERVICE @ 250 HOURS) OR BLANKETS SHALL BE REMOVED BEFORE THAT TIME IF OIL IS SEEN DURING POST JOB/PRE JOB OPERATING INSPECTIONS. ALL COMPONENTS WILL BE CLEANED AND A TEST OPERATION PERFORMED TO DETERMINE IF THERE IS AN UNDERLYING PROBLEM THAT NEEDS TO BE CORRECTED. TO PREVENT EXCESSIVE OIL IN THE EXHAUST SYSTEM DURING OFFSHORE OPERATIONS IT IS SUGGESTED THAT THE 6X6 JET PUMPS WITH  DETROIT DIESEL ENGINES SHOULD NOT BE RAN AT IDLE AND NO LOAD FOR MORE THAN 60 MINUTES AT A TIME.

Summary of Events:
On the morning of June 9, 2018 at 01:17:54 hours, Helix had an AVR cabling short circuit fault in Generator 5 onboard the Helix Producer #1, creating amps overload condition on electrical bus. After a series of events as seen in attachment #1, a "loss of DP Signal" was caused. Within 6 seconds (01:18:00 hours), the DPO on watch informed Talos production to initiate a controlled shut-in of the wells and prepare to disconnect. At 01:19:57 the red emergency DTS disconnect is activated. At 1:20:30 the buoy is released and clear of the vessel. At the time of disconnect, 0.528 gallons spilled from cavities of buoy.

Subsequent Actions:
Talos Operations attempts to contact BSEE after hours number at 01:35am. A notification email was sent to the after hours contact at 02:13am.    

On June 16, 2018 Helix is informed that the vessel is fit for service and does not pose a DP risk by USCG. On June 16, 2018 Talos receives approval from BSEE to reconnect the buoy, test/repair the RIV, and return to production after successful testing. 

On June 16, 2018 Talos lubricates the Gas Export RIV and successfully tested to confirm "bubble tight" integrity and began to come online with production. 

Investigative casual factors:
The identified Generator 5 is owned, operated, and maintained by Helix. An investigation by Helix personnel and Helix contracted investigators has identified a RC (root cause) with resulting corrective action request (attachment #1) for review.

Conclusions from the Helix Incident Investigation Report (complete copy also attached)
1.27  The failure of generator number 5 was initiated by cable insulation damage due to vibration, causing a short in the AVR module that shorted directly across 2 phases, thus causing a current imbalance in the port side of the buss. This imbalance caused the 1kV tie breaker and also generator 4 breaker to trip resulting in a blackout of that bus section. The tripping of the tie breaker prevented the faulted bus from taking out the healthy bus and only caused a voltage dip which initiated thruster ride through.

1.28  Generator 4 tripped due to its breaker protection sensing the same overload current as Generator 5. Further programming can be implemented in each generator breaker to initially send a "blocking" signal to all healthy generator breakers until the unhealthy generator can be first tripped offline.

1.29  Thrusters T3 and T7 (the drives on the Port buss) successfully rode through the voltage dip, but the DP system automatically deselected them after the 2 second timeout. This resulted in the DP system seeing zero thrusters available and kicking the DP system out of DP mode, into monitor mode. The data logger shows that both thruster 3 and 7 became available again after 2 seconds, however the DP system does not automatically reselect thrusters, so this would be left to the operator.

1.30 From the DP operators perspective, this would have looked like a complete black out, as all the thrusters were automatically deselected and the thrusters were all unavailable for a few seconds. The DP system should have shown T3 and T7 as running and available during the ride through, but it did not, because the timeout for thruster available was set at 2 seconds. This was not enough time for the drive to fully finish its AC Loss Ride through.

1.31 With a longer timeout (5 seconds or longer), thrusters T3 and T7 would have stayed selected into the system while the drives go through the AC loss ride through. The DP system would keep sending its speed demands to T3 and T7 to keep the vessel on station. The vessel could have had a slight loss of position, but it would have held position with those 2 thrusters. The DP System would not have changed to monitor mode. The operator and engineers would have not have had to take any actions to prevent a loss of position.

Recommended Actions:
1.32  All wiring in the AVR modules should be replaced with 1 kV high-T

Description of incident:
During a required flowline decommissioning procedure at PL 5B on 6.25.18 at 17:30 hours, a stop work was called when personnel near the open top flow back tank sensed a potential H2S gas release. 

Initial Action:
.  With the stop work order all pumping to/through flowlines was shutdown.  
.  All personnel safely mustered and moved to an upwind position onboard the support services liftboat.  Roll call accounted for all personnel.  
.  No injuries or sickness reported by the crew.
.  Onsite job construction supervisor found an initial tank at gas buster reading of 100 ppm.  These levels would be checked near hourly until 0330 on 6.26.18 a reading of 0 ppm existed.  
.  Job construction supervisor called out 5-man third party cleanup crew with all equipment to work with SCBAs at 1830 hours on 6.25.18.
.  On 6.26.18, that crew was onboard, secured the tank with H2S scavenger and blinded incoming flowlines and outgoing gas lift flowlines to/from the 5B platform.  Satellite platforms that were also part of job scope has flowlines blinded.  All personnel and equipment have been safely demobbed.

Talos Investigation Team Findings:
.  There is no history of H2S production from this field,
.  The production and gas lift flowlines as part of this job scope were previously flushed some 2+ year ago.  It appears bacteria remained within the lines and produced some element of H2S.  
  
Talos's corrective measures and actions to prevent recurrence:
.  Talos is preparing a remobilization to complete the scope of these required flowline abandonments.  To minimize associated H2S hazards, the design of this abandonment flush will be through the unmanned PL 5B production process equipment and not a flowback tank.  With this new flow path, Talos will request BSEE procedural approval before mobilization.  Personnel and equipment will be under an expected H2S environment and properly outfitted.

At 2:19 am on 11 July 2018, the LEL gas sensor in the shaker house was triggered meaning the air composition had reached 20% of LEL threshold, or 1% methane content by volume which subsequently activated the general alarm on the rig.  All personnel mustered to their designated areas as per emergency response procedures. While personnel were mustered the well was continued to be circulated to remove the high gas bottoms up with the mud logger gas sensor eventually reading 5,000 units and the shaker house exhaust fan gas sensor reading air composition reached 100% of the LEL threshold or 5% methane content by volume.  The bottoms up was expected to have high gas levels as the preceding operation involved bleeding down a supercharged formation of injected drilling fluid and cement spacer; commonly referred to as bleeding a ballooning formation.  Gas break out at surface and / or the presence of formation fluid on bottoms up was recognized as a potential risk and therefore the wellbore was isolated with the annular BOP element closed and circulation was occurring up the choke line through the mud gas separator prior to the mud reaching the shaker house.  The mud in the shaker house that set off the high LEL alarms had already passed through the mud gas separator and it was the residual entrained gas that gave rise to the high LEL readings.  Previous bottoms up circulations from this same interval have had similar gas responses.   All personnel were accounted for during the muster, no injuries to any personnel were reported, no pollution to the environment occurred, and no rig equipment was damaged.  While this is a BSEE reportable event, Chevron considers the occurrence to be within the basis of design of the vessel and an expected event at various times during the drilling and circulating process.

At 12:05 pm 7/18/2018, while eating lunch, platform crew noticed lights flicker and power go down. Upon investigation, crew noticed smoke and small flame at area near the exhaust pipe of the #2 diesel generator. Crew members retrieved nearby 30lb. dry chemical extinguisher and put out flame. There was no pollution or injuries associated with this event. The platform crew removed the insulation wrapping around both exhaust pipes and found both had corrosion holes at base of muffler.  The unit had shut-down on high engine temperature reading. Door, battery near radiator and insulation wrapping were damaged. Estimate of damages is still under investigation. 

On 8/1/2018, I (person1), person2, person3, and person4 met at the Linear Controls yard  to examine the # 2 diesel generator involved in the recent fire. The panel covers were pulled from the unit allowing access to the engine and exhaust/muffler portions of the unit. Upon examination, battery located next to the engine package showed damage to the battery, with the plastic covering of the battery melted and damage to area between terminals. The battery terminals, however, were not damaged which would infer that a short or arching at the terminals did not occur. A test meter was used to verify voltage and polarity of the battery, battery still contained voltage of 12.8 volts, which indicated that there was no damage to individual battery cells. It is the opinion of the investigators that the source of the ignition did not come from the battery. 

Further, the investigators believe that the insulation wrapping on the exhaust above the battery could have had some oil contamination which ignited and a portion of lit wrapping insulation dropped down onto the plastic covering of the battery. The radiator fan for the generator engine is a "pusher" which means it was taking air from the engine side and pushing it through the radiator to the muffler side.  Had the fire started on the exhaust piping by the forward mufflers, the air flow would have kept the fire outside the engine compartment. The engine shut-down on high cooling temperature and it is believed that the fan circulation pulled the flame upward toward the high jacket water temperature shut-down, which shut-down the unit. The damaged battery was removed from the unit, and a new battery was installed. The unit was started (it started immediately) and ran properly (alternator and fan belts, fan), no wiring was changed out prior to start up. 

It is believed that only the exhaust above the battery would furnish enough heat for a fire, absent any arching or shorts (which could not be found). Although this scenario of lit insulation dropping down onto the battery cannot be proven conclusively, the investigators feel that this a probable cause of ignition. Estimates to replace enclosure wiring and battery will be $500.00.

Description: Approximately 517 bbls of synthetic drilling fluid (SBM) was accidentally discharged into the Gulf of Mexico.

Cause:  The accidental release of SBM occurred when a butterfly valve failed during the transfer of the mud from the work boat to the platform.  After inspection it was concluded that the valve properly closed but that the rubber seal on the valve failed causing the valve to leak.  

Correction:  As soon as the release of mud was noticed the transfer pump was immediately shut-off.  This was an unanticipated occurrence which was dealt with quickly and appropriately.  To minimize recurrence of such events, a new butterfly valve will be installed along with a redundant gate valve on each transfer station.  The crew also plans to implement a testing procedure before each transfer that tests the integrity of the line and valves under 100 psi air pressure.  This procedure will be added to the standard operating procedures and the JSA.

.	Replace all current slight glasses with "Bull's Eye See Thru Flanged Sight Flow Indicator"

A shrimp boat trawling net snagged a gas lift pipeline; SN 15815 (6") and dragged it out of its ROW to the west. 
An investigation by the DSV person discovered that the 6" pipeline had been severed roughly in the vicinity of an 8" to 6" tie-in spool.  Additionally, divers discovered two areas where pipe was positioned above the seafloor.The divers surveyed the pipeline from the point it leaves the ROW back to the riser at WD 133 F and found no further damage or disturbance.  

Arena plans to mobilize a pipelay barge to location and complete the following steps:
1) Anchor barge in the area.
2) Locate both severed ends of the 6" and install end connectors w/ blind flanges to prevent any fluids from escaping. 
3) Locate pre-determined cut point on 6" and 8" pipelines.
4) Cut pipe at both locations and install appropriate sized pollution capture domes to prevent uncontrolled release of any residual hydrocarbons.
5) Starting with the 8", recover all damaged pipe to the barge and cut into sections
6) Repeat step #5 for 6" pipe.
7) Install approximately 500' of new pipe between newly installed connectors.
8) Install tie-in spools for new pipe.
9) Dewater using production equipment at WD 133 F.  

Arena is working with the BSEE Pipeline Group and will be submitting a Pipeline Repair Plan.

Description of incident:
On 9.12.18 at ~ 1330 hours, company and contract personnel were preparing to demob (swing off) the SS 224E satellite platform to a support field marine vessel due to oncoming weather.  Several personnel had safely swung when the IP started their transfer on the knotted swing rope.  The IP successfully completed the transfer, but the ring finger of their right hand slid onto the safety knot and they felt a sharp pain.
      
Initial Action:
* The incident and injury were immediately reported to the contract supervisor and Talos company personnel.
* The injury was initially reported as first aid pending medical evaluation.  The IP mobilized onshore where that evaluation determined a spiral fracture of the left ring finger.  The IP's finger was splinted and the IP put on restricted duty.

Investigative Findings:
* A swing rope transfer was properly filled out and signed by all involved personnel.
* All transferring personnel were initially brought upon the unmanned SS 224E satellite via crane and personnel basket that AM.  This platform crane was later put OOS that day for maintenance.
* The platform helideck was unavailable for use due to construction equipment and storage onboard.
* Weather deteriorated during the day and a safety decision was made to remove personnel via standby boat early afternoon.
* Investigating team reviewed individual statements, JSA and pictures taken of swing rope location. 

Causal Factors:
* IP mistimed their swin to the boat and hand slid down to swing rope knot where the impact led to the injury.
* With building weather and seas in the 4'-6' range, boat was non-stationary during transfer.   

Talos Corrective Measures and Actions to Prevent Recurrence:
* Talos HSE will distribute a Safety Alert detailing swing rope transfers in inclement weather as a last resort and when possible defer to "other" available transfers.
*JSA should evaluate "sea conditions" and how they might change during operations.
* Re-emphasize that all Talos employees and contractors are empowered to utilize SWA when applicable.
* Talos will investigate the rope for its current wear and tear condition.

Crane Operator had positioned a gas buster (back loading from platform) just above the deck of the motor vessel.  The vessel's deck hand pushed the gas buster towards the bulk head for final positioning.  In doing so, the unit's leg had inadvertently went under the bulk head's top railing. Simultaneously, the vessel dipped into the trough of a wave swell causing the gas buster leg to make contact with the railing.  This action resulted in the leg separating from the unit itself at its weld.  The unit was lifted back to the platform.  No injuries occurred during this incident.  Fieldwood has initiated an investigation and has taken the crane out of service to ensure there was no damaged to the crane boom that has not been visually seen by the crane operator.  A final report will be submitted as soon as possible as required.  Person - HSE Supervisor (Fieldwood Energy).

Final Report 09.27.18:  Fieldwood's investigation revealed that the at-risk condition of the gas buster protrusions (legs) inadvertently being positioned under the bulk head's top railing were not recognized by the attending deckhand or Crane Operator relative to equipment loading configuration.  The unit could have been turned in direction to avoid contact by the leg extension.     Fieldwood has inspected this crane for possible shock-loading damages (None identified - see Gulf Crane Inspection attachment).   The learnings of this incident have been discussed with site leadership and crane operators in effort to prevent a reoccurrence with any equipment that may have protrusions extending outward of the unit's main body.  Finally, information requested by BSEE:  the Gas Buster is owned by River Rental.  It is a high volume unit with three (3) stacks.  It's weight is 7500lbs; I D # RR T # 7531.  Included with this report are the following attachments as requested:  Photos of Gas Buster, photos of the leg damage,  a sketch of the vessel's position relative to the platform during the lift, and third party crane inspection.  Notable, at stated before, the unit was lifted back to the platform in which the leg was re-welded to the unit  - there is no damage cost associated with this incident.  Nor were there any injuries. 

October 10, 2018 response to BSEE request.  A provided attachment of the platform drill deck layout indicates there is only one crane on board the facility (west side). Key Finding:
The impact gloves the IP was wearing have a cut in the impact area, despite being rated "Cut 5." 

Root Cause:
The IP lost positive control of the piston and piston liner which caused the piston liner to fall. The investigation team did not find any indication that they lost their grip due to the equipment being being oily, slippery or too heavy to handle. Initial Report, submitted 10/29/2018
Incident Summary: IP was in the process of walking across gangway from the Lift Boat New Orleans back to the Lift Boat Myrtle, when they stepped on pallet used as step for gangway access when one of the pallet boards broke and the IP tripped. The IP fell, struck their head on handrail, and landed on the gangway walkway beneath him. The IP shortly lost consciousness and was woken up by a nearby employee. The IP was evaluated by the onsite medic and then send in for further concussion symptoms. 

Follow-up Report, submitted 11/13/2018
Initial Action:
* IP was immediately witnessed falling and striking their head by a fellow co-worker and taken to the medic onboard.
* Medic evaluated IP and they were sent in for further evaluation.
* IP was released to full duty with the diganosis of a minor concussion.

Investigative Findings:
* Reason walkway was installed - Corrective action from previous liftboat jacking with diver in the water near miss on 9/21/18 was to install gangway to allow personnel to transition easily back and forth to participate in all safety meetings, SIMOPS and JSA reviews.
* Due to different deck configurations of the two vessels, it was determined that the gangway between the two would need to be placed near the bow of the New Orleans.  This placement required the gangway to be elevated and placed over a boat bit.
* Past practice in place involved utilizing wooden pallets to provide the elevation required between vessels and act as a friction reducer to allow the lift boats to move independently of one another in high sea conditions.
* One pallet was placed on the L/B Myrtle and three were required on the L/B New Orleans. 

Root Cause:
Incorrect preparation and construction of gangway between vessels.

Causal Factors:
* No standard guidelines for safe pathway or gangway installation or use.
* Use of pallet material was not considered a hazard 
* Unavailability of suitable materials to construct a proper gangway ingress/egress.
* Obstruction under gangway caused gangway to be installed improperly, causing friction reducers to become a step-up or trip hazard.
Talos Corrective Actions:
* A solid wood frame structure was built and placed in lieu of the wooden pallets.
* All projects requiring the use of such walkways in the future will be evaluated for the best materials and course of actions to take prior to installation.  Including the length of walkways and their placement location on decks, including the buffer material required for said installation. 
* A Talos-wide communication was sent out about the incident and the corrective action taken to prevent recurrence.

On November 17, 2018, Renaissance notified BSEE orally of a welding flash fire incident that occurred at Lease OCS-G 01034, SS 266 "B" Platform.

As the welder was cutting grating loose from the top deck/cellar piping with a torch, the Fire Watch noticed that a flash fire had started at the field line gathering caisson located approximately 33' below and 8' to the side of the work area. 

The source of the ignition was the falling slag material from the torch.

The departing gas lift line is SN 406.

Renaissance is currently preparing a plan to remediate and place the line back-in-service.

At 22:50 hrs on 18 December 2018, the LEL gas sensor on Pit #5 in the active pit system was triggered as the air composition had reached 20% of LEL threshold (1% methane content by volume) which subsequently activated the general alarm on the rig. The maximum LEL reached 33% (1.5% methane content by volume).  The LEL level was greater than 20% for a total of 8 minutes.  All personnel mustered to their designated areas as per emergency response procedures within 12 minutes.  

The bottoms up from the liner cement job was expected to have high gas levels since ballooning occurred during the cement job.  Gas break out at surface and / or the presence of formation fluid on bottoms up was recognized as a potential risk and therefore the well was being circulated with the BOP closed up the choke and kill lines and through the Mud Gas Separator.  When contaminated mud (ballooned fluid) was at surface, this fluid was transferred from the common active pit system to empty Pit #5 to separate this contaminated fluid for proper disposal.  The contaminated fluid exiting the discharge line contacting the wall of the empty pit caused additional gas break-out that caused the LEL sensor to trigger.  Previous bottoms up circulations from this same interval on other Chevron Norphlet wells have had similar gas responses. All personnel were accounted for during the muster, no injuries to any personnel were reported, no pollution to the environment occurred, and no rig equipment was damaged. While this is a BSEE reportable event, Chevron considers the occurrence to be within the basis of design of the vessel and an expected event at various times during the drilling and well construction process.

Description of Incident
During the process of back-loading two contract personnel via a personnel basket to the M/V , the crane operator boomed up to close to the platform in order not to lower personnel directly over the M/V and struck a navaid light with the personnel basket resulting in minor damage to the navaid lens.

Investigative Findings:

The riggers picked up the un-damaged tote lid from the deck and re-installed the lid onto the tote tank and re-tightened the lid retaining band.  Routine lift then proceeded successfully to move tote tank from vessel deck to platform top drill deck.

Immediate Corrective Actions:

A release of gas originated from a pin hole in the surface flow line.  The well was remotely shut in from the SCADA unit located onshore.  This is an unmanned platform.  Note that no sheen(s) were reported from this event.  As this is a gas well, no hydrocarbon contamination nor oil residue was observed on the platform.  Additional Information:
The cause of the leak is thought to be corrosion in the weld area of the reducer downstream of the second choke. The well flows at approximately 200 F temperature and contains 1.27 mole % CO2. The well also produces approximately 45 BWPD. This water is very low in chlorides, 400 ppm, and has a ph of 5 which is acidic. Coupled with a low total dissolved solids in the water there is little to no buffering effect to help combat the effects of the low ph and CO2.  The operators reported that the corrosion inhibitor was not being pumped on a continuing basis due to causing problems with our water treating equipment. The operators also reported taking at least the majority of the pressure drop between the tree and the production equipment  through the second choke. This caused a much higher velocity and more turbulence downstream of the second choke and into the reducer. Coupled with the high temperature and the presence of CO2 this caused a corrosive and erosive environment in this area which resulted in the leak. 
To prevent future leaks from developing, Walter is fabricating new flowlines that will include a blast joint downstream of the second choke that has a 2-9/16" inlet and a 4-1/16" outlet and will also take the majority of the pressure cut from the first choke in the flowline to help prevent any erosional problems . The spool piece downstream of this blast joint will contain a 4" X 6" reducer and will be fabricated with a corrosion resistant alloy. In addition, Walter is working with our chemical company to start injection of a different corrosion inhibitor that does not cause issues with our water treating abilities. These measures should prevent future leaks from happening.

Four construction workers were moving a piece of grating (approximately 3' wide x 13' long - 240 pounds) into position by hand to facilitate replacement when one of the worker's suffered an injury. 
Investigation Findings
A JSA was in place for the activity being conducted.  "Gathering and moving material to work area" was listed as a step in the job task.  However, the limited pathway and piping obstruction in their path (hazard) was not mentioned and therefore the corresponding mitigations for maneuvering in the area were not documented.  In addition, we determined that there were other properly barricaded areas where grating had been removed that further limited their travel path to event location.  Reconsideration of grating replacement sequencing in that area could have improved accessibility and path for accessing work areas.  Simply said, we could have started at event location and worked backwards to lay down area thus improving accessibility. 

Human Factors
. Manual material handling is frequently utilized in field maintenance activities.  
. Having four individuals involved in the task minimized the consideration of the per man weight imposed by the grating - weight of grating exceeded recommended lift limit specified by contractor (50 pounds for men).   
 
Root Cause
. Inability to identify hazards in congested work area - worker placed his hand between grating and bolt on flange (pinch point) 
 
Contributing Cause(s)
. Congested work area with no access from platform crane.   
. Previously removed grating, which was properly barricaded, further limited travel paths. 
. Supervisor was on location but occupied by other job task when the event occurred. 

Corrective Action Plan
The following key actions are recommended as a result of this investigation:
1. A safety stand down was conducted on the facility following the event.
2. A conference call was conducted by Company Maintenance Supervision with other field maintenance crews to discuss event details.
3. A safety alert will be distributed by contractor addressing event details.
4. Contractor to evaluate the need for enhanced Hazard Hunt and JSA training.
5. Contractor will notify all supervisors and mandate a document safety meeting covering their manual lifting policy.   
6. The event will be reviewed and shared in Company's 2020 1st Quarter Safety Meeting.

Operators heard a compressor go down, an operator investigating the incident saw a two-foot flame coming off the coupling area that joins the engine and gas compressor.  A 30# Purple K fire extinguisher was used to extinguish the flame. There were no flames inside the guard. No one was injured.

The compressor was pressured up and nothing was found leaking on the compressor frame. The check valve in the discharge line for the starter was leaking. When the compressor shut down it blew down and the gas backed up through the check valve and escaped through the nose cone of the starter. The gas blowing backwards through the starter spun the bindex of the starter enough to contact the flywheel and that is where the spark happened to ignite the gas. 

The 2" check valve and the starter were changed out. The starter was sent to T&B to be disassembled to see which seal was leaking.

A safety blitz will be sent to all mechanics to check all check valves on all gas compressors throughout the GOM on their next maintenance to verify there are functioning properly.

Corrective Action Plan The following key actions are recommended 1. The damaged gasket has been replaced. 2. The separator is back online and has been pressure tested with no further leaks.  Investigation Findings

The test separator was recently switched from its historical LP mode to HP mode. The new exposure to high pressure caused a ring gasket on the 8" outlet to develop a leak.

The crane operator was putting the crane boom in the boom rest when a loud noise was heard by the operator. Upon investigation, the main line end cap was found laying in the boom access walkway. No personnel were injured and no facility damage incurred. The crane was removed from service and the OEM called out for further assessment and installation of a new cap. Q: Provide additional information in the remarks section to the cause of the incident and the issues with the crane.
A: Investigation with equipment owner determined the shaft flat end cap design allowed contact between the end cap and gear box. This contact caused contact stress over time which could cause the retaining bolts to loosen or weaken to the point of failure, resulting in the cap to fall. 

The new style end caps allow for an expansion gap to prevent the transfer of stress between the gearbox and end cap.
