column24: A member of the catering/steward staff discovered smoke coming from a dryer in the laundry room on the main deck. The individual immediately went upstairs to notify his supervisor (Chief Steward). The Chief Steward and the steward went back to the laundry room to discover small flames in the dryer drum. The Chief Steward called the Captain immediately and notified him of the fire. The Captain sounded the alarm at 0857 while using the PA to dispatch the fire team and to notify personnel to muster. All personnel not involved with the emergency team mustered and were accounted for.

The cook smelled an unusual smell and saw a small flame coming from a crack in the Steam Table. The cook doused it with water and notified the Campboss. The Campboss noticed a small amount of black smoke coming out of a crack of the steam table on his arrival and immediately unplugged it. The cabinet doors were opened where no flame was seen. The Chief Mate was notified via the bridge and he assessed the situation. The electricians arrived and removed the electrical panel access cover and found the terminal block has smoldered. No system alarms were activated and no other fire fighting measures were used.

Operators observed a minor leak on the V-5 bonnet where the ring gasket connects to the SSV. The operator attempted to tighten the flange; however, the leak did not stop so the operation shut in the well. On 01.03.2021, the gasket was replaced and the well was brought back online.

During weekly run of Emergency Generator, the PLC was reset which resulted in the emergency buss losing power, effecting the emergency powered lights, air handlers, and the Firewater Pump B. Main power was uninterrupted and there was no impact on the production monitoring or safety systems or main firewater supply. Firewater pump B was restored when Emergency Generator was back online.

Personnel were in the process of raising the FRC back to the stowage position after retrieving marine debris from the water. The FRC was approximately 10 inches from the stowage stops when all personnel exited the FRC and began to use the hand crank to raise the FRC the remaining distance. During this process, the cable broke and the FRC fell to the water. No personnel were injured. There are no boats in the area at this time to capture the FRC. Stowage height is 135 feet and the FRC weighs approximately 3900 pounds.

Crew was working on the boat landing hanging scaffolding to access the 12" horizontal from the outboard side. IP, our scaffold builder, slipped and fell 3' into the water. IP was attached to their SRL which did catch the IP; but, not until the IP was already entering the water. IP was able to hold on to the outboard leg of the scaffold; but, unable to lift theirself out of the water. the IP's designated helper attempted to assist in self rescue. Our rope rescue system and personnel were in place and standing by as indicated in our rescue plan. Rescue personnel used the rescue pulley system to hoist IP to the boat landing where they were able to stand and walk without assistance. IP was in the water less than three minutes and sustained no reported injuries as a result of falling into the water. A Safety Stand Down took place, discussion held and the employee walked from the boat landing to the lift boat unassisted and under his own power where he showered and changed into dry clothes. Work has resumed after Safety Stand Down was completed and JSA's were reviewed.

IP was a signalman and one of the riggers for crane operations. They were moving drill pipe on the deck to make room to offload the M/V. IP instructed crane operator to raise boom and lower load. As IP was watching the load, he lost awareness of his hand placement and was caught in a pinch/crush point resulting in a crush laceration to the left ring finger.
Immediate Corrective Actions:
Safely landed load and reported to onboard safety/medic and night abandonment PIC.
Investigation Results:
Both riggers had their hands on the load. Load was overhead and hand placement not in direct site of riggers. IP was signalman. Other rigger was in a potential pinch point. Neither rigger or crane operator stopped the job to reposition and utilize tag lines or push sticks (available on site).
Prevention Corrective Actions:
“Safety Stand-Down” was held to discuss incident with both day and night crews on platform. Emphasize the responsibility to utilize Stop Work Authority by all on facility. Discussed hand placement and the availability of other tools (tag lines and push sticks). Hands free movement of loads is to be part of JSA. Verification of hands free tool presence/use to be made prior to lift. Discussion was shared with crews on other facilities.

A muster event occurred on the platform: smoke station 24 on the lower level in main LQ was triggered which activated the general alarm. Non-essential personnel mustered at their primary lifeboats (5 mins). The incident command team to the ICC to assess the situation. The On Scene Response Team (OSR) was dispatched to investigate but found no smoke or fire on the lower level of the LQ. They proceeded to investigate the second level and laundry, but no smoke or fire was found. Background information:  It is believed that a brief power outage caused the exhaust vent over the stove to shut off and it was never restarted after the outage. During the time that the exhaust fan was not on, galley personnel were cleaning the stove. The steam from the cleaning may have activated the alarm.

During routine leak-off testing for DC221 commissioning on 12/19/2020, a hydraulic leak from the XT compensation system vent on DC122 was identified. After troubleshooting concluded on 12/20/2020, the leak was deemed non-isolatable and continued even when well was shut-in. Therefore the leak was most likely associated with an internal failure to the Subsea Control Module (SCM) of DC122. The SCM change out was completed on 01/06/2021. After completion of the activity, it was confirmed that the hydraulic leak was terminated. Based on data trends, the total estimated volume of glycol released is 797-gals or about 19-bbls.

Rig crew was breaking down chicksan lines from TIW valve. When chicksan line was disconnected the TIW was picked up via the air hoist with the IP guiding the TIW valve using a sub-strap with his right hand, lost his footing and sustained an injury, IP reported to his immediate supervisor. IP was seen by the medic and returned to work. IP was still experiencing pain from the injury and was sent onshore for further evaluation. After injury repair, IP was released to light duty. Beginning 11-Feb-21 the IP will return to work as scheduled, working on a special project and course development for hazard identification training.

Was notified USCG reported a ship contacting our un-manned and OOS platform. Between 0700 and 0800, USCG notified BSEE, who then sent us a copy of the NRC report (#1295614) filed by the striking vessel, stating no pollution was noted from the vessel  nor around our platform. Personnel via helicopter assessed the initial damage to the platform and took additional pictures. It was confirmed that the fog horn remains operable. Only one of the four Nav-Aid Lights was accessible (without getting into harm's way) and that one was confirmed operable. With all four Nav-Aids being connected, it is our belief that the other three are operable as well. Last Quarterly inspection of Nav-Aids was October 22, 2020 and all four were operable. At present, we are still assessing the damages and have estimated a minimum of 1.5MM in damage/repairs.

While troubleshooting a gas detector oon the production facility, IP was changing the combustible sensor head on the gas detector. IP was standing with his left foot in the generator housing and his right foot was situated on piping between the generator enclosure and other piping. IP's right foot slipped, causing him to fall, resulting in an injury.

The control room operators were alerted to gas reading on Booster Gas Compressor #1. This compressor was in the process of being started when the event occurred. Technicians in the area were notified of the gas reading witnessed by the control room.  They quickly identify the gas leak coming from an 8" Daniels Orifice Meter located on the discharge of the compressor. A unit and process shutdown was initiated by gas detectors in the area and an onsite technicians pulled an ESD while evacuating the area. Upon inspection it was determined that 2 failures occurred on the meter. The gasket on the seal bar had been changed, but small pieces of the old gasket material had not been removed prior to installing the new gasket. The gate in the valve was passing allowing gas to migrate to the seal bar on the valve. An all stop was called and a plan is being developed prior to continuing moving forward with placing this unit into service.

A short spreader bar was pre-slung by vendor using a choked flat web nylon sling and loaded on the motor vessel. Spreader bar was safely transferred from the boat to the platform using the whip line with no issues. When the bar was unslung after setting on deck, the sling was found to have damaged stitching and no label or inspection tag. All negative conditions were unidentifiable as slung. The sling was removed from service and reported to office. The rigging was not checked by the transport company dock crew or boat crew to ensure it was correct prior to each transport stage. All assumed it was good since the vendor installed it. A task to check rigging prior to connecting to the crane hook is to be added to boat transfer JSA's both at the platform and the dock.  Verification that the rigging is inspected and correct will be verbally stated to the crane operator prior to the lift.

IP had sustained an injury. IP had on impact gloves and all other PPE required for the task. IP recieved aid. IP continued to work with no issues. Five days after incident, IP's employer requested that he is sent onshore for further evaluation. IP was cleared to Full Duty with No Restrictions.

This morning, operators discovered a pinhole leak in the gas compressor suction piping. We are requesting permission from BSEE to install a 6 inch, 2000 psi Plidco clamp on the 6" 150 Series piping in reference in order to bring the facility back online. As a result of this incident there was no loss of containment and no pollution was observed. We are requesting a 14-day waiver to make the needed repairs. We will advise your office once repairs are complete.

column24: While displacing the wellbore from 14.8 ZnBr to 14.8 packer fluid, it appears that the downhole ECDs sheared the upper and lower FLCDs. The rig immediately began to experience fluid losses of 600 bph. A 50 bbl fluid loss pill was spotted and losses slowed to 345 bph. A second fluid loss pill  was pumped which significantly decreased the losses eventually resulting in zero losses. After losses stopped, the rig experienced approximately a 14 bbl gain on the trip tank. The well was shut in on the annular and circulated out using the driller's method. Oil was observed in the returns. While waiting on additional fluids and materials, wellhead pressure was managed by bullheading 14.8 brine when required. The well was killed via bullheading down the annulus followed by bullheading down the workstring with 3 CaCo3 pills. NOTE: Changed Occurred Date from 1-13-21 to 1-9-21 for 2010 (rwl 1-9-22)

Personnel noticed smoke from the cigarette butt can in the designated smoking area on the facility (SE corner of Main Deck). When the top of the container was removed, flames were noticed in the container and were quickly extinguished with water. All cigarette butt containers on facility were emptied. Initial notification to BSEE made via phone and followed by email at 11:13am day of the incident.

During heavy rain the evening , a plug for a deck light on the Vessel blender arced, causing damage to the male and female end of the connection. The light was installed with the female end of the plug angled up at about a 45 degree angle and the male end plugged downward into it. No injuries, no flame only an arc. 
Immediate Action Taken: Isolated power to the light and removed from service.

Rig Manager and two co-workers were in the process of moving a 4" x 5' piece of temporary pipework using handsfree straps. The temporary pipework slid into place and contacted the IP, causing injury. The job was stopped, and rig leadership was notified of the event. The IP was evaluated by the rig Safety Medic, given aid, and released back to work. IP was sent onshore due to foot being sore and tender.  IP was evaluated by a Physician and there was bruising on the foot with no broken bones. IP is on Restricted Duty and working onshore.

While attempting to position a riser insert into riser hold via air hoist, a rigger grabbed the air hoist cable in attempt to prevent the insert from contacting the scaffolding. There were two workers using hands-free equipment positioned on the fifth level and the  IP was above on the sixth level.  The IP was wearing welder's gloves and placed their hand on the air hoist cable, as the air hoist operator raised the load, the IP's hand subsequently squeezed between the cable and the sheave.  
Immediate Corrective Actions - The IP  hand signaled an all-stop.  The insert was lowered to the deck and IP reported to medic.  IP recieved aid.  IP was sent onshore for further evaluation. IP is expected to need approximately 8 weeks of recovery time.

A muster event occurred this morning. The abandon alarm on the NE subcellar was triggered. All non-essential personnel mustered at their primary life boats. Incident command team mustered in the ICC to asses the situation. A response team was dispatched to the NE sub-cellar to determine the cause of the alarm. It was determined that painters doing fabric maintenance (needle gunning) on the alarm panel accidentally triggered the alarm. All personnel were then instructed to stand down at due to false alarm.

The fire alarm was activated in response to TSH-9613B tripping in the "C" Living Quarters. On-scene personnel found that a pipe ruptured, spilling water and steam into the room. All personnel were mustered and energy sources to the building were secured. All clear was sounded at 1550.  Cleanup and repairs began. 
Update: per BSEE request: On the Incident Report also, check the Other Box not Listed...and in the rectangle box put- ruptured hot water pipe.
Note: No actual fire/flame. This was a thermal detector that activated, as designed.

While making rounds on the facility an operator noticed a plug leaking gas to atmosphere on the wellhead. BSEE has been made aware of the situation and a meeting is planned to discuss further action.
UPDATE:
This issue is still being investigated and information is still being gathered. Once the investigation is complete the requested information and additional information will be shared with BSEE.
RESPONSE TO REQUESTED INFORMATION:
*What are the plans for plugging the D-36 well since the wireline crew was unable to set the plug? 
-Rig up flowback equipment, cut paraffin to gain access to tubing, set tubing plug to remediate SCP, replace alignment pin on casing pool (X and Y have been fully approved, the crew has mobilized on location and is presently rigging up flowback and wireline equipment). 
*Confirm that the well is an H2S well. 
-This is not an H2S well.
*Why wasn't this incident reported to X within 15 days? (See below)
.Management was notified the afternoon of Aug. 24th
.Internal meeting was held on Aug. 25th
. Notification was made to X at 15:30 on Aug. 25th
. Incident was put into the BSEE eWell system the afternoon of Aug. 25th
. Meeting was held between us and X at 14:30 on Aug. 26th to discuss the path forward. 
REQUEST #6 ADDITIONAL RESPONSE: 
We are presently looking into what occurred with this well. As stated in the previous correspondence, we presently have flowback equipment on it to attempt to secure the well and address the issue. We will report any finding(s) back to X once this process is complete and we have gathered the information.

While troubleshooting gas compression, pressure built up in the closed drain system. This pressure back fed through the sales gas compressor crank case atmospheric vent. The resulting release from the 0.5 inch vent lasted approximately 1 minute and triggered a deck gas detector. This resulted in a PSD of the facility and full facility muster and response. An estimated 5.1lb (0.103 mcf) of natural gas was released during the minute long event.
BSEE RFI: What was being troubleshooted on Gas Compression? The inability to move liquid through the dump valve from the discharge scrubber.

Minor gas detection around the suction of the X alarmed the control room. A fast-stop and blowdown on the X was initiated. After a few minutes, four gas detectors picked up gas readings, so the control room informed the deck operators to stand down and go to their primary muster stations. 
Immediate Corrective Actions - An ESD was immediately pulled and a full platform muster was initiated. A full muster was completed and the gas eventually dissipated from around the X. After a walkdown from emergency response, it was found that the source of the leak was from the packing of FCV-1053B (recycle valve). Once the pressure was bled down and the release isolated, personnel were ordered to stand down from the muster.

While reaching up and extending their right arm to install a cursor pin into Cursor frame on ROV, located overhead, the IP felt an injury.
*What was the scope of work? 
-ROV maintenance
*Was the IP evacuated and if so, when? 
-IP was sent onshore for further evaluation two days after the date of occurrence.

Personnel was in the process of checking rotation on a pump that is in use at this time to ensure the rotation meter properly worked before testing a new generator. The personnel powered-down the electrical bucket to connect a 3 phase rotation meter and when the personnel powered the electrical bucket back up with the pump motor off and the meter instantly popped and smoked throughout the electrical bucket and meter. Stop work was immediately initiated and the personnel reported the incident to the Production Foreman. Company provided the final investigation report 15 days after the date of occurrence.

While lowering a sub from the flowhead pup joint to the deck, an IP sustained an injury. The rig medic provided first-aid treatment and consulted shore-based physician. IP was sent onshore for further evaluation. IP is on days off and will return to duty next rotation.

While backloading an air compressor onto the M/V, it took a swell from the sea, causing it to contact the air compressor. The impact caused the air compressor to start swinging as it was coming down. During this time, the deck hand was signaling the crane operator to lower he lift to the deck. The air compressor hit the handrail on the boat and came to rest on the steps leading up to the jump deck. The platform operator advised the crane operator via radio to pick the load back up and allow it to settle out. Once load and seas settled, the air compressor was lowered on to the boat without further incident. 
Return Comments:
No damage to the air compressor. Minor damage to the vessel. <$200 to repair handrail.

While picking up 9 7/8" tieback one of four body guide inserts fell to rig floor while lowering the elevators. It was also identified that one of the leveling bars sheared and fell to rig floor as well. 
Red zone barriers on rig floor were controlled at time of incident. No personnel were injured during incident. 
*How much did the insert and leveling bar weigh?
- Insert: 104lb
-Leveling Bar: 8lb
*What was the distance the insert and leveling bar fell?
- 90ft
*The closest personnel to where the both objects fell?
-The closest person was 15ft away outside of the red zone.
IP stepped on a piece angle iron, causing an injury. IP will be sent onshore for further evaluation. IP was released to full duty.

While backloading sections of the Crane #3 boom, the top section of the boom was being picked up from the Ram Powell Top Deck (RPT Deck) when it swung forward and struck one of the outer edge handrails, bending it outward. Workers in the area attempted to bend the handrail back in place when it broke free from the welds on the deck. The handrail was placed off to the side and a temporary handrail barricade was erected until permanent repairs could be completed. After reviewing the report and corrective actions, if further clarification is necessary, we can schedule a call with the BSEE district office at the district's convenience.

During the offloading and back loading of the weekly supply boat a grocery box made contact with the aluminum ladder cage and ladder pole on Life Boat A's davit. During the lifting operations, the grocery box contacted the ladder and the aluminum ladder cage on the davit of Life Boat A. The grocery box was then lifted up, repositioned and set down on the deck with no other issues. The mechanical integrity of the ladder and aluminum cage were inspected and no issues noted besides for being bent. There were no injuries as a result of this event. The ladder and aluminum cage are still functional and may be used to access the upper portion of the davit if need be. Further details will be reviewed during an internal investigation.

A worker entered LB 4 to inspect VHF radios. As required, the worker attached the maintenance pennant while performing his inspections. When work was completed, the worker attempted to remove the maintenance pennant and return the LB to service when he dropped the nut for the 4-part shackle overboard.
Action Taken - Remaining maintenance pennant hardware secured to prevent further dropped objects. New shackle ordered.

Work scope for rig crew included lifting items out of the work basket in which they were transported to location. A roustabout rigged a small portable pressure washer and signaled to the crane operator to initiate lift. At the onset of the lift, the lifting eye/bracket on the pressure washer failed, resulting in an immediate stop of lifting operations. It was determined that the roustabout was unaware, and did not observe, that the pressure washer had been strapped down to the interior of the work basket to prevent movement during shipment. As a result of lifting under these circumstances, the lifting eye of the pressure washer unit failed at the onset of the lift. There was no damage to the work basket, rigging or crane; only the soft-metal lifting eye/bracket on the portable pressure washer (aluminum angle-iron bracket). 
Update for BSEE questions: 
- Which crane was used for this operation? The West rig crane was in use during this event.
- Estimated cost to repair the equipment? Estimated by equipment owner at $350.00 to repair the aluminum lifting bracket.

While in the process of removing the pump deck hatch-covers the hatch cover contacts a Floor Hand. As the crew began to hoist up the east side hatch-cover, an adjacent hatch-cover flipped over towards the IP and landed such that the IP sustained an injury. The crew removed the west side hatch-covers successfully without incident.   
Immediately Corrective Actions - The crew stopped the job, contacted rig leadership and the Safety Medic evaluated the IP. The IP was sent onshore for further evaluation where the specific injury was confirmed. A safety stand-down was held with all crews.

An IP felt an injury while performing their normal duties (riser running operations). The IP notified the Toolpusher who advised the IP to visit the onsite Medic.  After evaluation by the Medic, a decision was made to send the IP onshore for further evaluation. The IP was diagnosed with the specific injury. 
Additional Information Requested:
*How many hours did the IP work before the incident occurred? -10 hrs
*submit the sequence of events:
   -Pre-Job plan to discuss the plan laying out MPD riser joint.
   -Crew proceeded to backout riser bolts using the hydraulic wrench. 
   -Whilste Picking up on the wrench the IP felt the injury. 
   -After the operation the IP informed the Toolpusher of his injury.
   -The Toolpusher sent the IP to see the medic. 
*Submit the corrective actions taken to prevent this type of incident from occurring again: -Not Applicable, IP had a previous injury. No event triggered the injury, just normal work motion assisting with the Riser Wrench.

While installing the umbilical control line, IP was progressing end of the umbilical control line through the last few rollers on the sheave. As the umbilical exited the sheave, the weight of the connection caused the hinged sheave to contact the IP. This case has been closed, IP had no injury and received a full duty work release.

While lifting the Supreme accumulator package a leg on the four part sling became hooked on the package structure causing it to tilt to its side. The operator immediately stopped lifting and laid the load on the deck (the package's side) which allowed hydraulic oil to leak from the vent of the package's oil tank. Estimated volume of less than one gallon. Oil pads were put down by supply vessel personnel to absorb the oil. 
Initial Actions Taken: Riggers cleared the obstructed sling leg from the package frame and the package was put back upright.
Follow up:  There were no damages associated with this incident.

While unloading construction equipment from the M/V the crane operator was in the process of lifting the construction tool house when the boat pulled out from under the load causing the load to swing and the cable to strike the side of the platform (BSEE onboard witnessed the incident). The PIC gathered witness statements and information for the incident report. We have the crane mechanic in route to inspect the cable for damage. It don't appear to be damaged but want to make sure. 
*(1/21) -Crane Mechanic is performing inspection on wire rope for any damages. There were No Injuries, No Damage to Equipment, No Pollution. Crane mechanic completed inspection of crane cable, No damage to crane was noted on his report.

Personnel were in the process of removing drip pan, located directly below the galley griddle, when liquid from the drip pan splashed on the lower controls of the unit. This shorted out the controls and tripped the galley breaker. No personnel were injured during this incident, no flames were observed but slight charring was noted on the electrical wiring behind the panel.

While replacing a corroded cooling media spool on a heat exchanger/cooler with the crane, we installed two bolts into the connecting flange then had the crane operator pick up on the pipe a little bit to align the flange and install the gasket and remaining bolts. I gave the signal via radio to come up on the pipe, which was rigged up with a nylon strap to the fast line and the crane line had started to come up too much and had jerked up slightly. I called the all stop and had the operator come back down on the load. The result was two bent bolts and a slightly bent flange lip on the interconnecting pipe. We had a toolbox talk about the possible jerkiness of the crane, and using rigging instead of the crane when fine tuning piping for flange alignment. We proceeded to also change out the second pipe spool that had the bent flange, with a spare pipe spool we had on location.

We had our emergency alarm sound today at 9:30 am. All personnel mustered. Currently have compressor #2 annual inspection going on. The isolation description in the SOP states to turn off the DC breaker to the Lube Oil Pump, but the main DC breaker to the panel was turned off due to improper labeling. Once the backup battery supply to the panel lost voltage, the fire & gas devices associated with the package lost communication with the control system causing the PAGA Emergency Alarm to activate as designed. Note: The fire & gas detection did not activate based on the presence of a hazardous source.

An unlabeled non-manifested package was discovered inside the area designated for helicopter cargo storage. After discussion with X, Logistic clerk from the drilling and operations side the PIC was contacted. The PIC made the decision to muster the location. Muster alarm was activated, Shell hotline was contacted, full muster was realized by 0803. Owner of package came forward and the package was identified as oilfield instrumentation monitoring equipment.

Crane operator was placing east crane boom into the boom rest at end of day. There was no load rigged up on to crane. The crane operator was putting the boom in the rest, and they did not notice the crane boom was not lined up correctly. Crane operator kept lowering the boom until it contacted the boom guide. After the contact, the Crane operator picked the boom back up and placed it in the boom rest correctly. Due to weather & lighting conditions, Crane operator did not realize any damage had been done. After visual inspection this morning, GIS supervisor noticed one of the boom lacings were damaged. Fortunately, a technician was on Site. The technician was able to inspect the boom and deemed it safe to continue to use. The estimated cost to replace the damaged equipment: Approximately less than $5000 with labor costs.

column9: Kosmos Energy Gulf of Mexico Operations, LLC
column24:
An employee or contractor to AllRig (a direct contractor to Seadrill), died while performing work on the Seadrill West Neptune drilling unit, which at the time was under contract to Kosmos Energy Gulf of Mexico Operations, LLC ("Kosmos") for operations on Kosmos'  Kodiak 3 well. Investigations are ongoing, both by the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement as well as an investigation by Seadrill in which Kosmos is participating. We understand AllRig may be conducting its own investigation.  
Subject in all respects to the final investigative report to be issued by Seadrill and Kosmos, below is information that Kosmos has received from Seadrill and which was extracted from an HSE alert sent by Seadrill to its fleet. The wording may vary somewhat from that alert.

On January 24th, 2021 at approximately 13:30 Central Time, two AllRig personnel were performing loose lifting gear inspections on and around the riser deck area of the Seadrill West Neptune. The task was to visually inspect slings. During the inspection, the inspection team leader observed two steel slings wrapped around a bundle of 5 metal plates which were stacked vertically, resting on dunnage, and secured to a stanchion by a single 2" ratchet strap. The slings had been left in place on the plates after they were landed by the crane for efficiency and ease of relocation when needed. The plates all measured 4 x 8 feet; three (3) were 3/8" thick and two (2) were 1" thick weighing a combined 1.8T (3,600lbs).
The inspection team leader was successful in sliding one of the slings from the plates on the inboard side of the plates, but he discovered the second sling was pinched between the rear of the plates and the stanchion, preventing it from being taken off on the outboard side. He then called his assistant to help free the sling and remove it for inspection. The lead inspector instructed the assistant to 'loosen' the ratchet strap. It is assumed that the inspection team leader thought that loosening the rachet strap would provide the opportunity to move the trapped sling. Prior to instructing the assistant to loosen the ratchet strap, the inspection team leader leaned his back against the plates. The reason for this is unknown, but it is assumed the intention was to support the plates in their standing position when the ratchet strap was loosened. Directly in front of the lead inspector was the framework of the drilling bail rack. When the ratchet strap was manipulated by the assistant, the ratchet strap hook released from the stanchion allowing the plates to free fall forward (away from the stanchion) under their own weight, fatally trapping the inspection team leader between the plates and the framework of the drilling bail rack.
An IP sustained an injury while pulling a tag line on a suspended cargo basket.

The #2 crane's whip line contacted the #4 crane's hydraulic gripper head line on the side of the crane boom. The #4 crane was in the parked position. When the whip line came in contact with the quick connect, it broke and released 0.57 gallons of Tellus -46  Hydraulic oil to the deck (none in the water). The quick connect end that broke fell 43 feet to the deck and weighed 1.2 lbs. The flagman ( Deck Foreman ) was the only person in the area and was 15 feet away.
Update to address returned comments: -The quick-connect fitting that broke off was not replaced as it was for the gripper head. The gripper will never be used on the #4 crane. Due to the pipeline pump not speeding up since 01.24.2021, the operator began to troubleshoot pipeline pump #1 and found that the wire had cracked and brunt the terminal connector on the power box. 
02.23.2021:  Investigative findings:
- The power leads for the junction block terminate inside of protective housing.  
- The power leads are secured by tightening machine screws set into the terminal block.
- Over time, the machine screws appear to have loosened causing an incomplete (loose) connection inside the terminal block. The loose connection resulted in line resistance. 
- As the current was passed through the connection, an arc was generated.
Root Cause:
- Upon investigation, it was determined that the plausible fault for the incident was due to vibration caused by Pipeline Pump #1. The vibration caused the machine screws used to secure the wire leads into the terminal block to back out. The result of the loosened connections was resistance (across the connection). The increase in resistance (>0 ohms) caused the connection to heat up and the resulting arc.

Technicians were testing battery banks, as part of the 3-year battery capacity testing maintenance activities. When testing the voltage of Cell 25, the voltage started at 1.212VDC and in 11 seconds the cell went into polarity reversal and voltage was -22.220VDC. VRLA (valve regulated lead acid) batteries are not designed to go into reverse polarity. At this point, with the cell going into reverse polarity as quickly as it did and how negative it went, caused the cell had a rapid expansion of plates and buildup of gases. This caused the plastic of the individual cell to give away and  the font cover to fail. In addition a cloud of smoke was released. No individuals were close by the Cell 25. No injuries occurred.  All connections and procedures were followed correctly. 
Specific information per NTL 2019-N05-
. where the fire occurred: UEB Battery room Testing a GNB 50A09 Battery from 2006
. if the fire was extinguished: N/A. No visible flames occurred. Only smoke
. what equipment was involved: LDA-85-BAT-1312 UM Emergency DC Lighting Instrument Battery
.  what equipment was damaged: LDA-85-BAT-1312 cell number 25
. what (if any) hot work was being performed: No hot work was being performed
. the duration of the fire: No visible flames occurred. Only smoke was observed and instantaneously dissipated. 
. if a muster occurred as a result: N/A. Event did not trigger a muster. 
. the cost to replace the damaged equipment: Cost of damage is still TBD 
. if an explosion occurred: Cell 25 had a rapid expansion of plates which caused a buildup of gases. In turn caused the plastic cover to fail. 
. the injuries related to the fire: No injuries occurred

Investigation Results: Changes made to operation/design without use of contractor's MoC process, availability of hydraulic pressure indication for umbilical reel operator was unknown by operator, no shut-off or alarm for operator of an overpull situation, pressure set-points for hydraulic motors was not verified prior to start of task onsite, and set-points were found to be out of range. Reel operator was an SSE. SSEs onsite was not communicated to FMOG. All personnel had safety training, but SSEs lacked operational training/experience for task. Project specs and equipment were different (larger/bigger/heavier) than previous projects performed by contractor. Did not take into account increased lateral loads in design of installation. Contractor did not utilize SWA when it was identified they did not have adequate personnel for project.
Recurrence Prevention Corrective Actions:
-Action 1 - Administrative
-Update planning process so that client provided sea-fastening is verified by internal engineering team.
-Action 2 - Administrative / Training
-Familiarize the operations team with the latest Project Management Process.
-Required reading will be assigned and monitored to completion.
-MOC Training for the team.
-Stop Work Authority Training
-Action 3 - Potential Engineered Improvement
-Bolt options for fastening the LARS & proving frame.
-Action 4 - SPAC (Standard Policies Administrative Controls).
-OMM Procedures will be updated to have a verification step for the set pressure at which the winch will not be able to pull greater than the pre-determined amount.
This will be verified during FAT and at the jobsite.
FM O&G

Operators were using the personnel basket to move several Glycol Charcoal Filters from inside the NW Hull Column to an area on the NW Main Deck. When the basket swung near (and about 15-20' above) the Booster Compressor #1 Exhaust; the wind pushed the basket over the exhaust. Once the basket came within close proximity to the (approximately) 1,200 °F exhaust; the ropes holding the personnel basket platform began to melt.
Initial Actions Taken:
-The riggers told the Crane Operator to finish booming down and land the load as quickly as possible.
Follow-Up Actions Taken:
-Once the load was safely on deck; the Operators inspected the personnel basked.
-The Ropes securing the personnel basket's platform tarp had melted through on one side, so the basket was placed out of service.
-To ensure that it is not used; the Operators attached an OOS Tag to the Personnel Basket's Upper Master Link. 
Response to RFI:
*Why did they use a personnel basket vs utility/equipment basket? -They did not think about using the cargo basket. (Complacency) 
Note: Both the OIM and our HSE Team Lead discussed this with everyone involved and the rest of the crew, so this does not occur again.
Recommendations from Incident Investigation:
-Contractors to review the (HSE.GOM.PRG-06.014) Personnel Basket Transfer Program and the (HSE.GOM.PRG-06.11) Crane Operation Program and amend the Crane Operations JSA to include requirements in relation to cargo transfers.
-Also consider identifying the high temperature Booster Compressor Exhausts as a hazard on the JSA.
-There is a "no fly / no lift" zone within a 30'-0" radius of the (approx. 1,200 °F) Booster Compressor #1 & #2 exhaust stacks.

The operations team was alerted of H2S readings of around 20 ppm at the Wemco and Water Skimmer vessels. This was discovered while taking manual samples (tubes) in preparation for putting a well on.  The well was unloading from an Acid Stimulation job, being unloaded through the test separator to Dry Oil tank and now wanting to put in our regular production system. The well from the Acid Simulation job was reading 0ppm at all sample points, which was the reasoning for the plan to put the well into the system. Upon investigation, samples were taken of the Fuel gas which supplies blanket gas and fills the Wemco, readings were 0 ppm. In discussions with the chemical engineer, there is a possibility that the water clarifier chemical being used is a contributing factor and has been known to create H2S. All necessary safety precautions have been taken to include exclusion zones, buddy system, personal H2S detectors, and respiratory protection when sampling. Samples at the Wemco and water skimmer have remained close to 20ppm throughout the night and morning of 2/3/21, while readings at all sample points within the current H2S contingency plan have been 0ppm.

While making up top drive to a full stand of drill pipe the driller set the parking brake after the saver sub was made up into the stand. After parking brake was set the driller then went to apply torque to the connection via the top drive control panel. After a minimum amount of torque was applied the driller noticed the block was traveling down with the parking brake set. The driller immediately stopped the block from moving via the brake lever. Total distance the block traveled down was 5 feet which resulted in bending 3 joints of drill pipe that were made up and the joint that was sitting in the slips. A Job-By-Design was in place for this task and all personnel were in safe step back areas.
Findings - Following discovery of air leaking into pilot line #12, maintenance team simulated and proved that when pilot pressure was in the 32 40 psi range, the park brake was unable to function.
Corrective Actions - 
1.  Emergency Caliper Pressure Gauge to be monitored and recorded every time setting of park brake is performed. This will remain until visual indicator light is installed.
2.  Brake handle will be secured as secondary means of block arrest.
3.  Drawworks HPU fluid will be flushed and replaced. Additional fluid filtering will be instituted to ensure acceptable fluid cleanliness.

Evacuation of personnel due to facility loss of power. Platform life safety systems were being powered initially by a primary 500 KW NOV rental generator. At 3:00 P.M., the rental generator went down. The platform's Emergency Generator was put online and ran for 1 hour before the mechanic manually shut down it down due to critical mechanical/electrical concerns. The primary rental generator issue was trouble shot during the time the Emergency Generator was online. The issue was initially identified as a control board malfunction and replacement part ordered. The part was sent out but the crew ran out of time to repair due to daylight and transportation availability. At that time, the Production Superintendent was notified that the facility was completely without power. The platform was secured and unmanned and the personnel transported to the facility for housing. The crew was not able to return to the Spar facility due to inclement weather until 2/18/2021. Upon return, a technician came out with extra parts to help troubleshoot and repair the primary 500 KW rental generator. The problem with the rental generator was found to be broken wires on the wiring harness to the control board. Once the wiring harness was replaced, the rental generator was put back on line. The platform Emergency Generator was trouble shot and determined that the generator's PMG wiring had failed. A second rental generator was procured for the platform and the Emergency Generator was placed permanently out of service. Power for the facility is now being supplied by the primary 500 KW NOV rental generator and a back up 350 KW NOV rental generator.

IP was injured while removing a hand rail to access platform's heat exchanger for repairs, IP was sent onshore for furhter medical evaluation. The Crane was being used to assist in removing handrail from sockets and when the handrail sprung loose, it struck the IP, causing injury.

Galley personnel were attempting to turn the power control to the "ON" position on the galley's oven/range which resulted in a small yellow flash and single "pop" sound. The range immediately lost power along with the galley's vent fan. No visible smoke or burning smell was identified.  

Follow-up Actions/Preliminary investigation Results: Galley personnel immediately turn the power control to the "OFF" position. Electricians were immediately dispatched to troubleshoot the incident. The electricians found that the main breaker for the DP-0008 panel had tripped along with the breaker feeding the range. The electricians isolated the range breaker and return the main breaker to normal service. The electricians removed the control panel for the range and identified the control switch for the hot plate had visual signs of arc flash. The control switch for the hot plate was removed to find the fault happened in the switch, as it has rungs of contacts that are made and broken by a rocker cam. The broken contacts rendered the oven/range hot plate inoperable. The electricians ordered a new control switch for the range/oven hot plate. The hot plate was placed in LTI and range/oven was placed in service. No injury to personnel was incurred as a result of this event.

IP was stepping down from a chemical injection skid walkway to the metal deck plate in the Riser Bay. As the IP stepped down and sustained an injury. While making rounds, IP and sustained an injury. IP was able to maintain balance and did not fall. IP reported to the medic concerning his injury in the morning. A banksman and crane operator reported a casing protector on 7-5/8" falling to sea while a bundle of casing was being hoisted from boat to the vessel. While pulling stands of 5.5" Drill Pipe out of the hole with the Pipe Racking System (PRS), the Driller released the elevators and the PRS started back with the stand. As a result the stand of drill pipe came out of the racker falling approximately 4' to the rig floor. The bottom of the drill pipe landed on the rotary table; and, the top of the drill pipe came to a rest on the North corner of the Derrick. Upon initial inspection of the PRS no damage was found to the dies, gripper, or the guides.  Note:  the PRS dies were inspected 5 stands prior to the incident occurring. At this time the only damage sustained in the incident are to the threads on the of the bottom joint in the stand. No injuries or additional equipment damage occurred as a result of the incident.  Red zone discipline was enforced therefor no one was the area at the time. The operation was stopped. A Safety Meeting was held with the crew; and, the stand of drill pipe was safely recovered. The damaged joint of rental pipe was separated, laid out, then marked as damaged to be returned to "Work strings" to be re-threaded.

Workers started the C-Pump to begin circulating WBM which is a twice daily routine. After the pump was started it was run at idle speed for approximately 5 minutes. The pump was then throttled up to circulate the mud at a faster rate. Both workers remained in the area with one inside the toolbox checking mud weights, and the other inspecting other equipment. After approximately 10 minutes of circulation one of the workers observed what he described as black smoke coming from the exhaust. Upon further observation he also observed what appeared to be glowing embers coming from the exhaust. At this point the observing worker immediately throttled the pump down to idle and shut the engine off by pulling the E-Stop. No flames or glowing embers were observed after the shutdown.
The pump is still on the facility and have not been sent in for analysis due to the East Crane repair currently out of service for repairs. Waiting on crane to offload pump to boat and send in onshore. The company will perform the analysis once they receive the pumps. Will add the analysis for the cause of fire to the report once complete. 
Incident - Embers and smoke observed coming from C-Pump Exhaust
Immediate action taken - The area was secured and Lead DSV notified.

Drill crew noticed an electrical arc inside the wire tray on the east side of the drilling rig. Once arc was noticed, the wires began to smoke and smolder. Crew member called Driller and told him to shut down mud pumps. After shutting down mud pumps smoking and smoldering stopped. Rig personnel completed repairs shortly thereafter. Investigating further for cause(s) and possible corrective actions.
Update for BSEE questions:
- What equipment was involved in the incident? The electric cables for Mud Pump #3.
- Was equipment damaged? There was no damage to Mud Pump #3. The only damage sustained was to the electrical cable.
- What is the estimated cost to replace damaged equipment? The cost of the repair to the electrical cable is approximately $1,800.00
- How long did the smoldering take place? It estimated to have lasted 10-15 seconds.
- Was there a muster? No muster resulted from the event.
Follow-up: Cause determined to be that the two cables rubber together or got smashed together, which caused them to short out with each other. Corrective actions consisted of repair to wiring/cables at point of arcing. Preventive actions include a pending third-party survey of all rig wiring for identification of other possible risks for arcing.

The blackout event occurred during routine operations to change out ESD and TSE lines onboard. The ESD line replacement was completed and crews were working on the TSE lines. As the TSE line was pulled, it activated the facility shut-in sequence.  This was due to the TSE line being unexpectedly fed by a different panel. A process upset occurred on the facility which lead to instability of the risers. At daybreak, about 7:00, a sheen was observed off the facility. Produced water samples were taken, water production was reduced by cutting back high water wells, and further stabilization of the production vessels and water polishing kit was conducted. By 10:00, water quality showed significant improvement and by 12:00, produced water samples were back within normal operating range. Based upon analysis of  samples during the produced water event, it was estimated that the produced water discharge between 00:30 and 12:00 contained approximately 2.0bbls of oil. Lab analysis of a sample collected February 24 was completed on March 10, 2021. The lab analysis of the sample showed an oil & grease concentration of 615ppm. Based upon the oil & grease concentration shown by the lab analysis and the estimated volume of produced water discharged between 00:30 and 12:00, it was estimated that a total of 4.5bbls of oil was discharged in the produced water over that time period. 
Return Comments:
*What was the process upset? -The facility was in the process of being restarted due to a full plant shutdown on the evening of Monday 2/22 attributable to an equipment failure causing the cooling system to go offline which cascaded into a full shut in of the production plant. As production was being ramped up, a recently stimulated well was brought online whose produced fluid adversely impacted the separation in both production trains when it reached the plant. 
*Explain "instability of the risers". -The plant and all associated risers were in restart condition with the risers being ramped back up to normal production rates. During this stage, riser slugging is experienced due to a combination of the lower production flowrates, fluctuating lift gas rates, and subsea topography.

The drill pipe remained in the elevators and in the upper and lower gripper arms of the PRS. Job-By-Design was in place with all personnel in their designated areas. The stand of drill pipe was released from the PRS and ran back in the hole. The PRS was then stood back vertical and safely secured awaiting repairs.

While POOH with WFR Clean out assembly the driller was in the process traveling down the derrick with the TDS to latch onto the next stand o f 5.5" DP. The facility PIC went to investigate the alarm in his office and smelt a burnt plastic smell from the MCC room. The PIC then went to the MCC room which is located on the back side of his office and observed no visible flame; however, a light smoke was observed which quickly dissipated upon entering the MCC room. Subsea Supervisor was in the process of moving the BOP Gantry crane from the STBD setback area approximately 20' port to align the STBD auxiliary winch over the BOP to install conduit. While positioning the Gantry crane the Subsea Supervisor and task participants heard a strange sound "like a pop". The crew called TOFS to investigate the strange noise. While investigating the source of the noise the crew found the forward leg traverse pulse encoder pinion and shaft assembly lying on the BOP transporter cart. Further investigation determined the dropped objected originated from the STBD forward encoder. The encoder pinion and shaft assembly dislodged from its housing and descended approximately 72 feet to the BOP transporter cart below. The pinion is made of Teflon and, coupled with the shaft assembly, weighed 2lbs . Note: The dropped object was not due to collision; nor was the Gantry crane bearing weight as the crew was not performing a lift at the time. No one was near the landing zone of the dropped object. The STBD setback area access was restricted via Red Zone management for ongoing maintenance. The Subsea Supervisor operated the Gantry Crane remotely from the LMRP level. The BOP transporter deck is located in the moonpool and only accessed during BOP lowering/recovery operations. Estimated cost for replacement parts was $7,784.00.

While conducting workover operations the crew was in the process of tripping in the hole. Slips were set on the pipe, with the top of the pipe at 12 feet above the rig floor, and the top-drive brake handle was released. However, the brakes were mistakenly left in the locked open position. The top-drive continued to descend contacting the pipe in the rotary. The contact caused an identification tag weighing 3.2 ounces dislodged from the pipe handler and fell 25 feet to the rig floor. A hydraulic cylinder and a pad eye on the top drive counterbalance broke, allowing 10 gallons of Aqua Marine AW46 hydraulic oil to spray onto the rig floor with no fluid entering the water. The pipe in the slips bent.

A plan was developed to secure equipment, clean up the released fluid and make repairs to the top-drive. Equipment damage was under 25K and included a broken hydraulic cylinder and a broken pad eye on the top drive for the counterbalance system.

It was noticed the busbar between cells on the electrolyzer was red and there was evidence of charring and soot. An investigation is on-going. 
Company response information request:
*WHERE DID THE FIRE OCCUR? please be specific about where the Electrolyzer is located, and which equipment is associated with it. - The MD Hypochlorite Generator system was found with an electrical connection overheating during the 3-month electrician inspection PM.  The MD Hypochlorite Generator system is located on the X Mezzanine Deck.  The Hypochlorite Generator package (ZZZ-7080) is located at MD Mezzanine deck within a Class 1 Zone 2 area.  The Electrolyzer cell enclosure unit (ZZZ-7087) is not rated.
*WHAT EQUIPMENT WAS INVOLVED? - The MD Hypochlorite Generator system - hypochlorite Generator package (ZZZ-7080) and electrolyzer cell unit (ZZZ-7087).  
*WAS EQUIPMENT DAMAGED? - Damaged bus bars (x3 or more). - Possible electrolyzer cell damage or internal build up within cell if the system is overdue for acid wash.  Several electrolyzer cells were removed and inspected. The electrode sleeves were each found to be more than 50% filled with white precipitates.
*>$25K (ESTIMATE)? - Yes, ~55K
*HOW LONG DID THE FIRE LAST? - Hypochlorite Generator incident is not a traditional combustion fire, it is related to an electrical hot spot where current (Amps) conductivity is generated either or for lack of surface contact or low/unbalance voltage conditions. Package immediately placed out of service via manual activation "off" push-button located on control panel upon overheating electrical connection detection, then package was electrical isolated from power supply source to perform corrective activities and bring it back in service.

At approximately 11:50am the facilities audible gas detection alarm sounded and a confirmed trip was identified on a gas detector located on the Lower Mezzanine Deck. IP reported to the medic they were working in a bent over position for about 45 min yesterday and they felt some tightness in the lower back upon standing up.  This morning they reported discomfort in the lower back and inner thigh.

Operator submits notification of a gas release that initiated a process shut-in.  While making rounds, production operators observed a pinhole leak in the fuel gas flare piping. Operator received approval from the New Orleans district on 03.16.2021 to install a Plidco clamp provided the following conditions can all be met: 1 - Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S) must not be present in the line; 2 - Operating pressure of the clamped line must be less than or equal to 285 PSI or safety devices must be set to protect this line (PSV or 2 independent PSHs) equal to or below 285 PSI; 3 - Clamp shall be monitored for leaks daily; 4 - Clamp shall be rated for greater than the Maximum Allowable Working Pressure (MAWP) of the connected piping; 5 - No more than two repairs per line segment are in place; 6 - An incident report is submitted in eWell for any gas release from the clamped line that results in a shutdown (automatic or manual); and, 7 - Installed clamp must be full encirclement type.

The crane crew was utilizing the gantry crane to install ram doors on the BOP stack as part of end of well maintenance. The gantry crane was moved forward to the stops in order to be centered above the BOP. Galley personnel were attempting to use the hot plate on the galley's oven/range when they observed a small arc flash and single "popping" sound. The range immediately lost power. At ~09:16 hrs there was an emergency shutdown due to "Fire in Turbine Generator-2 Enclosure". The shutdown was initiated automatically by the fire detection devices in the enclosure. Full muster of 26 POB completed and firefighting teams dispatched to location. Emergency Generator auto started as designed. The CO2 fire suppression automatically activated when the alarm came in. No signs of fire detected from outside the enclosure. After CO2 suppression was fully discharged (approx 20 minutes) fire team able to open doors on enclosure. No signs of fire detected during the initial inspection. After unit was ventilated and facility was back on main power a more thorough inspection of the Turbine Generator was performed. During this inspection a small piece of rubber was found lying in the bottom of the enclosure skid. This rubber was under the drive coupling between the gear box and the generator close to the generator side. There were also a few spots of melted rubber on the bottom of the skid by the piece of rubber. After unit was isolated the fiberglass drive coupling cover was removed. This revealed where a piece of the rubber skirt on the coupling cover had broken loose and rubbed against the drive coupling likely causing the fire detection devices to trip.

While running 14" casing the rig crew was stabbing the first stand of casing out of the derrick. At approximately 8:45 am, while performing a 24 hr soak with xylene in the well and with the safety head and PIV in the closed position providing two well barriers, we experienced an Auto-Shear event when the UTA and mud mat on the seabed tipped over due to current at depth. As a result of the auto-shear activation the upper ram closed along with the open side outlet valves in addition to the two already closed well barriers. UTA was identified by beacon and ROV visual to be at the PP Plem on the north side. The well control package wellbore was free of any tools, wireline or coil tubing at the time of the event. The Atlantis PQ Control Room was contacted and asked to monitor pressures. No environmental leaks or anomalies were observed and the ROV did a survey showing NO damage to any structure.

The team reported a strong sour odor throughout the production deck downwind of the float cell.   Upon investigation, a meter reading of 124 ppm H2S was documented directly at the vacuum breaker opening from the floatation cell vacuum breaker.  Readings 5' away from the vacuum breaker were documented at 10 ppm.  At ~10' from the vacuum breaker, meter readings were at 0. The team red barricaded the area off as a Do Not Enter Zone.  All H2S readings were 0 ppm around the perimeter of the isolated area.  The team then isolated the manual valve underneath the vacuum breaker in order to prevent the fumes from relieving to atmosphere.  In parallel, the team worked with the Champion X (Nalco) technician onboard and advanced biocide treatments were introduced to the production separation system and the floatation cell to kill the bacteria and reduce/eliminate the H2S gases. Biocide treatments are planned to continue with samples and readings documented.  While not expected to be needed, the self-contained breathing apparatus (SCBA) available onboard are positive pressure masks that can be used for an emergency response event if necessary.   The Stampede field is located in an area that was determined to be H2S Absent.  The H2S is bacteria-generated topsides and not from any of the producing reservoirs.

On 3/23/21 Field Gas Compressor #1 was being started after a compressor change-out and repairs to its associated gas cooler unit. The compressor was started at approximately 19:02 with personnel positioned in various areas around to the compressor to check for any abnormalities. As the compressor went through its start-up sequence and began to build pressure, a noise was heard coming from the cooler deck directly above the compressor and the unit was immediately shut down. column14: Main Pass Area, South And East Addition
column24: CI using cutting torch to cut apart base of old brine tank for demolition and scrap on top deck of platform. It is supected that a hot particle dropped to the well head on lower deck and ignited some gas inside casing valve. The well had been previously temporarily abandoned and was part of a sulfur mine operations well, as are all wells on this facility. Call for halt of all work. Fire Watch stationed on lowered deck immediately extinguished flame with dry chemical extinguisher. Continue to check for unsuspected gas sources. Talos Third Coast LLC respectfully submits a notification of a disabled safety system that occurred on 03.27.2021 at 15:00 hours. The platform was having issues with an ESD/TSE leak.  The TSE loop over the Wet/Dry oil tank is tied into the AFFF unit and separated from the rest of the platform TSE by a check valve. The check valve keeps the loop over the wet/dry oil tank charged when the TSE is pulled anywhere else on the platform preventing the AFFF unit from going off. It is surmised that the check valve leaked, and bled the TSE over the Wet/Dry oil tank down,  causing the AFFF unit to go off while the operators were trying to find the ESD/TSE leak rendering the system inoperable.  The platform remained shut-in until Talos Third Coast LLC could secure the proper equipment to safely bring the platform back online. The AFFF unit was repaired and back in service on 03.31.2021.

On March 28th, a shallow water flow was observed from one of the ports in the 38" wellhead housing following cementation of the 22" riserless casing string at Caramel Keg (GB 962 #1).  This flow was initially communicated to BSEE via phone call and email to the Lafayette district office on March 29th.  Additional wireline logging (casing bond log and temperature log) runs were performed to gain additional insights into the potential source/location of the flow, as well as the quality and presence of cement behind the 22" casing string.  Subsequent engagements with BSEE were held to review ROV images and video footage of the flow, data from wireline logging runs, wellbore structural integrity analysis, and monitoring plans.  Approval from BSEE Lafayette district was received on April 1st to proceed with running the riser/BOP and continue with subsequent planned operations.  Flow from the wellhead was monitored in alignment with the approved proposal and a general reduction trend in flow from wellhead port was observed.  Additional engagements with BSEE district and regional representation were held throughout April 1 - April 19, and approval was received from BSEE on April 19th to install and close ball valves on two wellhead ports to isolate flow from wellbore.  On April 20th, the ball valves were closed and flow from the wellbore ceased, approximately 23 days after initial observation.  Approval to temporarily abandon the well was received from BSEE on April 25, along with a monitoring plan of the wellbore and the surrounding area.   TA operations concluded on April 27th. The ongoing monitoring program has since identified no indications of flow/broaching at or near the GB 962 #1 wellbore as of May 7th.  No personnel were injured or evacuated as a result of this subsurface shallow water flow.

At 09:45, while lowering a 45' cargo basket onto a motor vessel using the platform pedestal crane, wind gust caused the basket to rotate and become caught on the davit of LifeBoat #3. Because the davit was in the crane operator's blind spot, the operator continued to lower the basket toward the boat, causing the basket to slip and swing away from the davit. As the basket turned outward and back in, the basket contacted the outer hull of LB#3, causing a 2" by 2" dent in the lifeboat. The impact caused the lifeboat to pivot inside the davit, causing superficial scratches in several external hull areas. The basket was safely lowered to the vessel and unhooked. Crane Operations PTW was canceled, and the UWA suspended all crane activity. The lifeboat was inspected and was taken out of service for further review. Supplemental evacuation lifeboats were available to meet the platforms' emergency evacuation plan. No personnel nor environment was harmed.

On 04/10/2021 at approximately 02:55 hours, operations personnel were making rounds and heard an unfamiliar noise. They quickly discovered that a needle valve for a pressure gauge had broken off the 3rd-Stage Suction Scrubber of a Flash Gas Compressor No. 2. As a result, a small volume of natural gas was released. Due to the location and minor volume of this release, the facility's gas detection system did not detect the release. Therefore, no alarm sounded and no muster occurred. There was no fire or injuries. There was no equipment damage other than the broken needle valve. The Flash Gas Compressor No. 2 was immediately and manually shut down by operations personnel. Based on the attached data, it appears that the release was approximately only 2.5 minutes in duration. Pressure indicated before the leak began was 862 PSI, 810 PSI during the leak, and then fell to zero (0) PSI (over the next 5 minutes) when FGC #2 was shut down. The broken needle valve was removed and a new valve was installed.

Renaissance Offshore, LLC production complex experienced a small gas leak that required manual shut down of components Compressors Recip. and Turbine Compressor. On April 11, 2021 at approximately 15:45 hours, a small gas leak was discovered proactively while personnel were making rounds. A crew member discovered a small gas leak on the CAE-2600 (C-160) centrifugal turbine's center housing between the housing and discharge capsule assembly. The small gas leak was not detected by the Turbine Compressor Building's Enclosure sensing devices lower or upper limits (Gas Detectors). The small leak was contained within a  Class I div. 2 area, and due to its size, being proactively identified by crew member no further escalation took place.  When the small leak was discovered, a calibrated portable gas detector was used to verify gas concentration lower and upper ranges in relation to Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) concentrations. At ~10" away  from the leak point, the lower ALM range registered and as sensor was moved closer to the actual location, the upper ALM range was denoted. The leak was approximately ~ 4.42' from an insulated exhaust system with ~ 1150 degrees protected. UWA was contacted, and a manual shut down response was conducted, the concern was the proximity to a nearby hot surfaces or if the leak progressed. The unit was successfully repaired, seals replaced, re-torqued, and placed back-in-service. No injuries, pollution, or damages occurred as the result of the small gas leak; no need for emergency musters.

At approximately 1655 hours local time on April 24, 2021, well abandonment personnel speared into the 18-5/8" casing on the C-4 well at the wellhead deck. The well abandonment team was attempting to start pulling and laying down the C-4 conductor. The top of conductor was at the mezzanine deck where a 9-inch pin hole was drilled. The team continued to lift the C-4 conductor to begin pinning operations. At 39.5-ft lift height, the 24-inch conductor separated from the 18-5/8" casing, likely from either poor cement bond in the 18-5/8" x 24" casing annulus or there was no cement behind pipe. The 24"conductor then slid down the 18-5/8" casing until it reached origination height at the well head deck. When the 24" conductor came to a stop at its originating spot, the descent broke the welds on the pollution ring. Three members of the well abandonment team were on the mezzanine deck where they had just completed drilling the 9" pin holes in the C-4 conductor, which consisted of the 18-5/8" casing and 24" conductor. Each were standing a safe distance, approximately 20', from the conductor that was being lifted. One heard a "rush of air", one heard a "loud sound" and the third heard "two metal objects hitting." At which time they saw the 24" conductor descending at a high rate of speed. All three personnel headed toward the egress point running. One team member slipped during the expedited egress resulting in a minor abrasion below the knee. It is worth noting that March 26, 2021, FM O&G verified the mechanical cut at 20' BML by picking up the C-4 conductor, 4' at 191,000 lbs. and set the conductor back down. The operation was performed using the same 18-5/8" casing spear that picked up the C-4 conductor on April 24, 2021.
Immediate Corrective Actions: The area around the well slot was barricaded until an assessment could be completed. It was determined that the 24" conductor had safely landing in its pre-pull position. The 18-5/8" Casing was secure and hanging from the spear assembly. Some grating will need to be repaired on the mezzanine deck. During the night and continuing today, the 18-5/8" casing is being pulled. Once on deck, it will be examined for cement pumped during the original well completion.
Investigation Results: 18-5/8" casing was not completely cemented above the mudline as was indicated in the well completion report. This lack of adhesion between the two pipes allowed the 24" conductor to separate from the casing when lifted with the casing spear. It was also discovered after the event; the casing head was a gravity type and not traditional. This information was not on the completion report.
Recurrence Prevention: On the platform we will be utilizing the proving clamp on all wells. The reason the clamp was not utilized in the incident is that a casing spear was used on traditional casing heads. So going forward an observation and evaluation is being completed before lifting the casing head to determine which type casing head it is. If the casing head is gravity held a proving clamp will be used and a 4" pin will be put into place before the casing head is cut to prevent any of the casing heads after being cut from falling off. If it is a traditional casing head it will be speared with casing spear, if possible, and we cannot get the proving clamp on the conductor.

On 4/26/2021 while tripping out of the hole with 26" drilling bottom hole assembly, the rig observed shallow water flow at LPWH.  The rig then displaced the well to 13.0 ppg at bit depth.  Then the rig pumped in hole to TD pumping 13.5 ppg mud. The rig continued weighting up till an 11.51 ppg estimated circulating density was reached. Well static.   The rig then pumped up the estimated static density from the bottom hole assembly and it was 11.4 ppg.  The rig then pumped out of hole with a 13.3 ppg water-based mud.

On 4/29/2021 while displacing the 22" inner string and casing from seawater to 13.3 water-based mud.  Inner string and casing were displaced to 13.1 ppg.   The rig then displaced to a 13.3 ppg.  Flow observed.  Weight up to 13.5 ppg until observed increase in returns. Weight up to 14.0 ppg and observed decreased return rate at LPWH.   Pumped in the hole with 22" casing from 5,900' to 9,110'. Land HPWH into LPWH.  From that point forward spent the next couple days spotting increased mud weight in the hole each time flow was observed after a few hours.   The rig attempted the 22" cement job.  After attempting the 22" cementing job the rig still observed flow.   While circulating around the 22" cement job back up mud made it to the rig and the rig circulated out the 22" cement job with water-based mud.  The rig continued to circulate spotting increased mud in the hole until flow stopped and a second attempt was made to cement the 22" casing.  The rig pumped the second 22" cement job on 5/5/2021.  The rig did not confirm cement returns to the mud line; however, the well remained static. The BOP was ran and initial latch up testing performed.  Wireline cement evaluation was performed to a depth, as far as, the tool could descend.  Cleanout run was requested to cleanout shoe track for cement evaluation.  Prior to cement evaluation the APD pressure test was performed and failed and well abandonment procedures commenced.

On 05-05-2021 the M/V HOS Captain was conducting cargo operations at MC 37. While utilizing the rig's crane, a frame being lifted from the deck of the M/V HOS Captain came in contact with the IP. No medical attention was requested and the AB continued to perform their job duties.  At the time of the incident the vessel reported their VSat communications was being blocked and stated this to be the reason for the late reporting.  The Ocean Blackhawk was not notified the incident had occurred until the evening of 05-07-2021.

Update 5-19-2021: The following activities led up to the event:
The rig crane operator positioned the rig crane and lowered the hook to prepare for the load. The senior AB (AB1/Mentor) advised a Short Service Employee Ordinary Seaman (OS/Mentee) to temporarily hold the hook while a tagline was being clipped in. AB1 knelt on the deck to attach the tagline to the underside of the metal frame. While the tagline was being attached, the OS clipped the crane hook to the D-ring which was attached to a four-part sling on the frame, making the load "live". While AB1 was still kneeling on the deck, the vessel rolled, causing the "live" load to shift slightly and strike AB1.

The root cause identified from Hornbeck's investigation were Inadequate hazard assessment - The JSA was completed at the beginning of the crews' watch and was "generic" to deck cargo. The hazards and risks of each specific lift were not considered. Therefore, the crew did not consider that the tagline needed to be attached to the frame prior to the crane hook being lowered into position. Corrective actions include (1) The crew did not consider the relative movement of the vessel to be a hazard to the load with the hook connected but the drillship crane not actively engaged (2) This event occurred after a 14-hour transit to the worksite in weather conditions that prevented the crew from resting fully.

Corrective action: Hornbeck launched a fleet-wide training module on
risk identification including threat controls and the accurate generation of risk tools.

During sandblasting operations a contract employee received minor injuries when an air hose connected to a sand hopper came apart. The hose was coupled with a crows foot connection, whip check and a wire keeper to prevent the coupling from disconnecting. When the hose parted, both the wire keepers and whip check failed. The contract employee was sent in for medical evaluation and released to full duty.

Follow Up: It was determined that the hoses were installed in a horizontal manner adding excess weight to the connections. When the employee reached to close a valve, his body pushed on the hose causing the connections to come apart. The contractor has updated its procedures to reflect the following.

All 1" air lines shall have safety pins and whip-checks on connectors to prevent inadvertent disconnection.
All 2" bull hose shall have tie wire (minimum 16 gauge stainless steel) and whip-chick installed at each connection.
A 90 degree fitting shall be used to prevent hose the hose from being in a horizontal position.

Evaluated by the onsite Medic, who in consultation with an onshore Physician, made the decision to have member sent to shore for further evaluation. There was no apparent life threatening injury. Update 6/2/2021: Dimensions of the accessway into the pedestal of the crane is 22" x 24.5". It is a square accessway, and the space into the pedestal below it is 72" deep (at it's deepest point). At the time of the incident there was approximately 18" of oily water in the bottom of the pedestal space below the accessway. The accessway is used to enter the pedestal for access to crane components/controls. The pedestal space is containment for the engine and accumulates rain water runoff through/from the engine compartment. It is pumped out as a maintenance function as levels of runoff accumulate, based primarily on the frequency, duration and/or intensity of rain.

The accessway cover consisted of a section of fiberglass grating that covered the space, which had been cut apart from the adjacent pieces to facilitate removal. The underside of the grating was covered with metal screen to prevent small parts from falling through. It was determined that the dimensions of this section of grating was one inch smaller than the dimension of the accessway. Over time, the metal screen underlayment had bent down and no longer was below the edges of the grating, which further allowed the grating to slide. According to the worker who fell, as member passed through the space and stepped on the grating accessway cover, it slid and fell into/through the accessway. Member fell into the accessway with it.

A survey of the other two cranes (of the same design/configuration) found that the grating coverings of the accessways were of sufficient dimensions to prevent the same occurrence. However, as a preventive action, the grating accessway covers of all three cranes were replaced with metal covers of an improved design. The new covers consist of 3"x3"x1/4" angle iron frames with steel grating permanently attached as an inset. The angle iron frames allow the cover to engage the sides of the accessway frame to prevent slippage in any direction.
