At ~ 23:45 last night in preparation for releasing the tubing hanger the ROV was staged at the tree and tied in to pressurize the gallery area via the THD circuit.  The THT was manually operated via a T-handle can-style valve tool to the open position and a hotstab was engaged to the THD receptacle with 1200psi applied ( ~500psi overbalanced to 11.9 SBM hydrostatic).  An FMC representative was stationed in the ROV shack as well as the rig floor where we were monitoring a live feed of the ROV pressure gauge for indication of TH release.  Upon indication of pressure drop and TH release the ROV operator was instructed to close the THD valve on the XT, FMC rep stated a satisfactory (6) amount of clockwise valve turns and a torque buildup indicating a full stop were achieved. Upon removal of the ROV hot stab SBM was observed releasing from the THD port, the dummy hotstab was retrieved from the top of the XT and placed in the THD port where all fluid release was stopped.  After installing the dummy hotstab the THD was re-engaged with the valve tool and 6 clockwise turns were achieved along with torque buildup indicating a full stop and valve closure. During the time of the fluid release the drill floor indicated a loss of 5.1bbls of 11.9 SBM from the trip tank. The THD valve status indicator has been noted to be inoperable in our previous crown plug operations and currently shows in the closed position.

Immediate notification and NRC report attached.

 On February 06, 2022, the main platform crane which is a Titan 5400 located on Eugene Island 338 K platform sustained damage to the boom heel section when it contacted with a square tubing pole. 
A third-party crane inspection team made up of a lead mechanic (operator) and a rigger (helper) were on location to perform maintenance on the involved crane. Inspection personnel participated in a pre-task safety meeting and conducted the job safety analysis for the task. The lead crane mechanic began to operate the crane and lower the boom to achieve 0Ã¿Â° degrees to grease the tip section and perform visual inspection of the components. As described in the operator's statement, the boom stopped lowering before he reached the desired position, and his initial assumption was that the anti-two-blocking (ATB) system worked as intended. The block was in a position that allowed the ATB valves to be lifted to reset the sensor so that he could continue to lower the boom, and the operator instructed the helper to perform the task. Following the physical attempt to reset the ATB valves the crane still wouldn't boom lower. At that point the operator acknowledged that he believed the low angle kick-out had engaged so he depressed what he believed was the bypass lever and continued to lower the boom. It was at this point that the operator noticed a difference in the structural uniformity of the boom and halted operations to inspect. 
Upon inspection it was discovered that the heel section of the boom had contacted a 4" W x 4" W x 7'6" H square tubing pole that was welded to the platform and a section of guard railing. The pole is not usually an obstacle during routine lifting operations however to grease and access the tip the boom must be lowered to 0Ã¿Â° degrees, and while lowering the boom as described above, it inadvertently contacted the pole. 
The crane boom was returned to the boom rest position and was placed out of service for further evaluation and repair. 
The involved crane was placed out of service and remains out of service awaiting repairs to the damaged heel and lacing section of the boom. (Estimated cost is $25,000)
No injuries or pollution occurred as a result of this event and based on the investigation the damages sustained were limited to a small section of the boom heel.

On March 4, 2022 at 0846 AM gas alarm activated in the FGC#1 enclosure.   The compressor was shut down at the time and not in service.  One detector in the enclosure reading gas.  Immediate action:  At 8:47 AM Fast response dispatched to investigate.  At 0850 AM Fast response arrived to location.  Fast response registered gas on a portable gas detector.  A second gas detector in the enclosure began reading gas.  Manual ESD and blowdown initiated along with a full ICS muster.  Crew was released from muster at 0916 AM after the issue was identified and isolated.  The Drilling team was allowed to return to work performing routine maintenance.  All other personnel not part of the operations team were released from muster but not authorized to return to work pending further investigation.  At 1130 AM all work groups were authorized to return to work. There was no hot work being performed.  There were work activities taking place on the facility but not on the equipment where the leak occurred.  At the time of the event, we were producing 23 wells and had 4 water injectors online.  There was no pollution to the Gulf of Mexico.  Initial checks found gas seeping from the lube oil tank vent.  A full LOTO was placed on the unit.  Production was ramped up on March 5, 2022 and full production has been restored. Estimated cost of repair is unknown at this time.  We are waiting for two replacement check valves to arrive on location before the repair work can begin.  March 24 Update:  Please see attached schematic of the lube oil tank and tie-in to FGC#1.  The FGC-1 was shutdown on February 28, 2022 and the leak occurred on March 4, 2022. Please note that the event occurred when another compressor shut down due to an un-related issue.  BSEE asked the question: "does the lube oil tank provide oil to an injection pump?".  No, there is no lube oil injection on this unit.  The lube oil tank supplies lube oil to the engine, gearbox, and compressor bearings as well as seal oil to the compressor seals.  The lube oil and seal oil are two separate systems, however they use the same supply (lube oil tank).  On March 31, 2022 BSEE asked "Two (2) failed check valves (FSV) have been determined to be the cause for the gas leak? Explain?".  April 12, 2022 Update:  Replaced BDV 1050 and FSV 1010 on March 25, 2022.  It was found that the FSV 140 on the second stage scrubber was leaking internally and repaired.  The rebuild kit for the vacuum breaker on the lube oil tank arrived and was installed.  We were able to complete the repairs and test FGC1.  However, we did identify another issue with a level control valve and an air intake vain valve that needs to be replaced.  FGC1 is isolated while we are waiting on materials. April 25, 2022 Update:  Level control valve 1010 is on order with delivery expected at end of April.  Preparing location to go into turnaround period and it will most likely be June before start-up of FGC1.

See attached PDF document for details of the March 18, 2022 release of the seawater / MEG mixture lost to the environment while trying to perform a cement squeeze on the Silvertip SA001 well.  Also attached is a MSDS for MEG, MSDS for TETRA sodium chloride solution, and the JSA. March 25 Update: BSEE asked for a  synopsis of how the incident happened to be added to the remarks section.  Operation at time of incident was RIH with coil tubing. A 5 bbl cement squeeze into the FR-12 reservoir in the Silvertip SA001 well was attempted on March 18, 2022, at 1800 hrs. This attempt was unsuccessful as squeeze pressure was not obtained and a subsequent test failed. After further investigation it was discovered the CIT1 valve on the tree was found to be leaking. Due to the CIT1 valve leak, a 50/50 seawater/MEG fluid was lost to the environment.  We first estimated the release to between 100 and 200 bbls.  After some logical estimates for individual activities, we came up with 188 bbls (max).  This is the amount that was reported to the NRC. The CIT1 valve was cycled to the closed position and tested to 3,500 psi against a closed PMV, the same pressure as the IRS is permitted for in the APM. The PMV was opened and test squeezed to 1,000 psi surface pressure as permitted in the APM.  Once test was verified per the CFR, the job was continued with the other approved APM steps. The NRC was contacted, and a report was made (NRC report # 1331496).  Future Action: ROV to perform more frequent inspections of the SST during operations.

(RUE G-30300) On 3/27/22 a smoke alarm sounded at 13:13 hours, full muster achieved 1:22 PM - the Maintenance team began test running the Emergency Generator after planned maintenance had been performed. The muster event was stood down and maintenance began investigating the detector location with fire and gas technicians. On April 1, 2022 at approximately 08:15 hrs, Helix Q400 noted on ROV monitor that the 5-7/8" HWDP (heavy weight drill pipe) and mule shoe were missing.   Silvertip was shut-in to allow for evaluation of any impact from this dropped object. ROV survey and other checks of the Silvertip field were conducted. Helix Q4000 moved to extended safe zone and started pulling pipe out of hole checking torque of each connection.  Helix Q4000 found that four joints of 5-7/8" HWDP drill pipe joint and mule shoe were missing.   Weight is approximately 6,000 lbs and 123 ft in length.  The Grant Candies' ROV located the pipe on April 4, 2022.  Approval to reinstate Silvertip production was received on April 4, 2022 at 14:03 hrs from District Manager (Lake Jackson District).  The likely cause of the drop is believed to be a single improperly torqued pipe connection on one of the 5-7/8" HWDP that resulted in separation of the 4 joints of 5-7/8" HWDP and the mule shoe from the pipe string. Mitigating Actions Going Forward: Torque on new bottom hole assembly will be made up to max value; written log will be kept of torque values for each connection; scribe lines indicating torque positioning will be monitored by ROV; pipe will be tripped in the extended safe zone.  Shell Offshore Inc. requested two weeks to provide a lift plan that will ensure the job is properly planned and executed. Pipe recovery is subject to said plan.

On April 1st at approximately 2100HRS the facility diesel generator was utilized to restored power to the facility after the #2 gas generator became inoperable because of a water pump failure. 

On April 2nd at 0500HRS facility power was interrupted again as the diesel generator shut down while it was in use. Facility personnel attempted to start gas generator #1 which was undergoing maintenance service due to an electrical booster issue but it would not function properly to support an electrical load at that time. 

At 0520HRS the mechanics began to troubleshoot the diesel generator and based on their assessment determined that the fuel filters were plugged. Once the filters were changed the diesel generator was started and voltage and cycles were checked. The diesel generator was engaged, and facility power was restored.
 
At approximately 0730HRS the diesel generator experienced stoppage again. As reported, this was the only operational generator on location therefore a production operator attempted to restart the generator. The attempt was unsuccessful, so the operator went to get the on-location mechanics.
The field foreman and facility person-in-charge (PIC) crossed paths with the production operator and the PIC shortly afterwards opened the left side engine enclosure and recognized a fire within the engine compartment within the incipient stage. 

At 0735HRS the PIC yelled, "fire" three times and retrieved the nearest fire extinguisher. Production operator activated the emergency shutdown system (ESD) and  immediately announced over the company radio for everyone to shut-in and secure their platforms. At the same time, the PIC was extinguishing the fire. He was then relieved by the field foreman and  sounded the facility alarm and another production foreman made a GAI-Tronics announcement that this was not a drill and that everyone  report to their muster station. Once extinguished, they cooled the generator's turbo with water to prevent reignition. Facility personnel mustered and this event ended without injury or environmental impact. The battery bank of the generator was then disconnected from the starter and the ESD engaged to prevent accidental start-up of the equipment.
    
Between 0500HRS and 1000HRS gas generator #1 was serviced operable and at 1000HRS facility power was restored using gas generator #1. 

Upon inspecting the damage sustained it was determined by mechanics that the oil inlet line's integrity was comprised which led to the failure of the component that is a portion of the root-cause. This line along with other hoses and gaskets near the fire is in the process of being replaced. 

No injury or environmental damage resulted from this event. 

Emergency muster did occur and all personnel reported accurately and were accounted for.

At 7:59 PM on April 8, 2022, Appomattox lost gas compression due to a compressor vibration alarm. This resulted in flaring in which the glare activated an ultraviolet/infrared safety high (flame detector) USH-040F12. Alarm logs revealed that another device, USH040F10 had went into a vote alarm fault at 7:50 PM which only sends a local console alarm to the control room. Due to these devices being on a 2oo2 voting (2oo2 is voting logic which means 2 out of 2 devices must activate to cause an action) and in the same fire zone on the upper deck, the fire and gas system automatically initiated a full platform ESD/production shut in and sounded the general alarm. A full muster was obtained in 6 minutes. Once it was deemed safe by the Incident Commander, the fire team was dispatched to investigate and confirmed the flare to be the cause and a fire had not taken place. The event did not result in a gas release nor was there total loss of power as the emergency generator operated as designed. There were no injuries as result of the muster.  The fault on USH-040F10 cleared at 8:01 PM.  Production ramp up began on April 9, 2022.   April 21, 2022, BSEE returned eWell report with three additional questions about the April 8 muster due to glare from flare:  What was done to correct the vibration problem with the compressor? The compressor vibration sensors reacted as designed to increased volume of gas from unloading wells. The VRU2 speed increased momentarily causing high vibration. CRO noticed and attempted to reduce the motor speed, but the VRU2 tripped before the motor speed could be lowered.  These trips are not uncommon.  Was it actually a vibration problem or a faulty vibration detector?  The vibration detectors were not faulty.  Will the glare from the flare continue to activate the ultraviolet/infrared detectors whenever the compressor blowdown and flare?  Investigation determined the cause of problem was suspected dirty optics which reduced the detector's ability to reject false fire events.  Actions taken:  Ongoing: Clean and iO calibrate 12 USH's pointed at the flare.  ETA: 5/10/2022  Completed: Develop a CM (corrective maintenance) plan to clean and iO calibrate remaining USH's on platform.  Develop a proactive PM (preventive maintenance) using PRM to routinely clean all USH's (Potential Mid to Long-term).

column24: [RUE G-30300] On April 14, 2022, at 4:45 a sling parted during the tail end securement of UGL-1. The deck Crew was prepping the 2nd end pulling head on UGL-1 before it was to be transferred over the tower. A rigging holdback sling was attached to the 2nd end of UGL1. There was extra slack in the stern tugger line to ensure there was enough wire to reach the pulling head. The winch wire had a direct path to the pulling head that was staged mid ship. The crew rigged the winch wire to the rigging strap that was secured around the pulling head. Once the winch wire was attached to the rigging sling the winch operator was informed to come up on the winch to take up slack in the wire. The Winch operator came up on the winch wire rapidly thinking he had a lot of slack to retrieve in before putting tension on the umbilical pulling head. The rapid recovery of the winch cable pulled out the slack in the wire faster than the winch operator anticipated, and as a result a shock load was placed on the rigging sling and caused the sling to part. All barricades were in place and all personnel were out of the line of fire. All rigging certs for the equipment used were up to date and in compliance. After the incident occurred an all stop was called on deck activities and a safety standdown was administered to all the deck crew.

After consulting with onshore physician, IP was taken by medevac on April 14, 2022 at 0836 hrs  to Terrebonne General, Houma.  Held safety stand down with crews. After reviewing mitigations Ultimate Work Authority (UWA) granted permission to resume job.  The Offshore Installation Manager (OIM) is the UWA.  The IP was stable and did not sustain a head injury.  IP was diagnosed with a fracture of the T12 (thoracic) and L1 and L2 (Lumbar).  IP was given prescription pain medication and a back brace.  IP to visit orthopedic doctor on May 3, 2022 for diagnosis.  Please see attachments for JSA and pictures of the work area. Oceaneering employee was installing a new ROV umbilical lubricator. The lubricator was placed on the umbilical and the two locking bolt nuts were finger tightened to hold the lubricator in place around the umbilical. The umbilical cable was then hauled in until there was a small belly in the umbilical. The lubricator was repositioned in order to tighten up on the umbilical, and the two locking bolts were hand tightened. When the umbilical was hauled in and made straight, the umbilical shook and the lubricator fell to the deck. The lubricator weighed 18.5 lbs. and fell from a height of 14 ft. Barriers were in place and isolating the deck where the lubricator dropped, and all personnel were clear by design. The only person working inside the barriered area was the single Oceaneering employee who was on a ladder level with the lubricator when it fell to deck. The ladder the Oceaneering employee was on at the time of the incident was necessary for the job, and was required to carry out the job as planned. ROV work is temporarily suspended until given ultimate work authority.

On April 18, 2022 at approximately 1:00 PM the control room noticed an increase in flare volume but no obvious source from the alarm log. After an hour of investigation, operators on deck were able to confirm that the Vapor Recovery Unit (VRU) suction valves had been closed (their fail-safe state) and the Blow Down Valves (BDVs) were open. The VRU compressor was still running at this time.  Electronic Technicians (ETs) found that the VRU Programable Logic Controller (PLC) Processor had locked up and stopped sending signals to our Data Control System (DCS) and the VRU skid.  The processor was manually powered down in order to turn off the compressor. ETs replaced the processor and reuploaded the VRU code.  Estimated cost of repair was $7000.00.  As of April 21, 2022, the VRU was back in operation.

On 04/22/2022 at 10:00 hours, a Production Operator was making rounds when he saw condensate dripping into the containment skid from a level bridle flange on the 1st Stage Suction Scrubber (MBF-2700) for the Flash Gas Compressor No. 2 (FGC#2). The Production Operator immediately reported the leak to the Lead Operator. The Lead Operator relayed the information to the OIM. They both went to inspect the leak and discovered that the leak was actually coming from a very small crack in a weld on the upper nozzle that connects to the upper flange of the level control bridle. The Mechanic confirmed the leak location and the decision was made to shut down FGC#2. The Mechanic MANUALLY shut down FGC#2 at 10:15 hours. Upon shut down, FGC#2 was blown down and locked out. On 05/21/2022 at 22:58 hours, the facility Fire Alarm sounded and the ESD activated, shutting-in the facility, as designed. All personnel mustered and reported to their Emergency Stations. The Fire Team responded to the Process Plant Power Generator No. 1 Enclosure (ZZZ-9000) because the Fire Suppression System (CO2) had been activated in this enclosure. Once the Fire Team had established and confirmed that there was no fire, the ZZZ-9000 enclosure was purged with fresh air. Facility mechanics inspected the enclosure and observed no evidence of fire or burning. However, facility mechanics did find a cracked flex joint in the generator engine exhaust system. Electronic diagnostics were conducted and codes indicated that cylinder misfires on random cylinders had occurred causing the engine to backfire, which in turn caused initiation of the Fireye system and activation of the Fire Suppression System (CO2). Once the facility was deemed to be safe, facility personnel began the process to return the facility to service._x000D_

6/29/2022 Update:
The CEC crew assigned is experienced with 5-10 years offshore work, is familiar with Platform Grace facility layout, safety equipment, hot work procedures, etc. Hot Work permit, JSA, SWC, prior to work starting was properly completed, filed, and signed off by the CEC crew and Beacon West Operations. Fabric maintenance workers mixed some expired two-part Carboline paint for disposal. After mixing, the workers poured the old paint in a bucket that contained some expired Belzona materials (2-part epoxy) that had also been mixed for disposal. After combining the materials, the workers placed the bucket inside the paint locker to allow the materials to cure. The blending of materials caused an exothermic chemical reaction that generated a generous amount of smoke and heat that was observed emanating from the locker after about 5 minutes. The workers removed the bucket from the paint locker and proceeded to add water to cool the reaction and eliminate the smoke. Believing they had eliminated the threat, the workers placed the bucket inside a storage bin next to their tool shed that had been filled with water and proceeded with their planned duties for the day. Several minutes later the fabric maintenance crew foreman came to the area and noticed smoke coming from the bin where the bucket had been placed. The foreman communicated the smoke to the production control room and the emergency response system was activated. General alarms sounded and plant ESD'd. Once the scene was secured, and the all clear given, a stand down conducted with the entire crew.  _x000D_

Event
While performing offloading operations and during the hoisting of a basket of scaffold materials off the back deck of a marine vessel (MV) the load contacted a rental generator and damaged the door and glass of the inspection window.

Event Description - Sequence / Timeline
On June 13th at approximately 09:30HRS crane operations were being conducted to offload materials from the marine vessel (MV) Elise Mary and set items onto the EI 252 G facility.
. The first lift, a 5'x5'x4' cargo basket (500 lbs.) was made according to plan without any issues.
. At 09:45HRS the second lift, a 6'x12'x4' scaffolding basket (11,600 lbs.) was attached, and the crane operator was given the signal to hoist the load.
o When hoisting the scaffolding basket, the load has been reported to have moved approximately 2-3 FT in the direction of the rental generator. The corner of the basket contacted the inspection window section of the generator door causing the glass to break.
o After contact, the crane operator raised the boom of the crane maneuvering the load away from the generator and it was lifted from the MV and set on the platform with no further incident.
. At 14:39HRS Port Captain with GOL addressed and sent an email to inform various representatives with GOL that MV Captain had called and reported the vessel's rental generator was damaged during a lift. The email identified that generator door and glass is damaged. Unit and all gauges work as directed without damage to engine or generator.
. At 20:00HRS the crane operator returned to EI 252 I where he was informed of the damage reported to have resulted because of load contact.
. At 21:56HRS an event to support the incident was generated within AOL's SEMS Portal and AOL management were collectively notified according to the system.
June 14th at 08:41HRS an email that contained GOL's Equipment Damage Report and a photograph of the generator's inspection window and door paint damage was received.
o Damage photograph received is labeled as (A.) within the photograph section of the attached report.

Event Consequences
Replacement of the glass for the inspection window of the generator estimated at a value of $300.00.

There were no personnel injuries or environmental impacts as a result of this event.

Root Cause
Marine lifting condition - The nature of the dynamic lift made from the marine vessel by the crane caused a minimal amount of horizontal movement of the load.

Contributing Cause
. There was little space between the position of rental generator in comparison to the material basket.
. Due to the weight and size of the load, and glass window being fragile, any minor contact made between the two pieces of equipment would very likely result in some degree of breakage. Considering the amount of damage sustained by the glass, it was determined that there was a very minimal amount of contact made.
. Inadequate room near the load for the rigger on the MV to effectively utilize the tagline in a way that would prevent contact of the two pieces equipment.

On 7/1/22 @ 11:15 am a radar antenna unit was damaged while preparing to lift the unit with the aux hoist of the platform crane. 10' Nylon straps were installed on the unit in a choked configuration before the retaining bolts were removed to allow the antenna to be lifted off the base. The rigger / signaler gave the crane operator instructions to hoist up enough to take some slack out of the straps before removing the final retaining bolts from the antenna. As the crane operator hoisted up the straps became tight before the hoist was stopped causing the fiberglass housing on the antenna to crack. The job was stopped and all parties discussed the cause of the incident._x000D_
_x000D_
Findings:_x000D_
The cause of the incident - The crane operator was hoisting up to remove slack from the straps, due to a delay in the electric over hydraulic controls the hoist was not disengaged before the strap tightened on the fiberglass housing causing damage. _x000D_
_x000D_
Learnings / Prevention _x000D_
- Basket hitch rigging should have been used instead of choking the straps._x000D_
-Longer straps would give more clearance / slack to allow more room for error as well as better depth perception for the crane operator._x000D_
-Cribbing material should be installed for protection between the rigging and thin fiberglass face of the antenna._x000D_

Final:  July 1, 2022, at 09:15, during facility safe out operations, when attempting to land a grocery box on the facilities' main deck, the load inadvertently contacted an existing storage diesel tank.  Doing so, the diesel tank's attached sight glass was struck causing the unit's bottom brass nipple to fail at its threaded connection. This resulted in fluid leakage (diesel) into the unit's containment pan (about two gallons) and an estimated 1/2 liter on the main deck.  Crane Operations were stopped, the leakage was immediately secured with a plumber's plug and the released fluid was removed from the containment pan as well as the main deck cleaned. There were no injuries nor any breach of GOM waters by this fluid.

An incident investigation revealed the following:

Contributing cause(s):
a)  Storage Diesel Tank (being within direct path of trans versing the lift) contained an attached site glass that protruded above the unit's top surface creating an at-risk condition of exposure.
b)  The 1" brass connector fitting does not have the integrity strength of a typical carbon steel /or stainless steel fitting that could have better absorbed the impact of contact by the load to the top of the sight-glass tube.
c)  Site glass was poorly secured at the top of the storage diesel tank (wire clasp around a hose reel bracket) allowing bending of the tubing to a point of stress failure at the bottom connection point with the tank's drain connection.
d)  Attending Rigger did not recognize the lack of clearance space between the diesel tank and grocery box and/or amount of residual load movement when the Crane Operator stopped lowering the boom on signaled command.

Root cause:  Though the Crane Operator was able to transition the load over & beyond the existing storage diesel tank, he did not allow enough clearance space between the load and tank to avoid contact caused by residual load Swing and/or motion when lowering the crane boom was stopped.

Full Description:
CI (crane operator) was attempting a vertical lift on a 10,000-pound riser with the load line. The load was to be transition to the horizontal position with the load balanced between the auxiliary and load lines. The auxiliary line was hoisted down the base of the riser. The base of the riser was then choked with a 2-inch 2 ply synthetic strap. The crane operator was instructed to hoist up on the auxiliary line to bring the load horizontal. As he was hoisting up the 2- inch two ply synthetic sling parted. 

The load was 2 foot off the deck when the strap parted, the load did not hit the deck and was suspended by the load line; no injury to personnel and no equipment was damaged. The crane has been inspected by a Qualified Crane Inspector and all found to be nominal.

Immediate Corrective Actions:
Ensured all were safe. Inspected crane for any damage. Lowered riser to deck using wire rope slings.

Recurrence Prevention Corrective Actions:
Woven synthetic (e.g. nylon) slings are not to be used for general rigging. Rigger will communicate sling ratings, inspection dates and condition to crane operator and receive acceptance of rigging prior to lifting load. Reinforce importance of SWA in prevention of incidents.

At 10:05 AM on 8-10-2022, Operations Personnel were informed of a sheen near the north east hull column.  Operations personnel responded to the area to investigate where the was coming from.  Personnel began checking the Produced Water System and the Emergency Sump System attempting the locate the source of the sheen.  Personnel went down to the top of the north east hull column and noticed a tarp in the area that had oil on it.  The personnel began checking the area and found a liquid dripping coming from above there location.  As the personnel continued trying to locate the source, they found a leak in a process piping segment.  Immediate Action: At this time, the control room and OIM was notified of the leak and the facility ESD was initiated.  The OIM also initiated a full ICS muster at this time. Before and during the event, the leak did not activate any gas detection systems as the leak was small.  There was no gas cloud and or excessive liquid release.  No hot work being performed and full production was online when the event occurred including DVA, Subsea, and Water Injector Wells. There are no injuries associated with this event and all personnel responded as per their training. The estimated volume of the sheen was .041968 gallons of crude oil.  Upon a closer look, the leak developed on / near a corrosion cell on the piping.  The size of the failure is estimated to be very small.  The piping segment which the failure occurred is isolated and not in service at the time of the event. The Facility is currently shut-in pending repairs. Corrective Actions: Facility was ESD's and Blown Down. Tapped blind flanges were installed on the affected piping to completely isolate the section of the piping where the leak occurred. Estimate cost of repair is unknown at this time.  It is believed that the isolated valves may be leaking internally but investigation is ongoing.  Full muster was completed and all personnel were accounted for.  Attached you will find the POB list and a photo of the pipe where the small leak occurred.

Description of Incident: Well work over crew was bleeding down the tubing in order to install a one-way check valve into the tubing string. During this operation low level LEL gas alarm was activated at the shaker pit. The peak reading was 23% and quickly fell back to zero. All personnel mustered in the Safe Briefing Area and all were accounted for without issue. The safety technician donned breathing apparatus and investigated the area. Upon arrival no gas was detected, and the sensor was reading zero. All Clear was announced and crews returned to work.

Questions were generated by BSEE and responses are from DCOR:

1.	The WAR report covering 8/20 mentioned "observation of oil and gas at the shakers." Yet no mention of the muster either in the text or in the significant well events.  Why is that?
a.	This event did not fit in any of the "significant well events" boxes.  The Incident was reported through the separate incident reporting function and so was not included in the WAR - we can add this to the WAR comments for the day on this well and future events.  
 
2.	When the incident was reported, the event was initially described as a 2 minute gas release for testing of the gas alarms.  Would you agree that statement was not accurate?
a.	The HSE on call individual failed to gather and confirm information regarding the incident prior to making the initial verbal report to BSEE. This led to an inaccurate initial verbal report.  The testing of the sensors was completed over an hour prior to the low LEL alarm being activated. The testing of the sensors is conducted using a calibration cap and 50% CH4 calibration gas with nitrogen balance. 
 
3.	If the crew was bleeding down the tubing why wasn't it routed to the production system and the gas processed or flared?
a.	During workover (and drilling) operations, fluid volume management and control is critical, so fluid movement is to and from the mud tanks/pits to allow for visual monitoring. Fluids (liquid and gas) are routed to the production system when initially bleeding off the well and turning it over to a known weight fluid to determine workover fluid weight requirements.  The well is disconnected from the production system when it is set up for rig operations.  The system used during rig operations includes a "gas buster" to allow gas associated with fluids circulated back from the well to be removed and safely vented away from personnel.  The piping allows for either the casing OR tubing to be lined up to utilize the gas buster.  In this case, we were bleeding gas off the casing side through the gas buster but despite attempting to pump down the tubing to push the gas to the casing, we still ended up with a small gas bubble in the tubing that we had to bleed off directly to the mud pits.  
 
4.	How do you plan to prevent miss-reporting in the future?
a.	DCOR is conducting a refresher training for all on-call personnel. This refresher will focus on gathering correct information as the potential need to involve other members of the HSE prior to making agency notification. The goal of this training is to avoid future misunderstandings during the agency notification process. 
 
5.	Do you have a plan to deal with gas and/or oil when performing "bleed down" operations in the future?
a.	As discussed above, we will continue to conduct operations to ensure the safety of all personnel on the platform.  During this operation, we maintained control of the well and bleeding gas off the tubing allowed us to install the back flow preventer in the tubing so that gas could be controlled and bled off through the casing side for the rest of the trip in to TD.  
 
6.	Did you consider any other options in your corrective action in the "Muster incident report"?  If so what were they and what reasoning was used to eliminate them?
a.	As stated in the above responses, the work over crew had taken steps to ensure the work being done was completed in a manner that ensures the safety of the personnel on board. We chose the corrective action as it was submitted to address a gap in our training and station bills. We hope to bolster the guidance for responding to a combustible gas alarm, similar to how our station bill covers the different responses for low and high toxic gas alarms.

Update 09/26/22: Please see below Root Causes and Corrective Actions provided by Helix.

Root Causes: 
.	The design of the torpedo guide does not allow for the guide clamp door to be secured in the open position. As the torpedo guide was hoisted it became unlevel allowing the door to swing freely.  
.	The JSA used for the task was incomplete, the JSA for Installing / Removing the Torpedo Guide only captured the task steps, hazards and controls for installation of the torpedo guide. Task steps for removing the torpedo guide is not addressed in the JSA.
.	Human Factor - The body placement near the torpedo guide door and cross beam was not identified as a potential pinch point. The torpedo guide historically has been manoeuvred with a hands on approach with no previous issues. 

Recommendations:
.	Recommendation to paint/stencil specific NO-GO Zones to highlight line of fire hazard in relation to the torpedo guide door and cross beam to make personnel aware of pinch/crush point.
.	Recommendation to create a task specific JSA for the removal of the torpedo guide. 
.	Engineering solution - Recommendation to install certified lifting points and procure designated lifting gear. Installation would consist of installing pad eyes at specific points as engineered for proper lifting of the torpedo guide in regards to levelness. 
.	Engineering solution - Recommendation to modify torpedo guide clamp door so that when the door is in the open position it can be secured to prevent movement. 
.	Engineering solution - Recommendation to evaluate feasibility and application to use mechanical devices i.e. tugger and snatch blocks, sand line crane or other rigging configurations for manoeuvring torpedo guide when suspended.

At approximately 12:30pm on 9/29/22 an incident occurred during lifting and hoisting operations on the starboard laydown area of the Turritella. A portion of the LER HVAC system (AHU cabinet 1 C) was being lifted out of its shipping container and onto the deck. When the load was being hoisted, it moved towards the side of the shipping container, struck the side of it and rolled on its side. According to the Crane Operator, the load was not being swung by the boom as this excursion took place. Dynamic movement of the FPSO was noted from the Bosun (DSP) as the load shifted. 

The unit was slung via its engineered lifting points designed for installation on the roof of the LER building. These lifting points are at the bottom of the unit, making the lifts center of gravity above the lifting points. This allowed for the lift to roll over on its side instead of just striking the edge and remaining upright. The unit was immediately up righted and set on the deck.  There were two tag lines attached to the load on the opposite corners. Radio communication and hand signals were being used and this was not a blind lift. 

Immediate Actions: Crane operations were shut down and the event was relayed to leadership. The A/C equipment had superficial damage that may be cosmetic only. Crane being operated by a Sparrow Crane Operator as normal complement of the crew. Crane operations were paused while load assessed. Estimated cost of A/C equipment is less than $10,000. While drilling ahead on Nov 16th 2022 with a 15.2ppg surface mud weight / 16.2ppg downhole equivalent mud weight at 25,000ft MD / 24,905 ft. TVD at the suspected base of salt exit, an influx was observed on the MPD flow-out system.  The MPD system was put into "flow control" mode to arrest the influx, however, the intensity was too great for the response time of the MPD choke.  Due to the increase in pressure, the MPD system pressure relief valves (PRV) opened at 1,300 psi and 12 bbls of 15.2ppg synthetic based mud was diverted through the dedicated MPD overboard line.  The well was then shut-in on the upper annular and secured.  A total of 37 bbl influx was observed before the decision was made to shut-in on the upper annular, and additional 22bbl while closing the annular (Total influx volume: 59bbl).  Drill pipe and casing pressure were monitored and climbed to 1580psi before leveling off.   With the pressure stabilized,  the influx  has begun to be circulated out at 40 strokes per minute.

Full Description: Offloading diesel tote tank from the M/V Mr. Mag. Deckhand hooked up the load and signaled to pick-up on load. The sling caught under the "snap ring" (lid locking ring bolt) causing the lid to detach. They immediately set the load back down to have it reattached, but it popped off again when second lift was attempted. The load was pulled from the boat slow and easy. No fuel spilled.

Due to sea state, and the potential for sloshing of fuel out of the opening, a decision was made to bring to tote up to the platform. Boat sent a undamaged lid from and empty tote up to platform allowing the sealing of the tote on a stable deck. No fuel was spilled during the process, and no fuel was found on the top or outside of the tote.

Recurrence Prevention Corrective Actions: Rigger needs to request slow lifting to be able to check that sling if free of components before full load tension is applied to load. Refer to FMOG Safety Alert on tote transfers. Safety Alert shared with all crews on current GoM projects.

On 12/11/2022, the drill crew was increasing tension on the drilling riser guide wire in preparation to begin riser pulling operations. As the tension on the guide wire approached 12,500 lbs., the 22 mm guide wire on the east side parted at turndown sheave and fell 3,258' to the sea floor. The remaining tail end backlashed into the winch with the tail landing on the deck in front of the control panel. In the investigation, further testing of the guide wire winches determined that the load cells were out of calibration by approximately 40k lbs. In actuality, the weight being applied to the guide wire was 52k lbs. rather than 12.5k lbs. as thought. The resulting winch pressure caused the guide wire to part. Operations were paused and management notified of the incident. 

Updated 12/27/ 22: The operator of the winch was qualified and has been trained by the mechanics which read and understands the Operators manual and does the repairs and maintenance on the winches. Operator knew how much to pull during this operation as it is posted on the winch and is in the Shell Olympus PROS Manual. Operator did not read the manufacturer's instruction before operating the winch, but the tension weight and low- and high-level weights were posted on the winch. If the power outages on the facility prior to the incident had anything to do with the system being out of calibration is a possibility, but power outages did not affect our subsequent outage.
K = 1000, 12.5k lbs. = 12500 LBS, 52k lbs. = 52000 LBS.
What is the max weight this winch can pull?  68000 lbs.
What is the breaking strength of this 22mm cable that was being used? 105,000 lbs.
Was everyone involved with this operation on the Job Safety Analysis? Yes.
If a Compass card was used is their documentation about what was discussed? No not required.
What caused the load cells to be out of calibration? Unknown currently.
Why was there an issue with getting the right amount of air pressure to the winch? It had adequate air pressure to operate as design.
What are the corrective actions? We recalibrated both winches, repaired constant tension mode, laminated operating procedure, weight of cable when on bottom with slack in cable, low- and high-tension alarm set point and constant tension weight. Also, the procedure to use if loss of power occurs to set winches back to correct tension.
Will there be an investigation done? Yes, initial findings have been sent.

At approximately 2245 on 12-20-2022, the Drill Crew was laying out 6 5/8" drill pipe on the Aux. At the time of the incident, the AD was coming up with a stand of drill pipe using the mousehole in manual mode. The PLS and PRS were both on the stand of pipe. No injuries resulted from this incident. An investigation has been initiated and is ongoing.

Summary from TOI TopSet report:

SP 93 A Compressor shutdown down due to PSH 3rd stage and as operator arrived to the compressor, a small flame was witnessed on insulation around the turbo area. once the flame was identified the flame was extinguished using a near-by water hose and the compressor was left shutdown. there were no injuries, environmental impact, or damages resulting from the flame. verbal and email notification was made of the flame at 06:50. 

Mechanics were dispatched to the facility to investigate, troubleshoot, and make repairs. below is the narrative from mechanic's report on cause of the flame, items checked, and repairs made: 

Items found; 
*The left bank air filter was plugged which caused a vacuum in the crankcase drawing oil into air filter causing saturation with oil on the outside, preventing air flow to the turbo charger.
*The exhaust piping had become miss-aligned with the engine expansion joint which caused a wide gap in the exhaust system.
*The exhaust venture piping was cracked due to the misalignment.
*Oil from the air filter dripped onto this area resulting in the small flame observed 
*The turbochargers spin freely and did not appear to have leaking oil seals or damaged turbine fins
*No wet oil residue was found in the exhaust Y-connection going to the exhaust pipe.

Actions taken; 
-Changed the air filters
-Changed the venture piping
-Changed the expansion joint and aligned it.
-Once repairs were made compressor engine was started to inspect repairs and no issues were identified.

At approximately 18:50HRS; the M/V deckhand hooked the auxiliary line of the crane to a four-barrel drum rack (1,000 lbs.) that contained (4) empty DOT Drums and then provided a hoist hand signal to the crane operator. At approximately 22:15, a BOP test mandrel fell to the main deck while performing a BOP chamber test with the middle pipe rams. The test mandrel was lifted with the Starboard Forward Crane and placed inside the BOP. Once in the proper position inside the BOP, the middle pipe rams were partial closed around the mandrel to ensure proper placement then the crane operator was instructed to lower the mandrel a few inches. The middle pipe rams were then closed with 500 psi (max closing pressure 3000 psi), at this time the crane weight indicator showed a reduction in weight from 1,000 lbs. to 400 lbs. The test mandrel and crane stayed in these positions until the test was complete. Once the middle pipe ram pressure was bled down the mandrel slid through the BOP and landed on the main deck. 

The total distance traveled was roughly 22 feet from the middle pipe ram to the main deck; 8 feet was outside the BOP from the wellhead connector to the test stump base. 

The mandrel was lifted into position using a 4-part shackle, which the banksman stated had all four parts were installed. The shackle body remained connected to the crane, and the nut and pin were recovered from inside the BOP using a magnet, but the cotter pin has not been found (search on-going). 

No personnel were in the area as it was designated a red zone with barrier tape and signage as well as an announcement made to inform personnel of pressure test and working at heights. Closest person to the object was inside the subsea workshop.

At approximately 11:45 hours, on Sunday, February 12,2023, a general alarm was sounded due to a smoke alarm notice which came from the HPU Subsea. Non-essential personnel were directed to their muster stations.  At approximately 11:51 hours, notification was received that it was a false alarm. The smoke alarm activated during routine maintenance operations. At the time of the event, Santorini Subsea was conducting maintenance on the Riser Tensioners. Operational procedures require that the Tensioners are lowered and drained of oil (Houghton Safe 273). This oil is then filtered. The oil is cleaned, and the Tensioners are refilled using the same oil. There are 2 valves located at the bottom of the Tensioners that are opened when adding oil. Once the MRT#4 was filled and calibrated, Subsea lifted the Tensioners without closing these valves. This resulted in pressurized air pushing the fluid out of the Tensioners and back into the oil holding tank. With the resulted oil volume and air pressure involved, the fluid rapidly discharged back into the tank. This created a release of atomized oil vapors which set off the smoke alarm. There were no personnel injuries or environmental damage.

At approximately 18:20 hours on Monday, February 13, 2023, the ZZZ-9200 Power Generator shutdown. Mechanics responded to the generator enclosure and bypassed the enclosure's fire system in order to safely enter the enclosure. Mechanics inspected the engine's fuel filters, replaced the fuel filters, re-started the engine, and observed the engine run without a load for approximately 30 minutes. Approximately 5 minutes after loading the engine, the mechanics smelled and then saw smoke coming from the insulation on the left side turbocharger and associated air filter. When the insulation was removed, sparks and a small flame was observed. The fire was immediately extinguished with a handheld dry chemical fire extinguisher. The area was also soaked with firewater to ensure that the fire was completely extinguished.

After disassembly and investigation to determine the cause of the fire, it was found that the air side of the left bank turbocharger had failed. The fins of the turbocharger made contact with the air side housing, causing sparks, which ignited the associated air filter.

There were no injuries, no pollution, and only minor damage to equipment. The turbocharger and air filter were replaced at an estimated cost of $8,000.

This facility was shut-in prior to and during this incident.

A load of 30-foot-long drill pipe contacted the handrail of a portable aluminum gangway and the handrails of the marine vessel Connor Anthony during vessel-to-vessel backloading operations. 

Event Description - Sequence / Timeline

On February 26, 2023, vessel-to-vessel backloading operations were underway utilizing the EC1100 crane of the lift boat Seacor Hawk. 

.	At approximately 05:50HRS; the marine vessel (M/V) Connor Anthony was positioned to receive a load of 30-foot-long drill pipe from the lift boat (LB) Seacor Hawk which was elevated at Main Pass 120 CA. 
.	As the load of pipe was lowered and approximately 8FT from the supply deck the M/V surged astern. 
.	When the M/V surged astern the load moved towards the M/V and off path of the desired landing area which caused the load to set on the top of a handrail of an aluminum gangway that was stowed near the forward crash rail on the supply deck. 
.	In an effort to prevent further damage; the crane operator began to hoist the load and swing the boom, but the M/V continued to move in reverse causing the load to contact forward crash rail and then the handrails on the cabin of the M/V. 
.	The crane operator continued to swing the boom to get the load free of the M/V's cabin handrails and the M/V stopped reversing and the load was lifted clear of the M/V.
.	The M/V then established a position where the load could safely be received, and the crane operator placed the load on the supply deck of the vessel without further incident.   
.	Once backloading operations were concluded the crane operator reported the event to the Person-in-Charge (PIC) on the platform and then the Field Foreman and AOL's incident reporting requirements were initiated which included reporting the incident to the Field Foreman, Production Forman, and HSE Coordinator for investigation. 

Event Consequences

1.	Aluminum handrail of portable gangway was bent downward slightly.  
2.	Surface paint of the M/V was scuffed on the handrails and forward crash rail where contact was made. 
3.	M/V handrail was bent inward and a weld was broken at a connection point. 

There were no environmental impacts, or injuries to personnel because of this event.

At 16:10 on 02/26/2023 the engine for the west side crane overheated causing damage to the engines turbo compressor, the emergency shut-off mechanism and rubber boots. 

The crane operator had had finished backloading 26" drive pipe onto the M/V HOS Commander, he was coming up with the main line when he noticed the reading on the engine water gauge was reading hot. The crane operator shut down the crane and called for the crane mechanic. When the crane mechanic arrived, he saw steam from the engine and smoke from the air filter box. He removed the air filter cover and found the air filter smoldering. (No flames). He removed the air filter and used a half bottle of water nearby to impede any further smoldering. The crane was placed out of service. 

Sequence of Events
1. 16:08 - Nabors crane operator finishes backloading the last of the 26" drive pipe (11,250lbs per joint) to the M/V HOS Commander with west side platform crane. While hoisting up on the main block crane operator noticed high engine temperature. He shut down the crane and called for the crane mechanic.

At this point the only people at the crane were crane mechanic and crane operator. The crane mechanic opened the air filter box and removed the smoldering air filter. The crane mechanic then used a nearby water bottle on the air filter to halt further smoldering.

It was found that the return coolant line had developed a leak, draining the coolant reservoir. This in turn caused the overheating issue, subsequently overheating the turbo, and air filter box.

ST 51 CJ Lift Boat "Lacie G. Eymard" Generator Alternator Belt Failure - March 04, 2023, Incident Date

Event Summary
On March 04, 2023, at approximately 07:45 HRS, the Starboard Generator shut down. Upon the L/B Lacie G. Eymard Captains' arrival to the fiddley at the upper engine room, light smoke and a heavy burnt smell were observed. The captain immediately sounded the general alarm to muster all 3rd party personnel and informed the Vessel crew of the smoke and burnt smell. The Vessel's crew had readied and stretched the port side fire hose and closed the upper engine room door and engine room vents while the cook conducted roll call at the muster station. Before the captain opened the fiddley engine room door, he felt the door for heat with the back of his hand. No heat was felt, so the fiddley door was cautiously opened, and the starboard engine room was assessed. Smoke was observed from the generator alternator's belt. No flames were present, so the vents were opened back up, and the port generator was put online for the blowers to air out the engine room to change out the starboard generator's alternator. Captain deemed the area and situation to be safe and to resume work.

Investigation Summary
The investigation determined the following contributing factors:
.	Starboard Generator's Alternator bearing seized, locking up and cracking housing; this caused the drive belt to degrade, resulting in smoke accumulation within the engine room.
.	All 3rd party personnel aboard dawned Type 1 PFDs upon hearing the general alarm and congregated at the muster station. Non-essential personnel roll call was then completed. Captain arrived after clearing the engine room, proceeded with his crew's roll call, and explained the current problem and that it was resolved. Captain deemed the situation safe, and all clear was given. Normal duties resumed. 

Corrective Actions
.	The port generator was utilized to engage engine room blowers to ventilate the engine room. 
.	The starboard generator alternator and belt were then replaced. Estimated costs: $175. Spare alternator/belts were available onboard and replaced following All Clear from Captain of Vessel by Captian/First Mate. 

**There were no injuries, fires, or environmental impacts due to this event.**

INITIAL INVESTIGATION: Two large electrical transformers (3121 and 3122) were taken out of service and loaded into a 10'x30' basket (GJ016) utilizing the East Crane. The transformers were secured using rachet straps to keep the load from shifting during transport prior to the lift being executed. On the night of March 6th, the M/V backed into C-Port #3 to initiate the offloading process. At that time, the Captain informed C-Logistics Team that one of the electrical transformers were leaking transformer oil (Manufacturer DSI; Product Name: Beta Fluid; Product Description: Fire Resistant Transformer Oil) to the basket and to the back deck of the Squall. The M/V deck crew had not noticed anything until they went onto the deck to tie up the vessel upon arrival in the slip. The source was identified, electrical transformer tank reservoir through the damaged insulator (see pictures attached to this IRIS Report). Absorbent pads and other spill clean-up material was used to keep the transformer oil from spreading and potentially entering the GoM.

It is unknown when it was damaged, but current evidence indicates that either the insulator was damaged by the 4-part wire rope sling or a load came into contact during the backload process by another load being set next to the electrical transformer basket. It is estimated, approximately 10 gallons of transformer oil leaked onto the deck of the boat and to the basket.

Description: At 05:30 hrs on 03/31/2023, our GC613A facility had a gas detector (GD-1702) that sounded the 10% LEL alarm (alarm only, no shut-in). At this time all personnel began mustering at their assigned location, with a full muster called at 05:35 hrs. The fire team was sent to investigate the gas alarm at 05:40 hrs. The team, once arriving in the area, determined that only gas detector (GD-1702) was alarming. The fire team then began to investigate the source of the gas. After a short investigation the team reported that the Cross Exchanger HBG-1525 was leaking oil and gas from the bottom of the unit. The fire team isolated Cross Exchanger HBG-1525 and the leak was stopped. The Cross Exchanger HBG-1525 is over a solid containment deck and all fluid from the leak was contained and cleaned up after the all clear was given at 05:55 hrs. The facility was shut in by operations personnel.

Our investigation into this incident shows that cooler than normal process liquids, caused hydrates in the system, which led to false readings in the level bridles for both the Inlet and IP Separators. This caused both separators to dump gas out of the liquid outlets (gas blow-by). This sent gas through the Cross Exchanger, cooling the plate's rubber gaskets. When the gaskets cooled, they expanded, and a leak developed.

Currently the facility is shut-in awaiting repairs to be made to the Cross Exchanger. Path forward is to get a crew out to remove the plates and then send them in to be repaired. Once the plates have been repaired, we will have them sent back to the facility with a crew to have them re-installed. The estimated cost to repair the Cross Exchanger is $180,000.00.

Please share investigation report, if any: Nor formal investigation report was completed due to severity and potential not meeting Shell's criteria for a formal root cause / causal. However, an abbreviated investigation was conducted, listed below.

1. Why did the Battery Load bank fail, emitting smoke, during testing?
Due to incorrect wiring - 240 VDC battery bank was connected to 120 VDC load cell (150 VDC max). 
The incorrect wiring caused electrical current to increase and resulted the thermal event at the load cell.
2.Why incorrect wiring was applied?
A. The vendor procedure omitted details to verify wiring configuration is correctly matching the test load cell to the battery bank.
B. The terminals of the load bank were not labeled. There are maximum voltage labels on the load bank terminals.
C. Batteries (all cells) are normally connected to the load bank. This is true that most batteries are below 120 VDC and connected in whole to the load bank, but this battery is 240 VDC and must be split in half to be tested. The technician had come across this before.
3. Why was the important detail was omitted in the procedure?
1. The vendor procedure highly depends on their technician's skill and knowledge to allow the flexibility to use the same procedures for different configuration which allow room for human error.
What is the solution(s):
To prevent this type of failure in the future, a step is being added in the procedure to verify the voltage of the battery under test and the configuration used. (Implemented by vendor).

At 2:26 pm, two expansion joints on FGC # 2 developed stress cracks allowing exhaust gas to accumulate in the vicinity of a nearby TSE (Zone 1) resulting in a total platform shut in. What Happened?
At approximately 08:22 on April 2nd while operating in a Split-Bus configuration (i.e., 3 independent, high voltage switchboards), the Starboard high voltage switchboard experienced a partial blackout due to low voltage from the online Diesel Generator (DG) #2. An automatic "All-Start" command was initiated due to loss of voltage. Subsequently, DG #1 started but failed to connect to the starboard bus, due to a sync failure caused by the voltage deviation caused by DG #2. As a result of the starboard engine room blackout, thrusters T2 and T4 dropped offline, and there was a loss of power to several critical drill floor systems (including the topdrive and drawworks). The rig was able to maintain station with four (4) thrusters with no issue.

Initial troubleshooting discovered a failed Phase Monitoring Relay inhibited the ability to close the ship's service transformer that supplies power to the auxiliaries. Continued inspection identified that DG #2 had a break in one of the windings on the exciter (i.e., armature winding). Once DG#2 was taken offline, DG #1 was restarted and placed online powering the starboard bus with no issue.

Event Timeline
20:22 DG #2 voltage alarm
20:23 DG #2 Automatic Voltage Regulator (AVR) alarm
20:24 DG #1 Sync Failure but running offline (Other two Switchboards had both engines running after "All-Start")
20:31 DG #1 Connected
20:41 DG #2 Shutdown
01:00 Check control system and change out Phase Monitoring Relay for Pre Mag-Distribution panel.
03:00 Failed Relay replaced; reset drilling equipment and bring T2 & T4 back online (Starboard bus). Perform Isolations in order
to continue troubleshooting & diagnostics of DG #2 generator (windings / diodes / rectifiers).


Early Learnings:

Subsequent Findings and Actions:
. The break in the winding appears to have initiated the failure of DG #2 to supply the designed output voltage and subsequent internal arcing resulted in voltage spikes that led to the failure of the Phase Monitoring Relay. This failed relay and the voltage imbalance from DG #2 inhibited the ability to close the ship service transformer and prevented DG #1 from syncing after "All-Start".
. DG #2 is temporarily out of commission, until the exciter is replaced, or rebuilt. The rig will remain in a Split- (Open) Bus configuration. An operational hazard assessment will be required prior to going to a 2+1 bus configuration for any for any Split-Bus deviation request, outside those necessitated by the Well Specific Operating Criteria (WSOC). A Common-(Closed) Bus arrangement is not recommended under any circumstances.

A contractor coatings tech discovered smoke coming from the control relay on the water softener connected to the UHP water system.  The relay was found to be in an open position with the board exposed. The tech disconnected the relay from the extension cord connecting it to the Titan power system. The equipment and the control relay had been inspected at the same time the day prior and had not been open and exposed. A small amount of water was found inside the control relay. The water softener was not running at the time the relay was discovered but it was connected to Titan power. There were no visible flames, but there was minor charring on the circuit board. No injuries.
The relay was immediately disconnected from power. The water softener unit will be replaced. The replacement water softener and new control relay will be inspected upon arrival at Titan and the control relay will be secured to protect against damage and exposure to the elements.

The FSV was conducting cargo operations at Olympus. A tote tank was lowered to the deck and landed by vessel crew, upon disconnecting the cargo hook from a tote tank. When the hook was disconnected, it drifted away from the tote tank with the crewmember toward starboard side of vessel. The crane hook snagged the lower strap on the work vest (PFD) worn by the crewmember (Deck Hand/ Rigger). Movement of the vessel due to sea states caused the crewmember to shift 2-3 feet across the deck while being lifted a few inches off the deck. The designated signal person called all-stop and the crewmember was able to free the strap from the hook. No injuries occurred during the incident. The vessel crew conducted a safety stand-down. The crew held discussions and reviewed previously completed JSA to identify any further mitigations in place to continue operations. BGOS management respectfully requested that the crew of the M/V take time to host an action review meeting once in port to reflect on the event and share thoughts about prevention.

The Affected Individual (AI) experienced a rupture of his Right Bicep Tendon while manually handling and maneuvering an empty wooden pallet. 

Event Description - Sequence / Timeline
On April 09, 2023, at approximately 10:30HRS, the AI was preparing discarded items for onshore disposal. The AI was engaged in organizing the contents within a cargo basket (4'x8'). Inside of the cargo basket there was an empty wooden pallet (4'x4'in size and weighting approximately 35-50lbs) lying horizontal on the floor of the basket. The AI leaned from his waist to the interior of the basket from the edge of the basket to stand the pallet up vertically against the side of the basket's wall. In this position the AI exerted physical motion from his elbow through the upper portion of his right arm and through this generated effort to lift the pallet he felt what he described as a "pop" followed by a burning sensation. 
. AI immediately reported his condition to Area 2's Field Foreman and AOL's incident reporting requirements were initiated which included reporting the event to the Area's Production Foreman, and the HSE Coordinator.
. Aircraft was contacted to transport the Field Medic to assess the AI's condition and following the field assessment the AI was transported onshore for a further medical evaluation and treatment if needed.
. 14:40HRS Aircraft departed EI 330D with an onshore destination onshore
. 17:30HRS AI was medically evaluated at a preferred occupational clinic of his employer, but a definitive soft tissue diagnosis required magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
. April 10th, 13:45HRS underwent an MRI. 
. April 12th, 15:30HRS an orthopedic specialist provided final diagnosis. 
. April 18th, AI underwent surgery and is currently absent while in a recovery status. 

Event Consequences
1. Musculoskeletal injury requiring evacuation for medical evaluation, condition determination, and treatment. 
o Diagnosis: Ruptured Right Bicep Tendon

While performing annual inspections on turbine generator starter cubicles, an electrician found evidence of charring and overheating inside the lube oil tank heater cubicle. The source was traced to the contactor load side terminals. Charred wiring and melted plastic from the contactor was visible from inside the panel. The breakers for this task were isolated and locked out prior to opening the panel doors to inspect. No visible flame was observed and no personnel were injured. 

Final Report:

The contactor was replaced and returned to service.

Response to RFI:

-Please attach all pictures associated with this incident.
Hess: Attached
-Was a muster required?
Hess: No
-What was the associated cost of damage? 
Hess: ~$300
-Please provide the component identification for the Turbine Generator? 
Hess: MCC cubicle
-Which area of which deck did the fire take place? 
Hess: Inside an MCC cubicle. There was no visible flame, only evidence of (melted wiring insulation/carbonization) overheating. Motor Control Center (MCC) is a pressurized building. This did not occur out on the deck in electrically classified areas.
-What was found to be the cause of the fire? 
Hess: The cubicle had bad starter due to a loose connection at terminal block. The cubicle was replaced and a new starter was ordered to put back in stock.
-What are the corrective actions to prevent future reoccurrence? 
Hess: This was part of a planned inspection/preventative maintenance that occurs on frequency. Terminal connections become loose over time and are inspected periodically, as in this case, to correct deficiencies.

At approximately 11:00 an inspection by an electrician in the maintenance team was conducted. The HMI in the control room gave the fault code of 64 (No Device Power) and after cycling the breaker the fault cleared. The Mechanics went out to the Air Compressor skid and had the CRO place it into Lag to make it start, as soon as the Starter closed the breaker immediately tripped and the Device Net showed a fault of 64, (No Device Power). When the breaker was cycled the first time it did not feel like the breaker was tripped. An LRP permit was issued to troubleshoot it was determined that the motor had experienced a fault to ground internally. The Motor was Megged from the Starter in MCC-3153 Phase to ground for all 3 Phases @500v and read 0.00ohms. Opened the Motor Termination Box and noticed a lot of soot on the Motor Leads and could smell that it was failed. De-terminated the motor leads and Megged the Motor and got the same 0.0ohm readings to ground. Megged the cable from the Motor back to the Starter in MCC-3153 and read 550m ohms, showing the cable was ok. 

Evidence of thermal effects were seen in the form of soot in the termination box when the motor power wires were disconnected to ensure proper isolation. 

Cost of damage...Estimated at $15,000 for the motor to be rebuilt.

Additional Questions:

1. What caused the apparent small incipient fire ...The motor windings seem to have shorted to ground. The motor will be removed and sent in for Root Cause Failure Analysis to determine the exact cause.

Event 
The Affected Individual (AI) was getting onto a rigid type of offshore transfer device (OTD) for transfer from the marine vessel (M/V) to the platform and wave action caused the M/V to subside between the wave crest and through approximately 3' from beneath the basket. When the vessel rose back to sea level, the supply deck contacted the underside of the OTD.

Event Description - Sequence / Timeline
On April 28, 2023, at approximately 07:20HRS, Personnel Transfer Operations were underway between the facility crane and the marine vessel (M/V). 
. Just prior to the event, the platform crane had lowered the rigid type of offshore transfer device (OTD) to the supply deck of the M/V. The OTD was received by a deckhand of the M/V crew and personnel were offloaded. 
. On the second transfer, the AI and two other persons were staged to board the OTD and once readied for transfer they would be hoisted onto the platform. 
o Once the OTD was positioned on the supply deck of the M/V, the affected individual (AI) was the first to board and was, as reported, positioned with one foot on the OTD and his other foot on the deck positioning himself ready for transfer. 
o Before the other persons could board the basket, the M/V sustained wave action that caused the M/V to subside between the wave create and trough approximately 3' from beneath the OTD, which was then suspended, and when the M/V rose again this caused the supply deck to contact the bottom side of the OTD where it remained close to its original position. 
o Initially, the AI did not report an injury or conditions of concern following contact between the M/V and the OTD. 
o The AI remained as he was positioned on the OTD, and the other two persons boarded the OTD. When all parties were safely positioned on the OTD, the crane operator was provided a hoisting signal and they were all hoisted onto the platform. 
o Once on the platform, the AI began position-related task. 
. At approximately 09:20HRS, the AI reported discomfort in his right knee to his supervisor and explained what had occurred while he was on the OTD earlier that morning. The person in charge (PIC) of the facility was also informed at this time. 
o The PIC then reported the AI's condition to Area 5's Field Foreman and AOL's incident reporting requirements were initiated, which included reporting the event to the Area's Production Foreman, and the HSE Coordinator.
. At 13:30HRS the AI requested to be sent shoreside for an onshore medical evaluation. 
. At 16:15HRS an Aircraft departed MP 123 A with an onshore destination.
. The AI was transported by their employer to an occupational medical clinic for evaluation, diagnosis, and treatment is needed.
. The medical evaluation provided a diagnosis of a knee strain. The AI received a release to regular duty as the condition did not require any medical treatment beyond the initial evaluation and first aid guidance on care. Based on this information, the employer acknowledged that the case was classified as a First Aid.

Event Consequences
1. Initially there were no event consequences beyond the contact of the M/V supply deck and rigid offshore transfer device. 
2. 2 hours later, a report of discomfort was provided, which required evacuation for medical evaluation, condition diagnosis, and treatment if needed. 
o Diagnosis: Musculoskeletal Injury/Right Knee Strain

There were no environmental impacts or property damages because of this event.

Incident occurred which required medical treatment for a contract mechanic on Cox's SM 99 A facility. The mechanics began job task by unscrewing the rod caps and checking the bearings within. At approximately 9:20 am on 6/21/23, Perdido experienced a Platform shut down due to a VFD failure. The "variable frequency device" is the controller for the caisson ESPs located in the platform's subsea MMC control room. The smoke detectors in the subsea control building were automatically activated by the smoke that was released from the VFD cabinet. This initiated a PSD - Platform Shut Down. A full muster was accounted for in 7 minutes. No escalation outside of the subsea MMC control room. The ICS team dispatched the fire team to a staging area and then to the Sub-Sea MCC. The fire team only observed smoke (no fire) from the VFD failure. Once the area was secured, an electrician was then dispatched to the building to begin surveying the cabinets.  No notable temperature differences noted on the outside of the cabinets.  Permission was given to open the cabinet on A and a temperature in excess of 350F was observed.  Continued survey of the B, C, and D cabinets and ~210F temperature was observed.  At that point, the team felt they had identified and isolated the source of the smoke which was detected.  A fire watch was staged and the fire team to report back to debunker.  The community was allowed to leave muster but not allowed to return to work.  

Recovery:
The building was ventilated, smoke cleared, and AHU's returned to service.  Once all smoke detectors were clear, the doors were closed to the building and smoke detection was continuously monitored.  A LOTO was installed on the electrical breakers for ESP-A VFD. The team then proceeded to apply power to the other available ESP VFD's in the building to verify their health (B, C, D). All appeared to have no issues.  General community was then allowed to return to work.  After speaking with Marco DeLeon w/BSEE and getting a verbal approval to start, the crew proceeded to run ESP - B to secure part of the sub-sea system for flow assurance (hydrate prevention).  The team then moved on to ESP-D followed by ESP-C, ensuring their health.  Once B-caisson wells were deemed safe they were started on initial ramps.  After all three ESP's were verified healthy, BSEE was notified through the afterhours hotline with an update. 

Costs: 
As far as repair costs, the crew is in the process of changing out the entire cabinet and start over with fresh equipment.  The cost of the new cabinet is approximately $65,000 with one currently on location.  The Perdido leadership team feels that this will be the safest and most efficient way to ensure safe production from ESP "A".

Go forward plan:
-Trouble shoot ESP-A VFD to identify failure
-Change the reactor cabinet and output switch section of VFD
-Commission and return to service  

Production Impact: 
Production loss estimated after failure -15,789 BOPD, 12083 GAS = -17803BEQ

Power:
ESP VFD's voltage rating is 6.9KV

1. DC321, DC323, and DC324's SCSSVs did not close during the 06/26/2023 Atlantis ESD event.

07/11/2023 Update:

SCSSV's Failed To Close on wells DC321, 322 and 324 (DC32X) During ESD Event - Logic Fault Summary and Corrective Actions

Background:
On 6/26/2023, routine maintenance work on the Atlantis facility inadvertently tripped an ESD, leading to a full field shut-in. During the course of this event, the CROs noticed the SCSSVs for DC321, 323, and 324 did not close in accordance with the active shutdown sequence. The CROs manually commanded the SCSSVs closed and verified normal operation of the equipment - confirming the command and hydraulic functions worked as intended. It should be noted that the USVs for the 3 impacted wells did close per the commanded shutdown sequence and all flow from the wells stopped in accordance with the ESD.
Once the system was verified fully safed out, onshore engineering support was notified of the SCSSV issues and a root cause investigation was initiated.

Investigation/Corrective Actions:
Engineering identified a fault in the existing subsea control logic directly impacting the operation of the DC32X SCSSV shutdown timers. This fault was introduced into the control system during the Atlantis Phase 3 development logic installation. The fault had the effect of sending a persistent reset command to the DC32X SCSSV shutdown timers, effectively stopping their operation and inhibiting the output of the SCSSV closure command at timer expiration.

Corrected logic was developed, verified through factory acceptance test (FAT), and then implemented offshore. Independent review of the newly installed logic was completed post-implementation by onshore and offshore resources prior to bringing the affected wells back online.
