A small flame was witnessed by two personnel on the turbo insulation blanket of compressor at our SM 99A facility. The flame was quickly extinguished by one personnel using a nearby water hose. It should be noted that the water hose used was utility water and not part of the fire water system. Although no damage was identified by the flame, the initial investigation revealed that a bracket, which helps support the expansion joint for the turbo, had broken. The resulting vibration caused the expansion joint to crack, and once it cracked, the hot exhaust contacted the exhaust's blanket. This led to oily/coolant residue on the exhaust's blanket to flame. There were no injuries resulting from this incident and current POB at the facility is 9. The facility remains on-line however, the compressor was shut-in and will remain shut-in until repairs are made.

Initial first report was made to BSEE Lafayette afterhours line. 

Update 6/29: Upon further investigation, it has been determined that the exhaust's expansion joint does not have a crack. However, oil residue was found on the blanket, and it was determined that the heat from the exhaust caused this residue to ignite. Extensive maintenance was conducted on the compressor prior to the incident, which involved replacing the turbo. It is believed that either oil from the replaced turbo or coolant during maintenance became the source of the residue on the exhaust's blanket. As a result, both the expansion joint and the exhaust blanket have been replaced. We are confident that we have successfully eliminated the cause of this incident.

On 07/03/2023, at approximately 0840 hrs. while preparing to load casing from the M/V onto Olympus, as the crane operator began to cable up, noticed the aft sling sliding forward up the stand of drilling riser toward the center of the tubular and the tubular sliding through the wrap of the aft sling moving toward the stern of the M/V. The DSP was placed in the middle of the load to observe the lift and guide the crane from an advantage point that could see the entire task. Two extra deckhands were placed on either end to observe the lift and slings, and two deckhands were placed on the ends on tag lines on the opposite side to place pressure on the slings and keep them tight.

Incident: July 03, 2023, 15:00 hrs. Pipe Spinner tail end struck IP in hardhat while backing out 5" drill pipe. The task was to rack back a 5" drill pipe stand in the derrick. The IP was at the controls of the pipe spinner, he received the go ahead from the driller to engage the pipe spinner to back out the drill pipe. When controls were engaged, the pipe spinner tail end moved away from the IP, then the IP engaged the controls in a reverse direction, causing the pipe spinner tail to move towards the IP resulting in the impact to the hard hat causing it to land on rig floor.

Initial Actions Taken: Both Floorhands approached IP to assist him as he was retrieving his hard hat. IP put his hard hat back on and all three moved back into position to continue the task of backing out the drill pipe to rack back in the derrick. 

Investigation Findings:
No malfunction of the pipe spinner was identified.
. IP failed to change body position when controls were engaged to change direction of pipe spinner rotation.
. IP was standing between the pipe spinner attached to the pipe stand in rotary and the single joint of drill pipe in the mouse hole.
. The standard procedure when changing direction of rotation of pipe spinner is to move with the pipe spinner as it rotates and stops when the snub line is tight.
. After the pipe spinner was attached to drill pipe, IP operated the pipe spinner to rotate the drill pipe into the drill string in the rotary, IP then waited for driller to give the signal to proceed to back the drill pipe out with the pipe spinner.
. The IP did not request any first aid assistance prior to resuming the task of operating the pipe spinner.

At approximately 3:30am on July 12th operators observed the tubing on a vessel tap on the subsea freewater knockout was parted at the fitting from the valve it connects to releasing hydrocarbons. A manual ESD of the FWKO was initiated and the release was secure. The amount released to water is still being determined. The event was reported to NRC, NRC #1372825.

Statement 08/25/23: At approximately 3:00 AM on July 12, 2023, Olympus operations discovered a ball valve separation in the sample line between the Subsea FWKO and the sample sink, resulting in a release of hydrocarbons to the deck. Initial spill calculations were made using a tubing flow restriction model. This estimate was based on tubing flow restriction - modeled flow through a 12" inch tube with full pressure drop indicated an 87.78 gallons per minute release rate. At this rate, approximately 31 barrels of hydrocarbon were released to the deck over the 15-minute duration of the event. The initial report to NRC was based on this estimate.

The first estimate was later updated because Operations informed the engineer running the calculation that the release did not come through the tubing, but in fact the tubing disconnected during the event, allowing the material to flow from a connection that has a nominal 0.5 inch, inside diameter, orifice. The first model run incorrectly assumed flow through a length of tubing. Consequently, the flow equations for flow from a tube were not appropriate since the tube disconnected. Therefore, a model designed for exit velocity from an orifice was used on the second pass. These model results indicated a choked flow that was limited by the maximum possible flow rate for this scenario. The revised flow rate of 46 gallons per minute, correlating to a 16.4-barrel release to the deck was then reported to the NRC.

A sheen on the water was observed during daylight hours. The 0.5 gallon released to water was estimated using a spill estimator, based on the dimensions of the sheen and US Coast Guard spill factors. Operations staff spent the day cleaning spilled material from the bottom deck, where the Subsea FWKO is located, and three decks above due to a significant updraft between the process modules and the well bay. Each deck was cleaned with a combination of absorbent pads, rags, hoses and sprayers.

However, the fire started to spread upwards through the grating where the day tank and transfer tank were located. The operators managed to extinguish the flames on the turbine compressor, but the fire had spread to the top deck where the diesel day tank and transfer tank were situated. They continued to use dry chemical extinguishers on the flames at the diesel tanks, but the fire kept burning. At this point, the flame reached a nearby 8-man sleeper building, which began to catch fire as well. ***Final Report***

Incident Summary:
Sometime between the hours of 1700 (07-24-2023) and 1100 hours (07-25-2023) the crane boom came into contact with the ISS owned gas buster vent line resulting in the vent line being bent. At 1100 hours on 07-25-2023, a lift was being performed which put the crane boom near the vent line of the gas buster. The UWA glanced up at the boom and saw the vent line had a slight bend. (Contact between the vent line and the bottom of the crane boom did not occur at the time damage was noticed). There were no injuries.

Immediate Corrective Action:
The UWA immediately called an all stop and had the crane operator inspect the crane boom while the ISS supervisor inspected the vent line. There was no apparent damage to the bottom of the crane boom, however there was an area where the paint had been scraped off. Paint on the vent line was cracked, however there did not appear to be any structural damage to either component.

Investigation and Recurrence Prevention:
The potential obstruction of the gas buster was identified in the JSA. The lift was not identified as a blind lift since the crane operator could see where the load started and was to be set down. It was identified during the investigation that during boom movement, there is a portion of the swing that the vent line was in a blind spot to the crane operator. 

Lifts planned for this boom path will be identified as a blind lift with a lift specific Lifting Operations Plan and lift specific JSA. These lifts may require placement of more than one Signalman in order to observe the entire load path; in these cases, both will be identified on the documentation. The Signalman is responsible for observing all aspects of the lift, including boom movement. Heightened awareness of this will be reviewed during the upcoming pre-tour SimOps / Safety Meetings.

At approximately 0700 smoke was observed coming from the main Living quarter laundry room Dryer #4.  Power was secured to the dryer and a muster alarm was initiated. The fire team bunkered, and two fire team members partially opened the dryer door and extinguished the smoldering contents in the dryer using a fire extinguisher. No flame was visible when this occurred. YSH 55001A in the area alarmed after muster had been initiated and the door was partially opened to extinguish the smoldering content.  
 
Once the smoldering contents were extinguished and cooled, the dryer contents were taken out. This included towels, mop heads, and one oven mitt (see attached photos). The oven mitt was the only item from inside the kitchen area. The load was described as the usual size, but it was noted that another cycle was run on this load because the contents were still wet after the initial drying cycle. This is not common with the dryers and when the smoke was first observed all dryers, including the one where the smoke was coming from had completed their cycle. No indication of lint build-up outside of the normal amount from a load of towels. The dryer vents had been cleaned one month prior.  
 
After the dryer was removed the fire damper (FD-5124) appeared to be in the closed position, but the Ruskin fusible link with a rating of 212 Fahrenheit appeared fully intact. The link was not connected to the damper indicating that 
the damper had been closed without the melted fusible link triggering it per design.  No issues with the motor belt on the dryer were found. 

FINAL INVESTIGATION FINDINGS-

Why did the incident happen? 
FD-5124 is a Ruskin Model DIBD2-WR Fire Damper that is installed on the exhaust ducting in the Main Quarters Laundry Room. The damper pre-maturely failed causing the flaps to Close in the Fail-Safe position. This in turn prevented the dryer from properly venting the hot exhaust air from the dryer. The dryer overheated causing the linen inside to overheat and smolder. The damper was found with the Fusible link lying next to the damper on the floor. The clips that hold the Fusible Link in place were found to be weakened which allowed the Fusible Link to be released from its working position that keeps the flap open. The damper is considered failed and will be replaced with a new one. 

Additional Action taken since the incident happened:
The camp boss will set expectations for crews to stop the job if clothes are still wet after one load and report. If clothes are damp, an extra 10-15 minutes can be added, but will not be set to another full cycle of 45 minutes. 

Damages did not exceed $25k threshold.

On Sept. 4th at approximately 09:00 hours an injury to an Contractor employee occurred after an unauthorized entry into a 10-foot diameter Heater Treater via a 24-inch manhole at HI 379-B.  The Injured Person (IP) was attempting to use a 3-inch hose to vacuum fluids and sediment out of the tank through a vacuum pump and into a cuttings box.  At some point in the operation the hose became vacuum locked onto a surface inside the tank.  At this point, the IP without planning, risk assessing, direction, or authorization, initially placed approximately 60% of his body into the tank to free the hose end to break the suction hold and allow fluid to enter the hose.  At some point, the worker completely entered the tank.  His absence caused a co-worker, who was operating the vacuum pump within line of sight, to stop the job, look for the IP and call his supervisor for instructions and assistance when the IP could not be found..
 
Using a flashlight, the Contractor Job Superintendent saw the IP inside the tank laying under the fluid and initiated a rescue response.
 
At this point of our investigation and analysis, it is apparent that Contractor personnel did not follow the restrictions and agreements made on the W&T Permit-to-Work that was issued on the day of the incident.  In addition, they also did not follow their own JSEA and tank cleaning procedures.  Lastly, the tank cleaner, who is a trained confined space entry supervisor as well as trained CSE rescuer also took it upon himself to enter the tank without planning, precautions, or authorization.  In fact, there had been no planned tank entry, and the team specifically discussed not breaking the plane of the tank manway once it was opened to allow the vacuum hose to be used inside to vacuum the sediments from inside the tank.

Immediate actions taken to prevent reoccurrence.

A. Stop all tank cleaning and confined space work with Contractor and require them to provide a comprehensive plan to complete the actions in this report and to measure and improve the overall safety culture at Contractor.
B. Contractor to provide the W&T Safety manager with re-training reports and competency evaluations to all staff who perform, supervise, or manage any work on W&T Offshore assets.
C. W&T Safety Manager to schedule in person audits and job inspections of Contractor' s management systems, processes, and activities that govern its adherence to safe work on W&T jobsites.

9.	Corrective actions
Contractor- Develop and Implement a plan to measure and improve the Contractor Corporate Safety Culture of safe work.	
Contractor- Call stop work and retrain and evaluate the competencies of all staff on safe work procedures.
W&T- Safety Manager to schedule in person audits and job inspections of Contractor's management systems, processes, and activities that govern its adherence to safe work on W&T jobsites.	
Contractor- Complete all Actions listed and provide a letter of affirmation when complete and submit to W&T Safety Manager for tracking closure & validation.

Initial notification: (Sept. 10th) at 08:00pm, a crane material handling incident occurred (no injuries) at WD 80D. Current site activity is the Plug and Abandonment of the D-12 well. Crew had picked up a drill collar with 2 7/8" single-joint pipe elevators and set into the slips. Then latched on to a joint of 2 3/8" tubing from the pipe rack and lifted it 6 feet when it released from the single-joint pipe elevators falling back to the pipe rack. All stop was initiated and it was identified that the 2 7/8" single-joint pipe elevators were inadvertently used to hoist the 2 3/8" tubing rather than switching to the 2 3/8" single-joint pipe elevators. Corrective actions included marking each of the elevator sizes with a paint marker and using a short pup joint of the work string size to verify the elevators size matches the size piping when hoisting. 

Sept. 24, 2023 - Final Update. The managements of both Whitefleet Operations (WFO) and Whitefleet Abandonment (WFA), (including field leadership) have conducted an investigation of this dropped-object event. Findings included the following: 
a) P&A Crewmen were given instructions by site leadership to ensure following the insertion of the drill collar into the slips to change out the single-joint elevators from 2 7/8" to 2 3/8" in order to hoist and trip the 2 3/8" tubing into the work string; the crewmen likely due to complacency did not change out the 
b) Work crew did not have within the task plan (JSA); a specific procedural step to change out the elevators from 2 7/8" to 2 3/8", the assignment of this task to a specific crew member, and/or a verification process to ensure the step was completed with the correct size elevators.

Immediate Site Corrective Actions:
a) Site leadership and crew (post) incident enacted STOP WORK to investigate this event and held a Safety Stand down with crewmen.
b) Job Safety Analysis (JSA) was revised to include an associate hazard (dropped object) when using single-joint elevators too large for the intended tubing to hoisted and verification of the correct tubing size elevators. 
c) Site leadership & Crew decided to identify each type single-joint elevator on site with the correct size (paint stick marking) on the unit's side matching the unit's stamped size.
d) Additionally, an equal tubing size pup-joint is being utilized to verify the signal-joint elevators are of correct size (GO/NO GO)
e) WFA has communicated to all Field operations the details of the event and to incorporate the above into their task activity.

Additional Preventive Actions:
1) Job Safety Analysis (JSA) will be further revised to include the specific procedure step of changing out elevators with verification when tripping In-or-Out the Well bore with different size work tools or work strings.
2) Whitefleet Operating (WFO) and Whitefleet Abandonment (WFA) will generate a "Safety Awareness Alert" for distribution to the fleet for awareness,
learnings of this event, and implementation of these corrective & preventative actions.
3) Both WFO and WFA will reiterate the learnings of this event in future projects of this type within pre-project "Execution Plan Meetings" with all contractors.
4) WFA will revise their Standard Operation Procedures (SOPs) for this specific task to include the above with verification process.
5) WFO / WFA will also spot check future operational JSAs to ensure continuous execution of the revised SOP.

At approximately 1:30 am, an alarm was activated as the #2 compressor shut down. The lead operator, who was leaving the quarters to address the production alarm, noticed a flame approximately 1-2 feet high. Acting promptly the operator grabbed a nearby fire water hose and successfully extinguished the flame. Upon contact with the water, the flames were immediately extinguished. 
To ensure safety and prevent any potential re-ignition, the area was closely monitored for the next 30 minutes. There were no injuries as a result of this incident. Initial report was made to the BSEE afterhours line followed up by an email  
The investigation revealed that the right bank's turbo lubrication tubing line was cracked at the flange where it fastens to the top of the turbo.
The crack in the tubing resulted in a spray of oil contacting the hot exhaust pipe causing the flame
Necessary repairs on the compressor at West Delta 27 A have been successfully completed. The issues that led to the flame have been addressed, including the replacement of both tubing lines for the right and left bank turbo. Additionally, all residue oil has been thoroughly cleaned, and the exhaust blankets have been properly cleaned as well.

On 10/03/2023, between 6-8 am, Crane # 4 was recovering the ROV basket to surface. The ROV basket contained a hydraulic flying lead (HFL). When bringing the basket through the splash zone, it was observed that the HFL was hanging out of the basket. Upon sitting the basket on the deck, the HFL was still hanging over the handrail. Then, the HFL hose came free from within the basket and began going overboard until it was caught on some equipment. The Crane crew got the HFL hose secured and used the crane to hoist the HFL up in sections. Upon getting the hose back up on the deck, it was discovered to be damaged and not fit for duty. Pictures that were taken on the seafloor indicate that the HFL was secured in the basket and had no damage prior to being raised to the surface. It is believed that when the basket was hoisted through the splash zone, the wave action caused the hose to come partially out of basket and damaged during retrieval.

It is estimated that a maximum of 6 gallons of Transaqua (hydraulic fluid within the HFL) was released to the water. According to the Manufacturer's Safety Data Sheet, Transaqua has a density of 1.071 g/cm3 and is composed of 40%-70% Ethylene Glycol (RQ of 5000 lbs.), 40%-70% water and 1%-5% Triethanolamine (RQ of 1000 lbs.). Based on this information, the event resulted in a chemical release to water below the reportable quantity threshold. The estimated amounts released are as follows:

Estimated release of Ethylene Glycol ~ 21.452 lbs. - 37.541 lbs.
Estimated release of Triethanolamine ~ 0.5363 lbs. - 2.6815 lbs.

The weather and water conditions at time of incident:
Sea state 1.2 @ 120, Swell 2 0.75
Wind was 16-19 knots.

The replacement cost of the Hydraulic Flying Lead (HFL) was $120,500 USD.

Human Engineering, Not Fault Tolerant System, Errors not detectable: During the investigation, it was determined that the replacement board had come from another facility (warehouse stock). Title:
PRS (Pipe Racking System) Roller jaw inadvertently functioned opened allowing stand of pipe to lean over to the Stbd side of the Derrick

Brief Description:
While making up diverter sub to the bottom of the stand of pipe using the PRS and AR5000, the diverter sub was clamped into the jaw of the AR with the pin end of the diverter sub sitting on the floor. The PRS operator positioned the stand of pipe over the diverter sub and the pipe pin was landed into the box of the diverter sub. The operator then opened the PRS grip jaw (roller jaw still closed), the AR was used to spin up the connection between the stand of pipe and the diverter sub while the stand was still secured with the roller jaw of the PRS. After making up the connection the AR was moved back to the home position. The PRS operator then proceeded to close the Grip jaw on the PRS so that the stand could be moved to well center and made up to the string in the Rotary.

While attempting to close the jaw the operator mistakenly pushed the button to open the PRS jaw instead of the button to close the jaw which allowed the PRS roller jaw to open and release the stand of pipe, allowing the stand to lean to the Stbd side and come to rest on a Derrick beam. The crew immediately secured the area and made notifications.

No Dropped objects or asset damage occurred due to this incident and the RedZone was clear of personnel with exception of the designated PRS spotter, who was positioned ~24 ft away from the pipe and in the opposite direction of that the pipe was leaning.

Human Engineering - Human Machine Interface - Monitoring alertness NI

Initial Report made to AH email at 17:56 on 11/8:
This evening, during a post-job inspection following welding operations to install a tertiary support beam for a Heater Skid addition, evidence of arcing (charring/melting) between the welding ground clamp and an aluminum cable tray was identified. The cable tray was located an estimated 2 - 3 inches from the ground clamp connection. Initial investigation of the cables secured within the damaged cable tray showed no visible signs of damage. 
No personnel were injured. 

The arcing event was caused due to the location/placement of the grounding clamp by the 3rd party welder. 

**Update**
Causal Factors/Remediation:
1). The grounding clamp should be attached as close to the welding area as possible. (The location of the clamp was observed > 3ft.) 

2). Ground clamps should be attached to clean, bare-metal surface. (The grounding clamp was attached to a coated support providing a barrier between the clamp and the support.)

The incident details, causes, and preventative measures were communicated to the PM Crew on 11/8 and the AM Crew on 11/9 by Stampede EHS and Topsides IHUC Lead. In addition, the prevention measures discussed are to be communicated in a PTW Toolbox Talk as an additional layer of awareness & prevention for all future welding operations. 
Damage was minimal, no repair was required.

This is the Initial and Final Report

Investigation Summary/Event Description:
On November 09, 2023, at 09:00HRS an alarm was automatically sounded, and the platform shut because of an activated Temperature Safety Element (TSE). All platform personnel immediately responded and convened at the muster station. All personnel were accounted for within a few minutes of the alarm. Production operating personnel then proceeded to the Master Panel of the platform to investigate which TSE Zone could be identified indicating TSE pressure was lost. Production operators determined that the activation was within Zone No. 3 therefore began inspecting all the permanent positioned TSEs equipped for the Float Cell and the generators. After inspecting Zone No. 3 without an activation discovery within the TSE loops, Production Operators moved to inspect the temporary TSE loops that support construction rental equipment, e.g., air compressors and welding machines. It was then that the temporary TSE loop on a welding machine was immediately noticed as having a hole in the poly flow tubing. Once discovered, it was determined that the poly flow tubing was positioned on the top of the welding machine and vibrations associated with normal runtime had moved it against the exhaust, which with the heat and vibrating against the heat wrap of the exhaust caused a hole in the material. The tubing was fixed and repositioned to prevent contact with the exhaust or elevated temperature components. The platform person in charge (PIC) then provided an all-clear notice and online operations were able to resume.

Event Consequences:
SMI 128 B Platform was emergency shut down as designed because of the sensor activation. 

There were no injuries to personnel, property damage, or environmental impacts because of this event.

Corrective Action:
The following mitigation was taken based on the investigation:
1. The TSE Loop was relocated to the side of the welding machine and secured with tie wraps/zip ties to prevent securing the line in place.

Reference Final Report attachment for extended details.

A material handling incident occurred during drilling operations. At ~01:10hrs on 04 Dec 2023, while hoisting the Aux Drawworks with an empty block, the Drawworks brakes inadvertently set, causing the drill line to backlash on the Drawworks drum. At this time, it is unknown as to what caused the brakes to set and our maintenance team will be working with NOV in efforts to find a cause. No equipment damage occurred from this event and the RedZone was clear of personnel. We will be working to put a plan together to hang off the block and remove the backlash from the Drawworks. The Maintenance team has isolated the Drawworks in the meantime.

Response to RFI:
*These two incidents were not related to the same problem but the system's reactions were the same
*The incident on the Main side was due to activating the Trip height setpoint while hoisting the block in close proximity of that limit
*The incident on the Aux was due to retracting the block in close proximity to the Fleet angle limit while hoisting up in the Derrick 

Corrective Actions:
We have created a supplemental Competency Assessment for our Drillers and Assistant Drillers to make them aware of the incident and how the Drawworks responds to set limits. We have documented operating parameters which instruct the operators to not retract or extend the block while hoisting up if the elevator position is above 60 ft. This will ensure that the Drawworks motors can react and stop the block without setting the brakes prior to reaching the Fleet angle limit.

Update 01/12/2024:
Below is additional information on the Closed Drain System - including some of the background/historical data and recommendations for going forward.

.	The LOPC earlier this year (June 23) was at the branch connection for the drain coming from "Sample Sink #2".  The defect was identified to primarily be from internal degradation, located immediately opposite/below the incoming flow, and was attributed to an erosion-corrosion or flow-assisted corrosion type mechanism.  Temporary repairs were made to this piping and the system was returned to normal operation.
.	After this LOPC, the PEI Team developed an inspection plan to assess other similar locations.  The other locations selected for follow-up NDE were at several branches for Sample Sinks (#s 3, 4, 9, 10, and 11), with the belief that more complex (atypical) chemistry and potential for unusually high corrosion rates may exist at these locations.  The inspection of these locations was completed in July in coordination with some additional inspection to assess external degradation associated with coating failure.  The lowest measured thickness found was 0.232" at the "Sample Sink #3" location.  This was evaluated at the time against the nominal thickness of 0.280" and a start date in 2010 and it was judged that there was not likely an immediate/acute concern with the system.  In this sample set the worst measured rate of 3.6 mils/year corrosion rate is effectively the same as the "default" 4 mils/year corrosion rate assumed for many of our systems where erosion-corrosion and/or underdeposit corrosion are anticipated.
.	The LOPC the morning (December 18) was identified as being at the branch connection coming from the "E" Flow Control Assembly gas vent connection (and was not part of our prior survey sample set).  Based on current understanding, the LOPC was likely made apparent during FCA checks on this ESP this morning.  The belief is this scenario may be an erosion-corrosion type failure given the potential for relatively high flow rates during the periodic usage of the branches - a slightly different lens than what the team has focused on after this summer's LOPC.
 
Additional RT scope was performed to further understand the overall condition of the closed drain header and ensure better understanding of the degradation mechanisms that may be in play more fully.

The crane crew was preparing to lift a tote of xylene from the main deck when as the slings were getting taught, one of the slings got caught under the bolt that tightens down the circular lid of the tote causing the lid to open. The lid was minorly damaged (cosmetic) when the sling was caught under the bolt that holds the lid, forcing it open. The deck foreman stopped the lifting activity. The team moved to close and re-tighten the lid. No xylene was released from the tote.

12/29/2023 Update:

Why did the incident happen?
Due to the slings being hung over the side of the tote for D ring hook up (tote is approx. 6+ ft. tall), one leg of the sling ultimately became hung up under the locking bolt on the tote lid. Due to the load's close proximity to the module, the flagger was looking up at the angle of the load line as the crane operator began to cable up. As the slings were becoming taught, the flagger immediately noticed one leg caught under the tote lid and called for the crane operator to go all stop. Before the crane operator could stop the lift, the tote lid popped off from hung sling leg. The tote was still on deck and no LOPC occurred from the tote lid being open.

Additional Action taken since the incident happened?
The job was stopped, and the lid was secured back on the tote. The lift was completed. PTL to ensure with vendors that totes coming offshore will have the rubber protection ring around the tote lid and locking bolt, which also reduces risk of sling legs becoming hung up under tote lid.

Oral Report was made by LLOG on Sunday, December 24, 2023, at 09:10 hours to BSEE New Orleans District Production Engineer (via After Hours Mobile Telephone).
A rental air compressor onboard the facility, used for blasting and painting operations, caught fire. Heat from the fire caused the temporary air intake filter media to catch fire on the nearby Platform Generator ZZZ-9000. The Fire-Eye detection system in the Generator enclosure properly activated, as designed, shut-in the entire facility, and automatically flooded the inside of the Generator enclosure with CO2. The facility's Fire Team was mobilized, and the fire was quickly extinguished. There were no injuries and no pollution. The only damage to equipment was to the rental air compressor and minor wiring on the external face of the generator enclosure.

On 12/27/23, the Deep Energy vessel was laying umbilical to the Rydberg drill center when a search light transformer adjacent to the bridge HVAC intake shorted out and produced smoke that was then pulled into the HVAC intake. The search light was not in use at the time.  Smoke entered the bridge thereby setting off the smoke detection system.

12.27.23: The crane operator was using West crane to lower bundle (6 joints of drill pipe) of 5" drill pipe to work boat. The crew had lifted and lowered 62 bundles down to the boat. The bundles were double wrapped on each end by cable slings and clamp was applied. During the lift of the 63rd bundle one end of slings slipped from pin end to box end of bundle causing bundle to go form horizontal to vertical. The boat deck hand and roustabout saw the rigging shifting and immediately moved away to the front of boat clear from the landing zone. Upon seeing the slings shifting, the crane operator lowered the bundle to the back deck of work boat and landed the bundle safely on the other stacks of bundle currently on deck of the boat. No personnel were injured, no equipment damaged, and nothing lost into the water. The crane was not shock loaded but the crane operator still performed an inspection on crane to ensure there was no damage to crane.

Corrective actions: 
1. A safety stand down was held. 
2. The drill pipe has completions fluid on it so the pipe will be washed prior to being rigged up to increase the friction of the rigging on the bundle. 
3. A longer two part sling will be added to reduce the angle and thus the inward pull force when lifting bundle.

On 01/14/2024 at 17:11hrs, Thunder Horse had a spurious trip by a line-of-sight Spectrex 900 series detector (AXT-J20215) in the Production Module, resulting in a PSD1 and full muster. Attached is a drawing showing detector location, PI data and field photo._x000D_
_x000D_
AXT-J20215 Troubleshooting, Corrective Actions, & History:_x000D_
AXT-J20215's high alarm is set at 1% LEL and its high-high alarm is set at 2.5%. AXTJ20215's ESS logic is a 1 activation trip to PSD1. Per the attached PI data, on the day of the event (01/14/2024 at 1711hrs), AXT-J20215 reached 3.133% LEL. The straight signal response indicates a malfunction. This can be compared to the expected curve response generated from a test with a lens on 01/14/2024 at 18:34hrs._x000D_
_x000D_
On 01/15/2024, the detector, including the transmitter, receiver, and HAWK cable gland, was replaced in-kind and put into service. Maintenance reported only slight damage to the HAWK cable gland. The detector that tripped will be sent to SOTEC for RCA to confirm the device failure and determine if the failure may be applicable to devices in the same batch._x000D_
_x000D_
AXT-J20215 was upgraded from a 200 series to a 900 series in June 2022 (MO# 100897642).  Per MO# 101352504, AXT-J20215 malfunction events were also reported on 11/27/2022 and 11/28/2022. These malfunctions didn't cause alarms and cleared without intervention. SOTEC had recently cleaned, calibrated, and aligned the detector on 11/11/2022. At the time, line of sight was verified to be unobstructed, and the device was put back into service. On 1-18-24 at approximately 2300 hrs. the drill crew was in the process of running a 4 1/2"" production tubing in the hole when the driller slacked off to the connection height and employees set the slips on the tubing. The driller signaled for the derrickman to install the collar clamp; the 3rd party elevator operator thought the driller was signaling him to open the elevators. When the elevators were opened the slips did not hold the string causing the string to slide down inside the slips stopping at the collar. 250' of TEC Line was stressed, & locally damaged at the rotary table and had to be spooled off, re-terminated, and tested.
The job was stopped, and leadership notified, the job was started back after a safety pause. A Joint of tubing was screwed into collar and string picked up and collar clamp installed.  The tubing that slipped was a new 4.5"" 15.10# S13Cr110 Vam Top.  The 1/4"" TEC control line was damaged (control line to the DHPG).  The Slips being used were 4.5"" DU long slips configured to be used manually.  Estimated cost to repair the 250ft of damaged TEC line is: $1,500.  It took 7 hours to make the required TEC re-termination and cut out the damaged portion of the line.  No other damages or repairs required and there were no injuries.  This is a pending ongoing investigation as corrective measures are still to be determined.   Please note this is not a lifting device incident -- the issue was a miscommunication that led to the tubing slipping through the slips without the safety clamp in place. Safety clamps are industry standard when running tubing. The clamps are designed to push down on the slips and make them bite harder if the pipe slips. Pipe slipping through the slips is not an uncommon occurrence in industry when there is not a significant amount of weight below the slips. Per [REDACTED_NAME]'s email, this eWell report is being submitted with the details listed above along with a JSA and photos provided as attachments.

An Electrician was working on an ESD push station when the facility suffered an ESD and total power loss. The emergency generator did not start as designed per the cause and effect according to the PIC. Power was restored at 12:59PM and production was restarted at 2:10PM. The seawater (firewater) pumps are electric driven and do not run on an independent drive. The pumps are powered from the platform 480V bus which is normally powered by the turbine generator and with the backup diesel generator. During the total power loss period of 15 minutes, all hydrocarbon production was automatically shut down (including up and over pipeline) and the facility had whatever sweater pressure was left in the system.
The Enchilada facility does have manual override capability to start the backup generator for firewater supply. However, since there was no fire alarm when the event occurred, the platform personnel utilized the time to confirm there is no real manual initial emergency before resetting and starting to restore power. There was no loss comm to Well and Safety System.  CCTV was working and Platform UPS power remain energized during the event. The root cause is due to ghost wiring issue from the generator water mist upgrade project. Same exact event occurred during commissioning of the project and claimed to be corrected. However, the issue was not fully addressed and caused the trip.

May 16, 2024 - Follow-up information and Final Submission for consideration for acceptance as Final Report for this dive-related event.

Following the event, an investigation was performed with participation by BSEE and USCG personnel.  Following the initial Evidence Preservation Order, equipment associated with the event including breathing air compressors and the dive helmet were removed from the vessel and sent out for third party inspection for evaluation to determine whether there were any identified malfunctioning units or components that may have contributed to the issues experienced by the diver.  All equipment and components inspected were verified to be properly functioning as intended during the inspection process.  After exhausting potential equipment issues as causal factors in the event, all indications at this time point to the diver experiencing a non-work-related personal medication condition.  

To date, the autopsy report and associated toxicology report remain outstanding.

This update is also being considered the Final Update and Submission for consideration as the final report.

Work-related cases involving cancer, chronic irreversible disease, a fractured or cracked bone, or a punctured eardrum must always be recorded under the general criteria at the time of diagnosis by a physician or other licensed health care professional.

On April 4th, 2024, maintenance workers conducted a run test on MTR-0201 (LACT Charge Pump Motor 201) following maintenance activities. During the 30-minute test, it was noted that the motor shaft ceased spinning. Upon checking with the CCR, it was confirmed that the motor was still receiving power (closed contact). Shortly thereafter, workers detected a burning smell. The team had people staged in the MCC Building when starting this pump motor up for the 1st time after a rebuild from the Vendor. {New Bearing on Motor} Smoke was not seen at this time. The workers then started the motor uncoupled from the pump and it ran for about 1 1/2 minutes when they noticed the contactor opened up and the motor stopped. The Electricians smelled some smoke in the MCC. After troubleshooting the Motor Contactor, workers noticed some soot around the Contactor control Circuit components (COIL). Promptly, the CCR was contacted to cut off power to the motor (open contact). No smoke detectors or ICS Muster was activated. Cost of repairs to replace the Motor Contactor Controls (COIL) is around $500. No hot work was being performed and no injuries.  During their search, a burnt coil was discovered on the control power circuit for the main contactor on the breaker. It was identified, a small faulty control Transformer was the cause of this incident. No investigation was needed as no work was performed on this motor contactor. This was in service for years. It was just a failed component of a control circuit.  The control components and the pump motor has now been in service for days with no issues. See attached photos.

On 05/21/2024 at 10:05 hours, the facility Fire Alarm sounded and the ESD activated, shutting-in the facility, as designed. All personnel mustered and reported to their Emergency Stations. The Fire Team responded to the Process Plant Power Generator No. 1 Enclosure (ZZZ-9000) because the Fire Suppression System (CO2) had been activated in this enclosure. Once the Fire Team had established and confirmed that there was no fire, the ZZZ-9000 enclosure was purged with fresh air. Facility mechanics inspected the enclosure and observed no evidence of fire or burning. However, facility mechanics did find that an exhaust flex joint in the generator engine exhaust system had failed, allowing the Fireye system to detect a probable engine backfire and activate the Fire Suppression System (CO2). Once the facility was deemed to be safe, facility personnel began the process to return the facility to service._x000D_
_x000D_
Answers to BSEE questions:_x000D_
1) Has the exhaust flex joint been replaced?_x000D_
   a. Yes. The flex joint was replaced on 05/21/24, the same day as this event._x000D_
2) And verified no additional exhaust leaks?_x000D_
   a. Verified. No other exhaust leaks were found._x000D_
3) Is there a concern for the probable backfire?_x000D_
   a. Yes there was. SEE ITEM 2 UNDER "Changes that were made to prevent recurrence" FOR ACTION TAKEN TO PREVENT BACKFIRES. Also, following a thorough investigation, the information below will provide the root cause along with solutions implemented to prevent recurrence._x000D_
_x000D_
What occurred:_x000D_
1) Due to onboard blasting and painting operations, fireproof filter media had been added to the enclosure louvers. This additional filter media restricted air flow and prevented the interior temperature of the enclosure from quickly cooling down following a unit shut down._x000D_
2) Following unit shut down and subsequent fan shut down, temperatures increased inside the enclosure._x000D_
_x000D_
Changes that were made to prevent recurrence:_x000D_
1) When the unit receives a signal to shut down, the engine will enter a timed, 10-minute running cool down period, before shutting down._x000D_
2) After the engine shuts down, burn times/spark timing has been set at 28-seconds to allow the gas to burn from the cylinders while the engine RPMs coast down, WHICH WILL PREVENT ENGINE BACKFIRES._x000D_
3) A 30-minute run timer has been added to the unit enclosure fan to prevent heat buildup inside the enclosure following shut down of the unit.

When the boom comes up high enough to trip the HAKO, the key switch will not override that HAKO function. If someone inserts the key and holds it on (spring loaded switch), the boom winch still will not operate to come up any higher.

At 17:25 hours, the facility Fire Alarm sounded and the ESD activated, shutting-in the facility, as designed. All personnel mustered and reported to their Emergency Stations. The Fire Team responded to the Process Plant Power Generator No. 1 Enclosure (ZZZ-9000) because the Fire Suppression System (CO2) had been activated in this enclosure. Once the Fire Team had established and confirmed that there was no fire, the ZZZ-9000 enclosure was purged with fresh air. Facility mechanics inspected the enclosure and observed no evidence of fire or burning. Presently, it is unknown as to why the fire detection system sensed a fire. Once the facility was deemed to be safe, facility personnel began the process to return the facility to service._x000D_
_x000D_
Following a thorough investigation, the information below will provide the root cause along with solutions implemented to prevent recurrence._x000D_
_x000D_
What occurred:_x000D_
1) Due to onboard blasting and painting operations, fireproof filter media had been added to the enclosure louvers. This additional filter media restricted air flow and prevented the interior temperature of the enclosure from quickly cooling down following a unit shut down._x000D_
2) Following unit shut down and subsequent fan shut down, temperatures increased inside the enclosure, causing a thermal element to trip._x000D_
_x000D_
Changes that were made to prevent recurrence:_x000D_
1) When the unit receives a signal to shut down, the engine will enter a timed, 10-minute running cool down period, before shutting down._x000D_
2) After the engine shuts down, burn times/spark timing has been set at 28-seconds to allow the gas to burn from the cylinders while the engine RPMs coast down, preventing a backfire._x000D_
3) A 30-minute run timer has been added to the unit enclosure fan to prevent heat buildup inside the enclosure following shut down of the unit._x000D_

BA538 Air Compressors/Air Compressor Dryers/Inverter Incident Report
	On Friday, June 7, the SISC Commissioning team began startup/ testing the platform Air Compressors/Dryers. First, the two Air Compressor Breakers in the AC Panel were closed to supply power to the Air Compressors. Next, the two Dryer breakers were closed, and then the two load contactors were energized from the HMI to supply power to the Dryers. At this point, all conditions were normal, and we were ready to start the air compressors. We first started CBA-80700 and successfully ran it for about 10 minutes, and then sent the start command to start CBA-80710. When CBA-80710 began to start, we heard a loud "humming" noise in the PCE building, started to look around and instantly saw smoke coming out of the Inverter. Upon seeing smoke, we immediately stopped CBA-80710. At this point, we called an all stop to confirm no personnel were injured, opened breakers for all previously mentioned equipment, report the incident, and to start investigating what could have caused this issue. All power feeding into the PCE building was de-energized and LOTO installed so that we could start identifying where the smoke came from within the inverter. After initial inspection, we found a faulted capacitor on one of the circuit boards within the Inverter. Once that faulted capacitor was identified, we continued to inspect the inverter. We were able to find internal factory installed cables (Lout & Nout-PE) with loose connections and there was no antioxidant compound installed on the connections. At this point, we determined the loose connections could have contributed to the inverter failure (pending confirmation from the manufacturer) but kept inspecting the remaining components in the system. We then inspected the AC Panel and megger tested the Air Compressors/Air Compressor Dryers wiring, and all readings were within acceptable tolerances. The next step is to consult with the Inverter Manufacturers' technical support team to review schematics and determine if the loose connections could have caused this incident.

The Fire Team responded to the Process Plant Power Generator No. 2 Enclosure (ZZZ-9100) since the Fire Suppression System (CO2) had been activated in this enclosure. Once the Fire Team had established and confirmed that there was no fire, the ZZZ-9100 enclosure was purged with fresh air. Facility mechanics also inspected the exhaust bellows and other exhaust components to ensure that everything was in place and working correctly. Once the facility was deemed to be safe, facility personnel began the process to return the facility to service.

Answers to BSEE Questions:
Is the sandblasting crew still onboard? YES.

What occurred (Root Cause):
1) Due to onboard blasting and painting operations, fireproof filter media had been added to the enclosure louvers. This additional filter media restricted air flow and prevented the interior temperature of the enclosure from quickly cooling down following a unit shut down.
2) Following unit shut down and subsequent fan shut down, temperatures increased inside the enclosure.

Changes that were made to prevent recurrence (Corrective Actions):
1) When the unit receives a signal to shut down, the engine will enter a timed, 10-minute running cool down period, before shutting down.
2) After the engine shuts down, burn times/spark timing has been set at 28-seconds to allow the gas to burn from the cylinders while the engine RPMs coast down, which will prevent engine backfires..
3) A 30-minute run timer has been added to the unit enclosure fan to prevent heat buildup inside the enclosure following shut down of the unit.

On 06/22/24 at approximately 13:23, the HP Oil Separator (MBD-115) level safety LT-115A was to be tested for the high/low shutdown. The HP oil separator was not in use at the time. An ACR, who has performed this task many times in the past, identified that there was sufficient level in the vessel based on the LT-115A level measurement. They started the testing process by closing the upper vessel isolation valves and opening the needle valve on top of the level bridle. The ball valve that allows gas to flow (bleed) to the skid was slightly opened to allow gas pressure to fall and the level to rise in the bridle by reducing the pressure above the liquid level. The indicated level in the bridle rose faster than expected and the ACR closed the ball valve. The control room operator (CRO) radioed that the high-level shutdown setpoint was not reached and the ACR re-opened the ball valve allowing gas to flow to the skid and allowing the level to rise. Again, the bridle level rose quickly and reached the LSH setpoint. The ACR then proceeded to prepare the draining of the liquids by closing the lower vessel isolation valve and opening the upper vessel isolation valve. Before draining the liquids the ASH-1017 and ASH-1008 detected sufficient gas (2oo45) with 1017 being in "Alarm" (25% LEL) and 1008 at least in "warning" (10% LEL) . This resulted in a platform shutdown (PSD) per the Cause and Effects.  The technician performing the check notified the CCR immediately. Note: Gas detectors that came into alarm that then caused shut down, cleared instantly. 11 wells were flowing (in service) during the time of event.  No muster was involved because it was known what caused the incident and it was not an ICS event.  The cause was due to the Technician bleeding a level bridal too fast causing the volume of gas to make its way to 2 Gas detectors. Since this was a human performance event, coaching was conducted with the individual.  There were no damages to the equipment, no injuries, and no hot work being performed.

Event Description: On June 27, 2024, at approximately 13:50HRS while attempting to fill a SCHMIDT Abrasive Blasting Hopper with abrasive material from a U-Panel Type FIBC/bulk bag personnel experienced a failure of one of the lifting loops. The crane operator had hoisted the bulk bag over the hopper and once it was in position to fill the hopper a crew member noticed an accumulation of water on the outside of the bottom of the bulk bag and liner. The crew then decided not to unload the blasting media from the bulk bag into the hopper, therefore, signaled the crane operator to hoist the bulk bag to set it back down onto the platform deck. Just after the bulk bag was clear of the top of the hopper and the load began to swing, the lift loop failure happened. Once the woven synthetic fiber of the lifting loop/strap broke resulting in the weight of the load shifting, the weight of the load was not equally disbursed. The bag then split open along the seam of the same side of the lifting loop failure causing unspent media to fall onto the hopper and the surrounding solid deck of the platform. The unspent media was contained in the deck and collected manually.

Event Consequences: FIBC damage and LOPC.

FIBC Cost: $44.00

On 06/29/2024 at 0430 hrs., the crew was setting the 250-Ton crane up for deck lifts utilizing the auxiliary line. To perform these tasks, the hold back tuggers were attached to the main block, and the Subsea Beacon was removed. After attaching the left and right tugger lines, it was noticed that the left tugger line came out of the spool flange and was wrapped around the inboard shaft. The deck foreman was instructed to pay out until the tugger line was back inside the spool, which in coordination with the crane operator required about 60' to be paid out. After the tugger line was corrected, the crane operator was instructed to come up on the main block and take tension on the tuggers. With the main block approximately 16 meters (approx. 52 feet) off the deck, the crane operator began tensioning the right tuggers. Once the right tugger was tensioned, the crane operator continued tensioning the left tugger line to complete the process. It was at this time the left tugger line parted approximately 30 feet from the attachment point on the main block. As a result of this event, the shock from the line parting and possibly the sur-loc hook not connected properly may have caused the hook to open, resulting in the 8-ton shackle with attached Sur-Loc hook, (weighing approximately 12.7 lbs. together), and remaining line falling an estimated 52.8 feet to the deck. According to the DROPS calculator, this dropped object event falls into the "Fatality" category. However, no crew members were impacted by the dropped object or incident, as the nearest crew member involved was approximately 15 feet away. towards the middle of the main deck area. All other crew members were about 30 feet from the impact point. No injuries were reported and nothing entered the water.
Crane operator used radio communication. Estimate cost of repair wire rope~$500. Please see attached deck layout, photos, CO and rigger Certificates, JSA and incident report.

- Stopped the job.
- Investigation initiated.
- Replaced the port hold-back pennant rope.
- The left and right pennant rigging consisting of shackles, slings, and Sur-Loc hooks were replaced with vessel spares.

- The rigging crew was reminded that while unspooling/spooling pennant lines positive control of pennants must be maintained with a tagline until fully spooled up or connected to the big block.

At 1157 on 6/29/2024, the fire alarm was sounded after an Ecoserv fire watch (FW) on the upper deck NW called into the control room to report the vacuum pump they were conducting FW on had started to smoke. The person fulfilled FW duties and shut the equipment down, monitored for incipient fire and mustered once fast responders arrived to the scene. The fast responders reported no visible fire and light white smoke emanating from the equipment exhaust. Fire team arrived at the scene and applied water to the equipment to eliminate the possibility of a fire emerging. Once the pump was cooled down the maintenance team began with inspection to troubleshoot the situation and find the root cause. Investigation is ongoing. Damage costs are estimated to be less than $20,000.

Facility attained full POB muster in nine minutes, no personnel were injured, and no damage to any other equipment has been observed. 

Please see the attached photos of the Ecoserv Vacuum Pump for reference.

Corrective Action Taken:  The mini vac 016 was received back at the Ecoserv facility on the afternoon of 7/8/24. On 7/9/24 shop foreman, two offshore supervisors, VP of Specialized Cleaning, Director of Specialized Cleaning and Safety Manager gather to begin the investigation.  A camera was run through the exhaust of the mist extractor and severe clogging of residual material was found.  The inlet filter screen was found to be clogged with blasting sand, which compromised the air flow through the blower causing the mist extractor to overheat. This is what caused the unit to smoke.

The mist extractor was removed and cut open to inspect the internal honeycomb and mesh. Replacement parts were installed.

Procedural Changes
1. Update Mini-Vac procedure to note the following steps:
    Remove three (3) eye-nuts
    Remove cover, secure O-ring on inside of cover
    Remove SS screen and inspect for build-up, wash if needed.
    Replace SS screen
    Replace cover, verify O-ring is in place inside of cover
    Replace three eye-nuts, hand tighten each evenly.

Maintenance Changes
2. Maintenance process will be updated to include an inspection of the mist extractor and inlet screen after every job. If any cleaning is necessary, the mist extractor can be soaped and/or steam cleaned and reinspected after cleaning. 

Improve supervisor / employee skills and knowledge
3. Safety bulletin to go out to all offshore personnel discussing steps to take to prevent overheating when utilizing a mini vac unit. NO dry product is to be vacuumed with mini vac units. This safety bulletin will be acknowledged by all personnel to show review and understanding.

On 7/27/24 at approximately 01:30 hours, while transferring Franks togs from forward to aft, crane #4 lifted the tongs from the Pod Shop rooftop to bring them aft to the Well Test Deck. However, when the tongs lifted off the deck, they moved aft horizontally, approximately 6" off the deck, and came into contact with a protrusion off of the headache rack which holds the Pod Shop hatch in place when it is open. This caused damage to the fiberglass pneumatic junction box on the side of the Franks tongs unit. A broken piece of the lid of the junction box fell about 4' to the deck. All crew were in the safe step-back area and the lifting area was barricaded off as a Red Zone. No personnel were in the vicinity of the junction box at the time. No taglines were used, and this was not a blind lift. Weather during the time was Wind 6 knots from astern, Sea 2 to 3 feet, with some vessel movement. A UHF Radio was used as a form of communication with the crane operator.  See attached photos of work area, prompt card and JBD board, and Crane and Rigger certificates.  There were no injuries during this time.  Cost to repair damages to junction box is about $848.95 which includes cost of labor and fees.

Corrective Actions: During handovers, both crews convened in the Marine/Deck office to review the incident. They emphasized the critical importance of maintaining vigilance and ensuring that the Banksman always has a clear line of sight. Additionally, it was reinforced that crane operators always have the option to request the use of tag lines to enhance safety and control during lifting operations.

As the crew was in the process of lowering a gearbox to the lower deck, through an open hatch on the upper deck, the load swung toward the northern part of the hatch. As the load swung, the retaining latch became entangled with a support beam. When the signal man realized the load was snagged, he signaled for the operator to "boom up". The subsequent lift caused the load to swing in the opposite direction (southward). This shift in the load caused the retaining latch to bend slightly outward. Upon completion of lift, the operator noticed a deformation in the crane latch.

[REDACTED_ORGANIZATION] notified the [REDACTED_AGENCY] District of the incident and the crane was placed out of service until a certified crane operator deemed the repairs adequate and the crane safe to operate (report attached). The repair was done on site, by [REDACTED_COMPANY] personnel at no additional cost.

In order to ensure this event does not reoccur, future loads will only be lowered through the center of an open hatch and a 20' stinger will be utilized to prevent the hook block from entering the hatch. There was no other property damage.

What is Oxy's policy that would determine whether a bleed down or purge of process piping is required during Hot Work or Spark Producing Work vs simply monitoring on the HMI?

Spark producing work requires continuous gas monitoring at the location and a permit. Stops work if combustible gas monitor registers over 10% LEL or when flammable gases are suspected.

Hot Work Policy- Using an open Flame within 35 feet of aboveground equipment containing flammable or combustible material. Using a non-open flame or an internal combustible engine within 10 feet of aboveground equip containing flammable or combustible material. Permissible atmospheric (Flammability) concentrations are <10% LEL/LFL, (Oxygen) 19.5-23.5% if condition are not met purging is then completed until achieved.

*In Megarme's JHA, there is no indication that Megarme was made aware that the control room was continuously monitoring pressure transmitters on the HMI and that there was an existing hazard present. All crafts report to control room to obtain permit to work and have discussion with CRO. This practice is to ensure CRO is aware of any activities that may affect any safety system/equipment/SIMOPS. Communications from CRO & actual performer of activity is achieved at this point.

On August 20, 2024 at approximately 04:30, the crane crew was making a lift of a 4x4x4 basket from the accumulator deck to the plus 50 deck below. The DSP advised the crane operator to come up on the basket. The basket was empty and located three inches to the side of the windwall and the lip of the basket was three inches different in height than the railing of the windwall. The crane operator said that the weight was good so he began to make the lift. As soon as the crane operator began to make the lift, the basket made contact with and was hung beneath the railing of the windwall. The DSP who was ten foot back and at a safe distance, told the crane operator, all stop, over the radio. Before the crane operator had stopped the lift, one leg of the four part sling had broken. The DSP again was at a safe distance away from the load. After further inspection by the crane mechanic it was also found that the crane hook had minor stretch to the opening of the hook rendering it out of service. The damaged items were replaced before putting the crane back in service. It should be noted that the basket was only lifted 3 inches off the deck when it hung up on the structure. There were no injuries reported. Cost of sling was under $500 and The crane hook assembly was about $19,000. Please see attached photos, permit, JSA and certificates.

Corrective Actions:
The damaged items were replaced before putting the crane back in service. A meeting was held with crane crews to speak about using a longer sling so as to keep the crane hook away from the Windwall. This will help prevent the lift from getting hung up. Disseminate the learning to all 4 of crews as lessons learned.

Axess will perform an initial NDT. Returned to operations with alternate turning device and yoke in place. Discussions with the crew were held on the importance of taking a time out when equipment does not respond as expected.

The fan was then grounded, plugged into an outlet, and powered on. During a test run, the fan operated for less than a minute before switching off. As worker moved towards the receptacle to turn off the power, the worker heard an arcing sound followed by an arc, which self-extinguished immediately. Further inspection revealed that saturated hydraulic fluid rags and absorbent pads stored in a garbage bag on a shelf above the fans, had leaked. After the incident, fluid residue was found inside the fan plug housing, which was not visible beforehand and was only noticed due to the hole caused by the arcing. No mustering took place and there were no injuries.  The only damage was to the receptacle and the electrical plug which cost approximately $500.  The arc occurred on the top of the Southeast hull column top.  There was no hot work going on, only test running the temporary air blower to be used for Confined Space entry into the Hull Column.  _x000D_
_x000D_
Corrective Actions Taken: The electricians checked out the equipment and both the receptacle and blower were taken out of service until repairs can be made. Before, the plug in the equipment was pre inspected and cleaned of residue Hydraulic oil that was spilled on plug while in a storage locker. After the incident and further inspection of the plug, it seems that they still had some residue Hydraulic oil inside of the receptacle plug which caused the short. The storage box was also cleaned and will not allow any fluid or other material stored in them except for the equipment needed for the ISIP inspections. _x000D_

1) Do not assume that the hook is high enough to clear surrounding areas when moving to pick up the next lift.  Ensure you have cabled up higher than everything surrounding your lifting area and then proceed to swing and position over the next lift._x000D_
2) Be aware of surroundings at all times. _x000D_
3) If you aren't completely sure you are clear, stop the job and call additional help (a spotter) to go to area in question and ask them to signal you. Only then will you proceed with crane activity once it is truly verified and there is no more doubt on if you are clear or not.  _x000D_
4) Always stay focused on task/lift at hand and not already thinking of next thing/lift to get done.  Focus only on one lift at a time so that if something changes during lift, you are prepared to stop and reevaluate immediately instead of being sidetracked on something else which will slow your response time. _x000D_

Incident Title:  Wireline Parting / Activation of Upper Shear Ram.

Description:  While recovering the BHA after the 2nd perforation run on October 24th , at approximately 05:30 am an unexpected increase in tension was noticed by the wireline technician.  The wireline crew immediately stopped the wire and called the client representative.  
 
Immediate action:  The well was shut-in at the choke and PWV/PIV.  The grease still was still holding well pressure and there was no release to sea.   Multiple meetings were conducted to risk assess options with offshore crews and onshore support.  Procedure amendments and clarifications were created to attempt recovery of the BHA into the lubricator.  Decision was made to eventually continue with approved overpull to recover the BHA into the lubricator.  The BHA was moved up-hole from 6,898-ft (initial stuck point) to 6,512-ft.  With 5,900-lbs of tension at 5,612-ft, the wire above the PCH in open water parted, leaving a section in open water connected through the PCH, and down to the BHA.    After discussing the status with the leadership team, decision was made to activate the upper shear ram to cut the wire and let the BHA fall to current TD.  
 
Additional Information:  Upon review, the wire parted at less than half of the maximum tension allowed per procedure.  More meetings where scheduled and risk assessments performed.  The consensus of the group was to cut the wire with the upper shear ram in the WCP and recover the PCH to surface.   Procedural amendments/clarifications were created, and the wire was cut per procedure.  The subsea assets were flushed per procedure and the PCH and wire were recovered to deck.  At no time during the event was well control compromised, and no wellbore fluids were released to the environment.

This evening while conducting lifting activities on the Mid Deck Production, a connex contacted an isolation valve downstream of the clay valve for Zone 12 of the firewater deluge system.

Summary: 
Starboard forward crane was attempting to set a connex in place. November 13, 2024 @ 1300 hours while offloading the weekly supply vessel using the Compression Crane, the crane operator observed what looked like a white piece of paper floating down towards the Main Deck. Upon further inspection, the object was identified as a piece of poly (plastic) about the size of an adult hand and weighed approximately 0.4 pounds. The poly is designed to prevent the crane cables from coming into direct contact with the metal boom frame, reducing the risk of damage and metallurgy issues. 2024-12-02 -  - In response to fire incident on GC-52-CPP on Nov 20, 2024. 
     On November 20,2024 an incident occurred on GC-52-CPP during cleanout operations being performed by Acadian Contractors cleaning crew on the Dehy Afterscrubber MBF-0233. Cleaning crew were on deck but not in immediate area, a loud noise was noticed, upon investigating the noise it was noticed that a flame came from the vessel, crew evacuated the area and notified facility PIC. There was no Hot Work being performed on GC-52-CPP at the time of the incident, there was no Injuries to crew, and no damage to equipment. The Platform had been shut in since Aprill 2024 for decommissioning activities and all vessels had been previously flushed, filled and drained utilizing seawater to reduce the amount of hydrocarbons in the vessels for cleanout. 

An onsite investigation conducted with BSEE and Operations personnel, along with interviews of all personnel involved, concluded there was no definitive proof of source of ignition, two possible sources of ignition were identified as 
.Static Charge due to the dry air conditions and cooler weather. 
. Possible Pyrophoric scale as explained in BSEE Safety Alert No. 462, May 12, 2023.  

Although filling and flushing operations were conducted with seawater, the vessel was never isolated from nearby vessels with the use of blind flanges or spectacles, nor purged of hydrocarbon gas utilizing an inert gas like nitrogen.  The manhole cover was opened facing the wind allowing air to enter the vessel and did not allow a true reading on the gas monitor. 

Since the incident MCOP has implemented the following 
.All vessels are to be isolated from all other vessels during the cleaning process 
. All vessels should be purged utilizing an inert gas prior to cleaning operations.

On 12/02/24 at approximately 1000 hours, while OSV [REDACTED_NAME] was offloading cargo to [REDACTED_NAME], a 90ft basket swung and broke the water tight call box on the aft deck phone. Radio communication was held during the time of the incident with the crane operator. There was no JSA. Onsite JBD was utilized for Boat Lifts and is not formal so after completion the board is wiped clean. While winds was gusting to 25 seas 8ft, [REDACTED_NAME] was angled providing a lee for the vessel to operate in. The crew was standing clear of the basket forward on the deck. The damaged box was noticed later. The call box was collected and brought inside to prevent damage to the phone. Cost estimate to repair the damage to the call box is $200. No other injuries or damages were noted and or reported. Please see attached [REDACTED_MEDICAL_DETAIL], witness statement, weather report, and photos.

Learnings: Elevated sea state combined with long lifts was the root cause of the incident. When lifting long baskets there is a chance the ends will get inside the headache rack. With the vessel rolling and the wind blowing on the basket, it's not always possible for the crane operator to keep the lift laying alongside the headache rack. When loading the vessel, the long baskets are accounted for and try to keep the ends from more critical sections ex mud, dry bulk and fuel piping and venting. With the elevated sea state, it's safer to keep the crew clear from the basket preventing injuries. As soon as practical, a documented safety meeting with all crewmembers will be held to share this scenario and the prevented measures above.

The corrective action from the rig's standpoint to prevent a similar situation in the future would be for the vessel to not mount such equipment on the bumper railing subject to and in proximity of lifts.

At approximately 17:00 hours on 1 October 2014, the offshore supply vessel (OSV)
Endurance lost station keeping while conducting well operations for Fieldwood Energy
LLC (Fieldwood) on Well A002 located at the Eugene Island (EI) Block 355A platform.
The Endurance is a dynamically-positioning (DP) capable OSV equipped with a DP-1
system and is owned and operated by Freedom Marine Services (FMS) of Houma,
Louisiana. The FMS Endurance had a cement pump staged on board that was connected to
the Well A002 production tree with rigid high pressure lines and had pressure tested
the wireline lubricator to 4000 pounds per square inch. When the crew was running in
the hole with wireline and was at a depth of 9000 feet (ft), for reasons unknown, the
FMS Endurance lost its station keeping and started moving away from the EI-355A
platform. As the vessel moved off location, the Well A002 production tree was severed
at the wellhead flange and fell overboard but was later retrieved. The well was
secured by closing the downhole safety valve and by installing a temporary flange cap
on the tubing head. The lubricator on top of the production tree and connected to
the wireline unit staged on the platform, fell over onto the platform deck damaging
some hand railing and grating in the vicinity of Well A002. An estimated area of 300
ft by 50 ft of oil was spilled into the offshore waters which was reported to the
United States Coast Guard (USCG) National Response Center (NRC), NRC Report #
1097096. There were no reported injuries associated with this incident. On 6
October 2014, Well A002 was secured by installing a new production tree for future
remedial work.
In a written statement to the USCG, the captain of the FMS Endurance stated that the
bow thruster alarm had sounded several times on 1 October 2014, but each time it was
able to reset into the DP mode without losing station keeping. However, at 16:34
hours, the bow thruster alarm sounded again and although power was not loss, the DP
system was failing to maintain the vessel's position. As a consequence, the captain
took over manual controls and put both throttles full astern, but the vessel
continued to move forward due to its initial momentum causing the rigid high pressure
line to shear the Well A002 production tree off the wellhead.
During October of 2014, FMS and USCG along with International Marine Systems, Marine
Technologies, Fugro, and Rhodes Electronics completed a series of diagnostic checks
of the entire DP systems. FMS was directed by the USCG to try to recreate the
circumstances that occurred on 1 October 2014 as recorded on the FMS Endurance's
event log. Several days of sea trials were conducted; however, and no issues were
found with the DP system. However, during the analysis of the FMS Endurance's event
log, it revealed that the DP system, gyro and throttles all went out at once due to
some type of electrical interference.
The FMS Endurance had a communication tower recently installed and according to the
communication tower vendor, it should not have been placed near any vital GPS
equipment. On the day of the incident, the communications tower was located 6 inches
(in) from the throttle system boards, 28 in from the gyro system and the DP system
was approximately 1 ft below the communication tower. Based upon this information,
all parties believed that since the communications tower was located within 1 ft of
the DP system, it may have caused electronic interferences as it received or
transmitted signals on the day of the incident.
FMS has since implemented a policy for all of their DP vessels that no communications
equipment can be located within 1 meter (3.28 ft) of the throttle control computer,
DP computer or gyros. In addition, a safety break-away hose coupling will be
utilized in future applications.
On 24 February 2015, the USCG and BSEE issued a joint Safety Alert that addressed DP
system failures on OSVs that are engaged in oil and gas operations in the U.S. outer
continental shelf.
MMS - FORM 2010 PAGE: 2 OF 4
­
EV2010R 08-APR-2015
­



For Public Release
The FMS Incident Investigation Report submitted to BSEE by Fieldwood indicated that
the probable cause of the FMS Endurance losing station keeping and stripping off the
Well A002 production tree was attributed to some type of electrical interference with
the DP system from a communications tower that was installed on the vessel near the
GPS equipment.

On October 13, 2014 at approximately 1335 hours, an employee was injured while
attempting to hydro test a pipeline.
The injured employee (IE) was part of a crew that was in the process of hydro-testing
the oil system on a new facility. The maximum pressure to be tested on the system was
9000 psi.
As the pressure reached approximately 8000 psi, the seal on a check valve failed on
the #6 flow line. The testing was stopped and the pressure was bled down to repair
the check valve. The crew stopped for lunch after bleeding the pressure.
Prior to resuming the check valve repair, the test gauges were checked and 2800 psi
was found on a gauge installed downstream of the check valve 2 (CV2) but the IE
failed to check the gauge installed downstream of check valve 1 (CV1). The trapped
pressure located downstream of the (CV2) was bled down utilizing a needle valve
located on that section of piping.

designee shall be responsible for system walk down. There was a foreman present
during hydro-testing operations but failed to detect the hazard.

removed to access the leaking valve, trapped pressure downstream of the (CV1) was
released striking the IE in the left side of face and head. The IE was found
unconscious due to his injuries. The IE was transported to a medical facility for
additional treatment.
