The following incident occurred onboard the Drillship Seadrill West Neptune on 5-May- 2016 at approximately 09:30-hrs. The incident occurred after a successful crane lift had been performed. The Injured Person (I.P.) is a rig roustabout and the incident occurred on the pipe skate deck aft of the rig floor. The injury (right arm) required an evacuation of the I.P. from the facility. After further medical evaluation, surgery was required to repair the Ulna bone in the right arm. The crane crew consisted of an Assistant Crane Operator (ACO) and two Roustabouts. A lift of a TIW valve from the rig floor to the sub-sea set back area had just been completed. Prior to conducting the lift the ACO noticed that one of the guide arms at the end of the crane boom was stuck at a 90-degree angle. (Each guide arm weighs approximately 300-lbs.). The ACO decided to proceed with the lift without notifying any supervisors concerning this issue. The ACO then positioned the crane boom over the handrail of the port riser skate bridge area. This was done in order for the roustabout (I.P.) to access the stuck guide arm. NOTE: Seadrill has a policy in place for all crane and lifting operations to be hands free. After instruction from the ACO the I.P. reached up with his left hand and touched the guide arm causing it to break loose. Witness statements state that as the guide arm was coming down the I.P. attempted to stop the guide arm with his right hand/arm from colliding with the handrail. At this time the I.P.'s arm was caught between the guide arm and the handrail causing the injury. Witness interviews have stated that this guide arm had become stuck on at least three previous occasions, although no written records or reports were available. No former risk assessment as per Seadrill Directive was performed prior to this task being conducted. This was also the I.P.'s first hitch on this rig and was directed to perform a task that he had never previously performed. Two of the three personnel involved in the operation were new to their positions.

On May 5, 2016, the H&P 205 crane crew was conducting a blind crane lift from the Safe Welding Area/Production Deck to the pipe rack. The crew on the production deck consisted of a Designated Signal Person (DSP) and two Roustabouts. Two tag lines (one 15 feet 10 inches in length, one 24 feet 8 inches in length, one half inch in size) were being utilized during the lift. The Crane Operator was given the all clear from the DSP and began maneuvering the cargo box. While the box was being maneuvered, the Injured Person's (IP's) right leg became entangled in the 24 foot tagline and he was pulled in the direction of the handrail. The DSP gave the "all stop" command to the Crane Operator who responded immediately, but the momentum of the cargo box continued and the IP was pulled over the water. While being pulled over the water, the IP grabbed the tagline and his leg became untangled but the IP could not maintain his grip and slid down the tagline falling 106 feet into the Gulf of Mexico. IP was able to swim to a ladder attached to the SPAR and climb to a small platform just above the water. The rescue team performed a rope rescue and IP was transported to the medic's office for evaluation and treatment. IP was later transported by Search and Rescue (SAR) helicopter to UTMB in Galveston, Texas, for further evaluation and treatment.

A Floorman was removing a 3" kill line from the storage area at the back of the rig floor. The hose was being hoisted by the rig floor tugger and hoisting straps. While doing so, a clamp on the hose hung up on a beam.  The Floorman stated that he used his right hand to push out on the hose while his left hand was positioned on the handrail.  When the hose came free from the beam, the worker's left index and middle finger were pinched between the hose and handrail. The floorman was wearing impact gloves.  _x000D_
The IP was transported to shorefor medical evaluation and/or treatment. We have learned that there are no fractures to his fingers nor were any sutures needed to close any skin abrasions.  IP has been issued a "Full Duty Release".  This case will be classified as a "First Aid". 
_x000D_Causal factor: The safety clamp on the kill hose created a hang-up point when lowered in close promitry to the structure..  Root cause:  Injured Person (IP) exhibited an at-risk behavior by grabbing the air hoist cable with his right hand to shake the hose off the angle iron. The position of his left hand being placed in the line of fire (between the hose and handrail) was not recognized when attempting to manually push on the hose.  Again, the IP suffered only brusing and minor abrasions.   The incident will be shared with the Ensco fleet to heighten awareness how work-teams can effectively manage the risks and hazards associated with this task.  Consideration is being given to installing a deflector plate to prevent future hang up points by the safety clamp on the kill line.

Operator saw smoke then fire coming from top of IP compressor. Operator shut in compressor and mechanic put out fire with 30lb. dry chemical extinquisher. It appears insulation caught fire. There was no pollution or injuries in this incident._x000D_
_x000D_After investigation, it appears that the cause of the fire was that an oil fill-up valve was left open which led to overfilling of the compressor engine crankcase. This overfill caused oil to be picked up by the crankshaft and moved into the crankcase air breather. The oil was then drawn up into the engine exhaust by the Venturi. The oil seeped out of a crack in the expansion joint which in turn saturated the insulation blanket. High temperatures at the turbo caused ignition. The estimated cost of replacing the turbo, insulation blanket and expansion joint is thought to be $1700.00. A company wide Safety Alert will be distributed to be used at Weekly Safety Meetings.

On May 13, 2016, a crane incident occurred at approximately 5:30pm on Fieldwood Energy’s West Cameron 130-B facility. The Crane Operator was attempting to transfer a cutting box from a workboat (Marine Vessel Commander) onto the platform. During this attempt, the cutting box contacted a stack of four-foot by twenty-foot grating that was also on the workboat’s deck. Upon contact, the grating was shifted and impacted the Rigger on the workboat causing a laceration to his right shin area along with a laceration to his left forearm. On the day of the incident three Operators departed West Cameron 100 via the workboat and arrived at West Cameron 130-B around 8:30am. The work scope for the day involved draining all the platform vessels’ fluids and chemicals on-board into cutting boxes. In addition to transportation for the operations crew, the workboat also contained the general cargo to facilitate the work scope. This included two cutting boxes and one four-foot by eight-foot basket with pumps and hoses. Additionally, the workboat contained miscellaneous cargo that was destined for other facilities, which included two tote tanks and a stack of loose grating. At approximately 10:45am, the Crane Operator successfully offloaded the four-foot by eight-foot basket and one of the cutting boxes onto the platform. Around 4:00pm a cutting box that was approximately seventy-five percent full was successfully back-loaded onto the vessel. At this time, an empty cutting box was effectively lifted from the vessel and onto the platform. Later around 5:30pm, the cutting box on the platform was full and there was still a small amount of fluids left to drain on the platform. Therefore, the full cutting box was back-loaded onto the boat and the seventy-five percent full cutting box was rigged up to bring back onto the platform. While offloading the seventy-five percent full cutting box the crane block was not properly centered over the load prior to lifting. This was primarily due to the insufficient positioning of the load block; the Rigger should have ensured the proper position prior to giving the hand signal to lift. Additionally, prior to giving the Crane Operator the hand signal to lift the load the Rigger should have ensured he was safe from the line-of-fire along with any associated pinch points or deck hazards. Due to the block being offset, upon lifting, the load swung and contacted the stack of grating. The stack of grating was tied together with half-inch twine but was not secured in place to the deck by adequate means which should have taken place prior to transport to prevent the load from shifting or breaking loose. This allowed the grating to shift which then impacted the Rigger due to his near proximity. Due to the Rigger sustaining injury the Crane Operator chose not to set the lift back onto the workboat but rather set it on the platform. At this time, the three Operators made their way onto the vessel and the decision was made to transport the Rigger to shore where he received medical treatment including twenty stitches to his right shin area.

A High High Gas Alarm on ASH-8042, located on the Booster Gas Compressor and skid, came into the control system initiating an ESD.  All personnel reported to the alarm in accordance with emergency procedures.  Confirmed that the "confirmed gas signal" originated from the topsides production area but was no longer reading a high gas level on any Gas Detector Sensors. The On-Scene Commander and Fire Team 2 Lead confirmed the area was all clear. The source of the release was identified as a 1/2" SS Tubing Line on the Fuel Gas circuit for the compressor which appears to have failed due to fatigue.  We completed muster of all parties and stood down crew at 06:10. _x000D_
After further investigation, it was found that the failed tubing was 1/2" x .035 WT. This tubing was included as part of the compressor package provided by Exterran;  however, this tubing is not suitable for gas service per the Swagelok catalogue.  The tubing was replaced with .049 WT prior to returning the compressor to service. 1/2" SS Tubing of .035 WT is not utilized for any service on the vessel in regards to process equipment;  the minimum purchased is .049 WT.  The plan forward is to inspect all Exterran Package tubing in gas service on the three provided compressors and replace as necessary._x000D_

On May 19, 2016 a Transocean Electrician received electrical burns to his right hand and forearm while performing maintenance on the drawworks motors. The incident occurred aboard the Transocean Deepwater Asgard which was working for Chevron USA Inc. The Injured Person (IP) was preparing to conduct a megger test at the time of the incident as part of the rig's yearly preventive maintenance program (PM). The megger test is a method of testing the integrity of electrical wires and components by applying voltage to the desired components and measuring it's resistance to flow. This test will detect if there is any leakage of electricity that otherwise may go undetected by other test methods. With the megger test, it is possible to detect deteriorated wires, bad motors, generators, transformers, etc... prior to components actually failing. On the day of the incident, rig management met and agreed the PM for the megger test on the drawworks motors would be conducted that evening once the well was in a safe state. During this meeting, procedures Rig Recommended Practice (RRP) DGD-543 and Written Work Assessment (WRA) DGD-1121 were approved to be used in order to complete the PM, and a Level 2 Energy Isolation (lock-out/tag-out) was going to be required. However, following the meeting the Electrical/Electronic (E/E) Supervisors agreed that the approved RRP and WRA were inadequate and needed to be revised. They knew that the Original Equipment Manufacture's procedure (OEM) had been used successfully for similar tasks and the OEM's procedure was less intrusive, so they decided to instruct the crew to use the OEM's procedure, Siemens Blue Drive 908.4401.09.1A. On the evening of the incident, the E/E Supervisors instructed the IP and Chief Electrician to perform the PM that evening and also to follow the OEM Siemens Blue Drive procedure instead of the approved RRP and WRA. They were also instructed to update the rig's RRP and WRA after they completed the PM, based off of the OEM's procedure. Neither had ever completed this task before, but the IP had performed similar isolations in this electrical panel. Around 1900 hours the IP completed the "Energy Isolation Certificate" and the "Try to Operate" paperwork and posted it on the Bridge. Around 2045 hours the IP and Chief Electrician reported to the Mud Module Electrical Room to begin the PM. They discussed the Siemens Blue Drive Procedure and agreed to work in adjoining cabinets and megger two inverters at the same time, with the IP calling out the procedure for both to follow. They proceeded to switch the breakers from automatic to manual mode to prevent anyone from accidently operating the breakers while they were working in the cabinet. At this point, they believed the breaker to be open (which would de-energize the cabinet). However, in order to actually open the breaker in manual mode a special tool is required to be inserted into the breaker and turned until the breaker is open. The Siemens Blue procedure did not mention the need for this tool to be used in order to open the breaker (nor did the RRP and WRA). The IP then viewed the Human Machine Interface (HMI) for the panel and observed no voltage present. He interpreted this to mean that the system was de-energized and they proceeded with the procedure. This observation would prove to be a misinterpretation of the system. The HMI was reading zero voltage because the drawworks were sitting idle. Had the drawworks been moving, voltage would have been observed. They considered using a multimeter to test the voltage across the busses, but their meter was only good for up to 1000 volts, and the voltage of the busses was known to fluctuate above 1000 volts. Other equipment to check for voltage above 1000 volts was available but they did not take the time to acquire the equipment. At this point a padlock should have been applied to the breaker in accordance with the Level 2 isolation requirements and the Siemens 17. INVESTIGATION FINDINGS: For Public Release MMS - FORM 2010 PAGE: 3 OF EV2010R 17-AUG-2016 5 Blue Drive Procedure, but the IP and Chief Electrician decided not to apply a lock. Had they attempted to apply the lock, they would have known the breaker was still closed (energizing the cabinet) because the lock can only be applied when the breaker is in the open position. Furthermore, only the Offshore Installation Manager (OIM) can give permission to deviate from isolation requirements, and he was not aware of their decision to not follow Level 2 Isolation requirements. The Siemens Blue Drive Procedure called for a jumper wire from the positive to negative DC bus bar. When the IP made this connection, the jumper short circuited the 1000 volt DC bus which resulted in an arc flash that burned the IP's hand and forearm. The moment the bus arced out, the lighting on the rig turned off and immediately back on. The on tour E/E Supervisor went to the bridge to investigate the lighting flicker and learned that the breakers the IP and Chief Electrician should have opened to conduct their PM were still closed. Knowing they were working in the area, the E/E Supervisor traveled to the work area to check on the IP and Chief Electrician. Upon arrival the E/E Supervisor asked if anyone was injured, to which both the IP and Chief Electrician both denied any injuries. They then began discussing the incident and assessing equipment damage. To discuss a plan forward they relocated to the Maintenance Office and during this discussion the E/E Supervisor noticed the IP appeared to be in pain. At this time the IP confessed that he was experiencing pain in his hand and forearm. The IP was taken to the Rig Hospital to initiate treatment and the OIM and Chevron Drill Sight Manager (DSM) were notified of the incident. At this time it was decided that the IP should be evacuated for further evaluation. The IP was treated for radiant heat burns and placed on restricted duty for one week. Multiple decisions lead to this incident. The procedures that were initially agreed to be followed in order to complete the task were found to be inadequate by the E/E Supervisors, so they instructed the IP and Chief Electrician to use the OEM Siemens Blue procedure. The change in procedure was not adequately evaluated for hazards or thoroughness by the E/E Supervisors, the IP, or the Chief Electrician prior to starting the PM. The tool required to be used in order to open the breaker in manual mode was not mentioned in any of the procedures for meggering the drawworks. The IP and Chief Electrician had not completed this task previously, and no one was present at the worksite with sufficient experience to properly isolate the circuit. They decided not to follow the approved Level 2 isolation requirements which required a lock to be installed on an open breaker. Had this procedure been followed, it would have been discovered that the breaker was closed and the circuit was energized. The IP filed the "Energy Isolation Certificate" and "Try to Operate" an hour and a half prior to actually doing the work, which should not have been done until the breaker was isolated and verified to be isolated by testing the system during the task.

On 29-May-2016 at 1310 hrs a Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S) gas release of 400 parts per million (ppm) occurred on Main Pass (MP) 299-FP Platform, OCS-G 12362, operated by Freeport McMoran Energy. The MP 299-FP Platform processes gas and liquids containing a high concentration of H2S. The field’s wells are all “sour” and are located on remote satellite platforms. They are flowline connected to the FP process facility. The FP Platform process system was designed to resist the H2S corrosion when installed in 1991. The system has not had issues with H2S release at a significantly higher occurrence rate than other platforms handling high concentration of H2S. The release occurred during pigging operations on the flowline from the MP-299 "A" to the "FP" Platform. While receiving the 6-inch pig from MP 299-A Platform to MP 299-FP Platform, the crew started draining the fluids from the pig trap. This trap ties into a common drain line header to the MBF-110 High Pressure (HP) vent scrubber. While the crew were draining the fluids, the H2S sensors at #81 and #83 located near the pig trap and the gas MBF-935 Buyback Gas Scrubber skid, were "amber light" activated. Then the H2S high alarm sounded indicating a release of sour gas and the monitoring panel located in the quarters indicated the sensors previously in a "orange" state had detected a high concentration of H2S. The release caused the H2S alarm to sound and the safety systems then shut in the platform. All personnel onboard mustered to the primary station where they donned the Safe-Contained Breathing Air (SCBA) and waited for further instructions. All nonessential personnel where then instructed to stay in the primary muster area. The response team (RT) that included the H2S Safety Burner Tech, the Field Lead Operator and the Deck Lead Operator masked up with voice active SCBAs and went to inspect both H2S sensors #81 and #83. The RT began using gas H2S detectors to check the area around sensors #81 and #83 to discover the source of the leak. At the same time, the Field Foreman was verbally reporting the H2S parts per million (PPM) readings for sensors #81 and #83. While the RT was still checking the area, the Field Foreman notified the crew that the H2S, as measured at sensors #81 and #83, had dissipated to a safe level according to H2S panel readings. He therefore declared an "all-clear" of the H2S high level. Following the "all-clear," the RT went upstairs to meet with the rest of the personnel onboard. Shortly afterwards, as the crew were taking off their SCBA packs, the high H2S alarm sounded again, activated by the H2S sensor #81 located in the buyback skid. The crew donned a new set of SCBAs to ensure there was enough safe breathing air to make it back downstairs to the safe breathing air manifold. The RT used gas detectors to again check the area around the MBF-935 Buyback Gas Scrubber. During this check the RT found a gas leak in 2-inch pipe outlet coming from the MBF-935 Buyback Gas Scrubber, below the south side cellar deck. BSEE Investigators arrived on 31-May-2016 to conduct an incident investigation of the H2S release of 400 ppm. Statements, pictures and initial reports were obtained. A safety walkthrough inspection was conducted of the 2-inch piping run that leads to a 6-inch common vent line, and then to the MBF-110 HP Vent Scrubber. Based on inspection of the equipment, interviews, and documents reviewed, the BSEE investigation found that during a pigging operation from MP 299-A to MP 299-FP platform, the following were causes of the H2S release: 17. INVESTIGATION FINDINGS: For Public Release MMS - FORM 2010 PAGE: 3 OF EV2010R 15-NOV-2016 7 1. The MBF-935 Buyback Scrubber 2-inch outlet piping was found to have extensive exterior corrosion which compromised the integrity of the piping. This allowed the release of the H2S gas. Interior corrosion related to H2S was not confirmed because inspection of that portion of the piping was not possible. 2. In addition to the above, the 6-inch vent piping connecting all vessels to the MBF-110 HP Vent Scrubber was found to have pitting corrosion. This was located on the exterior in the form of relatively small isolated “tubercles,” or rust mounds, on the pipe and on the flange fasteners. 3. During the investigation, the BSEE determined the condition of the piping showed evidence of a lack of routine maintenance. Conclusions Failure of the Operator to perform routine corrosion assessment maintenance on piping was the primary cause of this incident. As a result of this incident, the BSEE investigation, and the condition of the facility the Operator shut in the facility because the continued operation was uneconomical. The Operator is developing a "plan forward" as a guideline to the future of the facility and the field.

On May-31-2016, at approximately 2:45pm, an incident occurred during crane lifting operations on West Cameron 616-A. The work crew was removing 381.66’ of 13.375 casing weighing approximately 25,953 lbs. from the well bore when a worker injured his hands. At the time of the incident, the operation being performed included the of use the crane to lift the casing through the casing jacks that were set up on the top deck of the platform, and then lay the casing down on the deck of the platform. The casing was attached to the crane load block with two separate lifting slings approximately 20’ in length. The slings were connected to casing using shackles and the looped ends of the slings were connected to the load block. When the load was lifted approximately 15’, the injured person (IP) instructed the crane operator “to boom up” in order to allow the casing to pass through the casing jacks. At the same time the boom was being raised, the IP put his hands on the slings to assist alignment of the lift through the casing jacks. The casing began to rotate and wrap the slings around each other, trapping the IPs left hand between the slings and momentarily catching the IPs right hand. In order to free the IPs left hand from the slings one of the sling had to be cut with a torch to remove the IPs hand from the sling assembly. The IP received injuries to both hands as follows: 1) the left hand had bruising, and 2) the right hand had a fractured thumb. The IP was released for light duty work on June-1-2016. On June-7-2016, BSEE Lake Charles District inspection team assembled onsite to conduct an investigation into the incident. Two of the three Job Safety Analysis (JSA) completed for the removal of the casing mentioned the need to use tag lines for controlling the load during lifting operations. Furthermore, API Recommended Practice 2D Sixth Edition, May 2007 section 3.2.3 “Moving the Load,” states “Appropriate tag or restraining lines should be used where necessary to control the load”. An inspection of the load block found that the hook would not rotate when a load was applied. The load block was sent to Seatrax for further analysis. During the analysis of the load block, the trunnion bearing was found to be unserviceable. Sand and other particles were found inside the bearing assembly. The sand and particles were found mixed with the grease in the bearing causing the bearing to seize and lock up with minimal force. The seizing of the bearing did not allow the hook to rotate on the load block, which in turn forced the slings to wrap around the IPs hands.

He then gave approval to resume work. _x000D_The fire's size can be estimated using standard paint can dimensions. Considering the flames were seen at the mouth of the paint can, and since a standard paint can has an approximate diameter of 6.5", the size of the fire is estimated to have been 0.23 square feet. With regard to duration, the Fire Watch (who extinguished the flame) stated that the flame caught his attention immediately upon ignition. The paint can was within his span of immediate response, and he had a portable extinguisher at his side. Thus, the duration of the fire is estimated to be less than 5 seconds.

The Braden Winch (Model PD 10-77-1) was dissembled by Gulf Crane Services (Shorebase) to determine a possible cause for the winch failure.  It was found that a Snap Ring was missing from within the inner Motor Output Shaft Coupling. This Snap Ring prevents the Motor Coupling from "Sliding" out of the input shaft. The motor coupling had slid over the Hydraulic Motor Output Shaft, allowing the Sprag/Brake Clutch to become disengaged from the inner splines of the internal brake friction disc. Notable, is the Sprag/Brake Clutch is the Internal Brake Component that holds the load when the hoist control lever is in the "Neutral" Position" thus preventing free-fall of the load. It was determined that through time, forward and reverse motion, the lack of the snap ring allowed the components to finally separate. _x000D_
_x000D_
This winch was rebuilt by Gulf Crane and passed load testing. The Gulf Crane technician who performed the rebuild did not notice the missing snap ring nor was he aware of a Service Bulletin issued indicating "Motor & Coupling Replacement on PD 10 Winches".  Fieldwood has identified (4) additional Model PD 10 winches that were also rebuilt by this specific technician. All were removed from the field and dissembled at the Gulf Crane shop for validation of the snap ring. Three of the four units did have the necessary snap ring required by the specific coupling used.  The remaining unit had a coupling of longer length (previous style model) that did not need a snap ring. Each winch disassembled and inspected._x000D_
_x000D_
Following are these processes:  1.  Full access into PACCAR/Braden Service's Portal to view the latest revised manuals and service bulletins associated with Braden winches, 2. the shop router (work order) has encompassed bulletin verification for signoff by technician and supervisory personnel listing critical components, photos, alerts, etc., 3. all out dated manuals have been destroyed to eliminate the potential for inaccurate information 4. all work though the shop router will be verified and signed off by the supervisor validating compliance with the latest alert, manual and API RP 2d._x000D_

On July 27, 2016, while performing riser running operations on Exxon’s JU104 well, an incident occurred onboard the Maersk Viking involving the rig’s riser skate system. The riser skate trolley, used to transfer riser joints from the rig’s riser deck to the rig floor, derailed from it's track. When the rig crew attempted to repair the skate using a chain hoist (3.2 ton Vital Lever Hoist), one employee was injured. A Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) onsite visit was performed on July 29, 2016. Onsite interviews were conducted and paperwork related to the incident was collected. On the day of the incident, the rig was running roughly 7,000 feet of riser in order to latch the subsea Blowout Prevent (BOP) to the wellhead. The Driller was using the riser skate to shuttle riser joints from the staging area into the derrick. The riser skate trolley was being operated in “trolley freewheeling mode” rather than “trolley drive fwd/aft mode” during the riser running process. The “trolley freewheeling mode” allows the riser trolley to move freely along the conveyer system’s track with no relative speed control. The only means of regulating the trolley’s movement is by restricting the rig’s Top Drive lifting rate when hoisting the riser joint into the derrick. The “trolley drive fwd/aft mode” operates a dual chain drive that attaches the riser skate trolley to the rig’s riser conveyer system. The dual chain drive is used to control the riser trolley’s speed and position when a riser joint is being hoisted up by the rig’s top drive. During this process, a riser joint got caught on the trolley’s front cradle causing it to derail on the rig floor. The rig had to suspend riser running operations until the skate could be repositioned back onto its track. In order to reposition the riser skate, the rig crew decided that a chain hoist (come-a-long) would be quicker than using the rig’s crane. The crew proceeded to anchor the riser skate to a rig floor snubbing post using a 3.2 ton Vital Lever Hoist with a braided metal sling. When tension was applied to the chain hoist, the hoist malfunctioned, causing the hoist handle to spin. The handle struck the employee operating the hoist on the wrist resulting in a bone fracture. The injured person (IP) was sent to shore for further evaluation. The IP returned to the rig the next day with a cast on his wrist and he was placed on restricted work duty. An investigation by Maersk and Exxon was conducted after the incident. The operator investigation concluded that the incident occurred due to a defective chain hoist still in service on the rig floor. The chain hoist was missing a vital retaining pawl latch that prevents the hoist from freely distributing chain from it's ratchet mechanism. Due to multiple chain hoist styles available on the rig, the crew was unfamiliar with the specific hoist selected. This resulted in a failure to notice the missing latch when the specific equipment was selected for the job. The selection of the proper lifting equipment was also brought into question due to a crane being available to perform the lift rather than the chain hoist method. The primary cause for this incident was the defective chain hoist, but poor job planning/hazard recognition, improper pre-use inspection of the equipment, and inadequate training also contributed. Had the crane been used to lift the trolley back onto the tracks, this incident could have been prevented. Had the chain hoist been properly inspected prior to use, the missing pawl latch would have been found and the damaged hoist would not have been used. If the employees using the chain hoist had been properly trained on how to use and inspect the chain hoist, this incident may have been prevented. All of these factors combined allowed this incident to occur. In an effort to prevent another incident like this in the future, the rig will consider all use of non-standard lifting and rigging (NSRs) devices to be a level one permitted activity. The operator will implement a new process checklist for all chain and lever hoist usage. This includes an evaluation for different alternative 17. INVESTIGATION FINDINGS: For Public Release MMS - FORM 2010 PAGE: 3 OF EV2010R 20-OCT-2016 4 lifting methods before work is started with NSRs. All chain and leveling hoists available for use will also be from a single source manufacturer to standardize the training and knowledge base for the rig crew.

On August 07, 2016, while running casing on Chevron’s PN010 well in Green Canyon 640, an incident occurred onboard the Transocean Discoverer Inspiration in which an employee was struck with a joint of 16“ casing. The incident occurred while the rig crew was positioning a double joint of casing on the rig's forward conveyor system in preparation for it to be trolleyed to the rig floor. The Injured Person (IP) was sent onshore for further evaluation. On the day of the incident, the rig was in the process of running roughly 5,000 feet of 16” casing. The involved crew, consisting of two Roustabouts, a Banksman and a Crane Operator, were lifting casing joints from the starboard side pipe deck onto the rigs forward pipe conveyer system. The joints were placed onto a dunnage (casing spacer), located on the conveyer systems belt, to elevate the casing in order to release the rigging slings used for the lift. At around 22:30, after placing the tenth (10th) double joint of casing onto the conveyer belt system, the top piece of dunnage was knocked off by the casing joint being set down. The Banksman signaled the Crane Operator to pick up on the load in order to reposition the dunnage. The Crane Operator proceeded to lift the casing from the conveyer belt as directed from the Banksman. Once Roustabout #1 correctly repositioned the dunnage, the load was again lowered onto the conveyer belt. When the casing joint contacted the aft dunnage, the casing joint began to shift. This caused the load to swing into the direction of both Roustabout #1 and the Banksman. Roustabout #2, standing forward of the conveyer track, noticed the load shifting and proceeded to duck. The Banksman also recognized the casing’s movement and also ducked down. Roustabout #1 was struck in the torso by the casing and forced over a 42” handrail, finally landing on the rig’s riser yoke spreader bar stored directly beside the forward conveyer walkway. The Banksman immediately pulled Roustabout #1 (IP) back to safety onto the conveyer walkway. All rig crane operations were stopped and a rig wide safety stand down was performed. The IP was evaluated by the rig medic and later sent onshore to a hospital for further evaluation. A Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE) onsite visit was performed on August 15, 2016. Onsite interviews were conducted with the employee’s involved in the incident including the Tool Pusher, the Crane Operator, and the Banksman. Roustabout #1 and # 2 were not available when the interviews were conducted. While on location, BSEE inspectors collected paperwork provided by Transocean and took pictures of the area where the incident occurred. An investigation by Transocean Offshore was conducted in the days following the incident. It was determined that the crew preforming the task failed to recognize the hazards involved when repositioning the dunnage’s in such close proximity to a suspended load. Normally, rig personnel are not allowed within the area that the incident took place once lifting operations have begun. It was also noted that the Work Risk Assessment (WRA) performed by the crew prior to the casing lifting operation failed to cover the repositioning of the dunnage on the conveyer system. Since the incident, Transocean has redesigned the dunnage used on their conveyer belt system for casing lifting operations. The new dunnage design consists of four pieces of conveyer belt bolted together which prevents them from separating. Chevron and Transocean have begun the process of reviewing all WRA’s involving tubular handling operations. Transocean has also implemented new lifting requirements as stated in their new Health and Safety Manual requiring additional control measures for tubular lifting operations. With these changes, Transocean hopes to prevent further incidents like this from occurring in the future.

A. DESCRIPTION OF INCIDENT:_x000D_
Riser Pup Joint lifted off the deck during the crane operations made contact with a 1-1/4" diesel fuel line. _x000D_
_x000D_B. BACKGROUND OF INCIDENT:  _x000D_
During the crane operations on the aft riser deck, a 37' riser pup joint weighing 17,400 lbs. was lifted off the deck to be temporally staged in the well test area. As the riser pup joint was lifted off the deck, the fin on the riser pup joint momentarily hung-up on the stanchion post. Once the riser pup joint came free, the riser pup joint made contact with the diesel fueling station located at the base of the riser skate, consequently damaging the 1-1/4" diesel fuel line / flange connection.  Approximately 3 to 4 gallons of diesel fuel leaked on the deck. The diesel fuel was captured in secondary containment on the riser deck._x000D_
_x000D_
C. INITIAL ACTIONS TAKEN:_x000D_
Deck crew immediately stopped the job. _x000D_
The ATWD OIM, STC, Chief Engineer & the Noble Energy LDSL and EHS were notified. _x000D_
_x000D_
D. FACTS KNOWN AS A RESULT OF THIS REVIEW: _x000D_
Diesel Fuel System was de-energized at the time of the event. _x000D_
The diesel fuel line on the aft riser deck was isolated. _x000D_
Spill Kits located in the area were used to contain the diesel fluid. _x000D_
Approximately 3 to 4 gallons contained and captured in the secondary containment.   _x000D_
Clean-up process has been completed. _x000D_
The 1-1/4" diesel fuel line / flange connection has been capped and closed off. _x000D_
_x000D_
E. Actions Recommended to Prevent Recurrence:_x000D_
Fabrication & installation of a bumper guard (steel barrier) to be secured in front of the fuel supply system on the aft riser deck to prevent contact to the system from re-occurring. _x000D_

The incident involved a 67lb. 3" piping spool piece manually lifted up by rope into an overhead rack approximately  8' feet off of the deck to be placed in position in the piping rack by a man standing about 3' up on a ladder._x000D_
 The man on the ladder grabbed the rope to position in the pipe rack pulling the spool off of the rack causing it to fall to the deck striking him on the right shoulder in the process._x000D_

 The incident investigation conclusion determination found that the two workmen failed to properly observe safe and workman like practices in providing for the control of the load (piping spool) in hoisting it by rope up overhead to be secured in the piping rack. A second safety rope could have been used to secure the load to minimize the fall distance if the hoist rope failed, or an additional man could have been in attendance on the lifting rope._x000D_
As such the root cause has been determined to be human failure to properly access the risk, hazards and process in planning and performing the activity to maintain control of the load via the lifting rope and or to use a secondary backup (safety rope) to minimize risk to personnel safety._x000D_
A safety alert directed at safe manual load lifting risk assessment safe work practices is being written to be included in the revised risk assessment training for all field personnel to raise awareness to the incident risk to minimize any future reoccurrence of this type of incident._x000D_

DP current was indicating approximately 1.4 Kts from SSW (215 degrees). The vessel excursion increased to about 2.8 meters from the latch-up position. The excursion and all data/information available was observed. Gain mode was switched from high to custom, with surge being the priority, as this was the direction of our excursion. After several minutes the excursion dropped by @ 0.1m to 0.2m, but did not reduce anymore. The system was put back into high gain. The excursion remained around 2.8 m from our latch-up position for some time. It was determined that making a heading change from the current heading of 150 degrees to 180 degrees would help bring the vessel back to the set point. The heading change checklist was completed, including making all the phone calls to all departments involved. ROV was at depth observing the IWOCS to ensure there would not be any issues while completing the heading change._x000D_
_x000D_
The present heading light turned green, indicating the present heading function was engaged, however the present position light did not turn on. The vessel finally stopped. The DGPS was indicating that the vessel was 8.6 m from well head. This included the 1.9 m offset which was the latch-up position set point. Total excursion was 6.7 meters_x000D_
_x000D_
After discussions with the Master, it was decided to bring the vessel back to the previous latch-up position. Vessel was slowly moved back to this position. Once the vessel was back at this set point, the present position light appeared. ROV did an inspection of the IWOC's and all was normal. _x000D_
_x000D_
Atwood town Management was contacted as per WSOC. Kongsberg contacted to retrieve information regarding the sudden change in current and to verify the DP data logger information._x000D_
_x000D_
Vessel is currently in previous latch-up position and in auto DP with no issues._x000D_
_x000D_
UPDATE: The results of the Konsberg evaluation of the Advantage DP system, in summary show there were no anomalies noted and confirmed that the human interactions were contributing factor to the excursion.

On September 11, 2016, the Diamond Ocean Blackhornet working for Anadarko Petroleum Corporation, accidently initiated the Emergency Disconnect Sequence (EDS) while pulling the Blow Out Preventer (BOP) to surface. The BOP was suspended approximately 1,550 feet below the water line at the time the EDS was activated, and the BOP stack fell approximately 2,330 feet to the sea floor. The rig was located in the designated safe zone at the time of EDS activation and there was no subsea infrastructure impacted by the BOP being dropped. There was no damage to the rig, no injury to personnel, or environmental impact. The EDS is an emergency system designed to shut-in the wellbore, disconnect the Lower Marine Riser Package (LMRP) from the lower BOP stack, and allow the rig to safely get off of location during emergency situations. The EDS is manually activated, and it is initiated via two buttons that must be pushed at the same time in order to fire the EDS. One is a "push to operate" and the other is the button to actually fire the system. There are multiple EDS stations located in various manned locations on the rig, such as the Bridge, Rig Floor at each drilling chair, and each BOP station. Once activated, the EDS will automatically close the blind shear and casing shear rams in a pre-determined sequence, disconnect the LMRP from the lower BOP stack, and pull the LMRP to a pre-determined height above the BOP so the rig can move off location without damaging the wellhead. In the days leading up to the incident, the rig had jetted in the 36 inch casing, and open water drilled and set casing down to the 22 inch surface casing. The 22 inch casing was cemented from its total depth of 7,954 feet back to the mudline on September 6th, and once cement was set the rig moved into the designated safe zone and prepared to run the BOP. On September 7th, the rig started running the BOP stack and in the process they were testing the back sides of the choke and kill valves located on the BOP stack. On September 8th, a mismatch alarm was observed for the Yellow pod Subsea Electronic Module (SEM) B. The BOP was pulled back to surface and after troubleshooting the issue, a solenoid in the Yellow pod was changed and the rig started running the BOP again on September 9th. On September 10th, the Remotely Operated Vehicle (ROV) observed a leak from the lower outer choke valve while pressure testing the back side of the valve, and the decision to pull the BOP stack back to surface was made. Also, previous to the incident, several software upgrades had been made to the BOP system which included upgrades to the EDS. On several occasions during the software upgrades and during the stump test, the Dynamic Positioning Officers (DPOs) were asked to initiate the EDS to test the system. During these tests the DPOs would receive a simple phone call with the request for them to push the EDS buttons. There was no pre-job planning or discussion that otherwise would have given them time to think about the test being conducted. On September 11th, the Anadarko compliance technician contracted through Onward LLC decided to conduct the weekly Emergency Shut Down (ESD) system test for the subsea infrastructure in the Marco Polo field. The Onward technician called the Bridge at approximately 0825 and informed the Bridge that he wanted them to function the rig's ESD. At the time of the phone call, only the Junior Dynamic Positioning Officer (JDPO) and the Senior Dynamic Positioning Officer (SDPO) were on the bridge. The phone call was taken by the JDPO. When the JDPO answered the phone, he heard, "I want you to function the ESD." When he heard this, he stood and looked at the SDPO and repeated out loud to the SDPO, "You want me to function the ESD." Upon hearing this, the SDPO stood up and walked the short distance to the EDS station. At this time the JDPO asked whom he was speaking with and the Onward representative told him his name. It’s noteworthy that the Onward technician’s name was very similar to the name of a BOP technician that the SDPO had been discussing BOP related issues with earlier this 17. INVESTIGATION FINDINGS: For Public Release MMS - FORM 2010 PAGE: 3 OF EV2010R 22-NOV-2016 5 same day. The JDPO repeated the Onward representative's name out loud to the SDPO, and the SDPO turned to the EDS panel, and activated the EDS sequence. Almost immediately the SDPO realized his mistake and he and the JDPO quickly started looking over the system to see if the EDS sequence initiated. Shortly thereafter they felt the recoil of the BOP being released, and they knew the system had indeed fired. The JDPO immediately called the Marco Polo production facility to notify them that they had just dropped the BOP stack, and at this time the SDPO started notifying rig management of what had just occurred. The time from when the phone call was answered until the EDS button was mistakenly pushed was approximately one minute. The ROV dove to inspect the LMRP and BOP stack, and confirmed that the BOP stack was not connected to the LMRP. The ROV then proceeded to the sea floor and found the BOPstack approximately 484 feet away from the well head, in the safe zone and away from all subsea infrastructure. The BOP was found with only a few feet of the BOP stack sticking up above the mudline. BSEE Inspectors visited the rig the following day, September 12th, and started the initial investigation. The Inspectors gathered as much information as possible at the time, and met with Diamond and Anadarko's investigation team. They also participated in the interviews of the personnel involved with the incident, but were forced to leave the rig early due to inclement weather. BSEE Inspectors conducted a follow up investigation on September 20th. BSEE Inspectors were able to conduct their own independent interviews of personnel and inspect the Bridge work area which includes the EDS station and ESD station. The EDS panel was noted as being only a few feet from where the SDPO was sitting at the time the phone was answered, and the ESD was noted as being approximately 12 feet away. The panels and buttons also look nothing alike. The EDS panel requires the “push to operate” button to be pushed as well as the EDS activation button. The ESD station is a pull type, where the button is pulled out rather than pushed in to activate its function. Though the acronyms are similar because the same letters are used in different order, the panels and functions are very different. It was also noted that the SDPO was an experienced employee with 6 years of experience as a DPO, and he has been a Senior DPO for 4 years. He understood the difference between the EDS and the ESD. His action to initiate the EDS rather than the ESD appears to be due to momentary confusion brought on by all of the EDS tests that he had participated in prior to the incident. Also, the Onward representative’s name was very similar to the BOP technicians name of which the SDPO had previously been discussing BOP related issues. He had been in the habit of assisting EDS tests by pushing the EDS buttons when requested by phone call from either Subsea Engineers or BOP technicians, and when the phone call came in for him to test the ESD, his mind processed the information as EDS. In interviews, the JDPO also stated that even though he heard ESD and even repeated ESD outloud, due to the previous EDS tests and BOP conversations, he was even thinking EDS at the time the phone call came in. The moment the EDS function was initiated though, they realized that it did not make sense to test the EDS at this time and this must be a mistake.

While conducting the pre-use inspection for the west side crane, the Crane Operator was checking the low angle boom kick-out.  When he boomed down stopping at 0 degrees, he exited the crane to check how much cable was on the winch. The off going crane operator was walking by and pointed to the handrails for the Crane Operator to inspect them.  At this time, the Crane Operator noticed that the boom was laying on the crane pedestal's hand rail. The handrail was bent and the deck was pushed down an estimated 6".  The Crane Operator reentered the crane and set the boom in the rest. Operations have been stopped and the onboard crane mechanic will be inspecting the crane to ensure that it is in compliance and can be operated safely. Early indications from the mechanic are that only a small amount of paint was chipped off the boom and there is no structural damage. A barricade was installed in front of the damaged handrail until such time it could be repaired. A Gulf Crane Mechanic did inspect the crane and deemed it safe for operation. Repairs of the handrail and decking were completed.  
_x000D_
The primary cause of this incident was due to operator error. Following the swing of the crane boom outboard from the boom cradle, the Crane Operator failed to verify boom clearance of the crane pedestal handrail directly below that would have prevented contact when having to boom down to zero degrees. Crane Operators have been informed of the importance of verifying boom clearance when checking the associated boom kick out system and/or performing boom inspections with the boom at zero degrees or less.

Personnel noticed that a spreader bar attached to the CT reel was sitting off-center in its saddle causing the aft spreader bar arm to rub against the CT reel. The crane crew, assisted by a CT supervisor used the 160 crane to attempt to reposition the spreader bar and center it in the spreader bar saddle. CT supervisor obtained and inspected a Halliburton nylon sling and rigged a basket hitch to the 160 crane. The nylon strap used was 2"x6" and rated at 6400-vertical, 4800-choker, and 12800-basket. The ACO came up on the load, lifting the spreader bar to an almost vertical position, before the flagger called all stop when he heard a popping sound. The ACO complied, stopping all crane movement, but the load remained under tension. Two or three seconds later, the nylon strap separated and the spreader bar fell forward into the saddle. The two RSTBs and CT supervisor had positioned themselves out of the line of fire and were not in jeopardy from any falling objects. The lead CT supervisor inspected the CT reel after the incident and determined no damage was sustained to the operational portion of the equipment. The spreader bar was bent during the incident and will be replaced._x000D_

column79: Note: The total for Injuries in the above worksheet will differ from the BSEE FY16 Annual Report due to a duplicate error discovered subsequent to the publishing of the report. Please find informtion below on how the values recorded are computed for each category.

General         
BSEE Incident Reporting Requirements can be found at: 30 CFR 250.187-190.         
Effective July 17, 2006, the Incident Reporting regulations were revised. Related to this chart, revisions were made to the reporting criteria for Injuries, Loss of Well Control incidents, Collisions. In addition, new incident categories were required to be reported, including incidents involving lifting operations and gas releases. The number of incidents shown in these categories for 2006 and beyond may be affected by this change when compared to previous years.         
Incidents may be counted in more than one category. For example, a fire resulting in an injury would be counted in both the fire and injury categories.         
Statistics in the chart above are based on Fiscal Year.  Statistics shown in the Incident Archive are based on Calendar Year.         
         
Injuries         
DART – Days away from work; days of restricted work; or days of job transfer.         
Effective July 17, 2006, BSEE reporting requirements were revised.  These revisions required that injuries be reported if the injured person was evacuated from the facility for medical treatment or if the injury resulted in one or more days away from work, restricted work, or job transfer (DART). A combined total for Injuries in the BSEE Annual Report includes:  1) injuries that resulted in more than three days away from work, restricted work or job transfer, 2) injuries that resulted in one 1-3 days away from work, restricted work, or job transfer, and 2) injuries that required medical treatment, but did not result in any days away from work, restricted work, or job transfer (DART). 
         
Loss of Well Control incidents include:         
Uncontrolled flow of formation or other fluids where the flow is to an exposed formation (an underground blowout).         
Uncontrolled flow of formation or other fluids where the flow is at the surface (a surface blowout).         
Flow through a diverter.         
Uncontrolled flow resulting from a failure of surface equipment or procedures.         
         
Fire/Explosion Categories are based on the amount of property damage caused by the incident:         
Catastrophic – destruction of a facility worth more than $10 million         
Major – property damage greater than $1 million         
Minor – property damage greater than $25,000 but less than or equal $1 million         
Incidental – property damage equal to or less than $25,000         
Incidents involving both an explosion and a fire are only counted once.                         
The total used for this category in the Annual Report are a combined total for the Fire and Explosion Categories.

Collision 
Categories are based on the amount of property damage caused by the incident:         
Major – property damage greater than $25,000         
Minor – property damage less or equal to $25,000 (this is below the reporting threshold, some of these are reported).  
Major and minor collision categories are a combined total in the BSEE Annual Report.          
         
Spills         
The calculation used for spill events in the BSEE Annual Report is provided by OSPD and the data is not contained here within.      
         
Gas/H2S Releases         
Only unignited gas releases are counted in this category; ignited gas releases are included under Fires/Explosions. Gas releases related to losses of well control are also not counted in this category and are listed under Loss of Well Control Incidents.         
Some H2S Releases counted here may be below the reporting threshold.         
The Gas/H2S Release categories are a combined total in the BSEE Annual Report.  

Lifting     
For statistical purposes, incidents that involve both a crane and other lifting device are counted as one incident for the BSEE Annual Report.

While backing up to the platform, the rear of the MV went down and came up during the rise of a swell and caught the boat landing. 
The estimated cost to replace the entire damaged section of the boat landing is in excess of $150,000.

An employee was injured when assisting with lowering flotation onto the ROV during maintenance. The IP was sent in for further evaluation.
_x000D_
_x000D_
During work related activities an employee was walking down stairs and injured himself. The IP was sent to shore for further evaluation.

During liftboat operations the elevators are attached to the LB crane.  The elevators had latched onto the pipe, the IP was trailing pipe as lifted, when the box end (protruding above the elevators) struck the power tong arm causing the pin end to kick up. IP is being evacuated for treatment.

At approximately 0810 this morning the facility powered down the main generators for scheduled maintenance activities. At approximately 1030 hrs the facility powered up the diesel generator to provide essential power to the facility.  At approximately 1040 hrs the FM200 system alarmed and the MCC was evacuated. Once the all clear was given,  the initial investigation lead to the Apache 480 switchgear tie in point. Facility personnel discovered that the wiring insulation was melted and soot was visible within the enclosure. _x000D_During troubleshooting, it was discovered that the like-in-kind diesel generator replacement did not properly communicate with platform logic controls causing a prolonged power loss. It was discovered that the conductors used for this application were inadequate._x000D_
_x000D_

column19: Semi Submersible (Column Stabilized Unit) Floating Production System
column23: The IP was involved with annual inspection of a ballast tank.   During tank entry, the employee was turning around to  climb down a ladder inside the tank, when he felt pain.  At a later date the employee was transported for further evaluation. _x000D_

A pup joint was use to screw in the hanger and pull it from the C-8 well.  When the pup joint and hanger were laid down on the pipe rack, the pup joint was unscrewed out of the hanger with the elevators still attached.  The pup joint was then hoisted up and transferred to a storage work basket that was adjacent to the platform's outer hand railing. Workers stood the 10' pup joint up (vertical) in a leaning position against the top edge of the workbasket.  When the elevators were unlatched, the pup not being physical held began to slide and roll towards the hand railing, falling over, and then rolling between the middle railing and kick plate over board. There were no injuries sustained in this event.

A fire was reported in the #4 Engine Exhaust on the port side of the rig. The Emergency Alarm was sounded, the Emergency Teams responded, and all non-essentials reported to the life boats for mustering.  The Fire Teams cooled the exhaust and the engine was put into idle mode to allow it to cool down. Tthe fire was caused by carbon build-up due to the engine running with a low load for a period of time prior to starting the anchor operations.

A smoke detector alarm in the a-deck General Equipment Room indicated a potential fire on the rig.  The general alarm was activated and the Captain ordered all onboard personnel to muster for evacuation.  When the Rapid Response Team arrived at the electrical equipment room "light Smoke" was confirmed but there was no fire.  It was determined that there was no threat of fire and there would be no evacuation.

The IP along with other personnel were preparing rig floor and staging casing equipment. Two personnel were sliding a control panel across the rig floor and were approached by the IP to assist.  The 3 workers then picked up the control panel (appx 150lbs) to finish relocating it. During this process the IP slipped and fell as he was walking backwards with the load. IP was sent to shore for further evaluation.

One of the FLET wing restraint rigging arrangements (turnbuckle & wire rope sling) was dropped by the OTS whilst securing the sling from the vehicle to the garage.  The turnbuckle weighs 12kg and the wire rope sling weighs 5kg. Water depth at this location is 2,000 meters. The incident occurred despite there being two safety lanyards attached to the rigging (one is always supposed to be secured).  A survey was carried out along +200 meter to -200 meters of the umbilical from the initial drops point, corresponding to 10% of the water depth. Further circular survey around the drops area also carried out however no rigging or damage to the umbilical was found._x000D_

Employees were moving power tongs onto 4 Yz" tubing to break out of the stand on Well A-17ST01. While pulling the power tongs onto the
pipe, an employee reached for the tong door handle to open the door while the floor hands were pushing the tongs in towards the pipe at the same time. The IP was pinched between the power tongs handle and the piping that was set in the slips in the rotary table. The IP was transported to shore for medical treatment.

The Lewek Express is performing the recovery to surface of pipeline SN19245. This pipeline was laid as a test trial for the pipelay vessel that performed Noble's Rio Grande Loop pipeline installation and has never contained hydrocarbons._x000D_ While recovering cut sections of lay trial pipe to surface, the Balltec Pipe-Lock tool failed causing a cut section of pipe to be released at 4860' water depth.  Water depth on location is 7310'. The dropped pipe did not impact anything during its decent through the water and has been located on the sea floor. Recovery of the dropped pipe section is in progress and an investigation is ongoing to determine the cause of failure of the Balltec Pipe-Lock tool._x000D_ The dropped pipe was 512' long consisting of 13 joints of 16" pipe. Weight is estimated at 40t._x000D_

While back loading the power pack for the HWO Unit the crane operator got the load in position then started to lower the load onto the back deck of the supporting vessel. When the load was a few feet from the deck of the vessel the vessel shifted forward, or a wave / current forced the vessel to shift forward. The crane operator could not get the load up fast enough and the vessel struck the portable cat walk on the power pack causing damage to the top rung on the handrail. No personnel were injured in this incident and 25' tag lines were being used during lifting operations. There was no cost of repairing the damaged hand rail. _x000D_
_x000D_

A employee was prepping the rig floor substructure for painting while standing in the basket awaiting lift. While coming up off the deck with the Moonpool Pal Finger Basket, the basket caught on the adjacent BOP cart rails on deck (skids) allowing the basket to tip. IP sustained an injury. _x000D_
_x000D_

The crane crew was in the process of rearranging cuttings boxes on the plus-40 deck. As the box was moved into position, it was observed that it needed to be rotated 180 degrees before setting it down. The DSP immediately initiated a Stop Work Authority and the lift was left approximately 6 inches off of the deck. The DSP then informed the crane operator and riggers that the lift needed to be rotated 180 degrees. As the two riggers used the taglines to rotate the lift, the pad eye from the cuttings box made contact with one of the riggers and briefly pressed the worker into another cuttings box. _x000D__x000D_
The cutting box had approximately 22 barrels of well bore fluid and cuttings weighing approximately 17,000 lbs.
IP was walking through the quarters to his office, when he experienced a pain. The IP was transported to shore for further evaluation.

An employee went to the platform to launch a 16" sphere. While lifting sphere off of the floor, employee slipped on grating causing an injury. The employee went to shore for further evaluation and treatment.

IP tripped on the door frame as he stepped up to go through the raised door and fell through the door to the deck outside. IP was off duty no work was being performed.  The IP was transported to shore for further evaluation.

A P&A crew was pulling the last joint of 26" grouted casing through the casing jacks on well A-13. The bottom end of the casing was flared out and as it passed through the bottom bowls, the flare picked up the 26" casing slips that we had tied off with a rope.  When the slips came off of the casing to go back into the bowls, the metal flare cut the rope causing the slips to fall through the bottom bowls, through the opening on production deck that we had just pulled the casing through, and then into the gulf.  There were no damages nor injures to personnel.  
Fieldwood's investigation revealed that the 1/4" manila rope secured to the casing slips (attached to two separate ends of the slips) was not cut by the flared bottom's end of the casing joint as it passed through the bottom bowl.  The casing slips rode the casing joint upwards while being hoisted by the crane due to the joint's flared bottom outer edge.  The casing slips no longer being wedged between the casing bowl and  the casing joint, then relaxed allowing itself to slide off the casing joint falling downward; the manila rope used to secured the casing slips failed allowing the slips to fall into the gulf waters. 
_x000D_

An employee was injured while utilizing a hammer wrench on a 3" 600 pound flange.  When a co-worker attempted to strike a hammer wrench for the flange, the hammer hit a cable tray causing the hammer to be deflected and hitting the IP. _x000D_The IP was flown in for further evaluation and treatment. 
_x000D_

The connector and bullet frame were landed on the EDP via shackle and crane stinger. Add'l rigging added to assist levelling the connector with the EDP (sling to chain fall to sling basketed around the bullet frame). The connector (with frame) was landed and torqued. The crane stinger was removed from the connector shackle. Before add'l rigging on frame could be removed, a radio command was given instructing the crane operator to pick up. An "all stop" was called, but not before the basketed sling parted. The parted sling fell straight to deck and the chain fall traveled upward, 2-3ft. The chain fall and sling were taken out of service.  There were no injuries associated with this incident. There was no environmental impact associated with this incident.  There were no damages associated with this incident.

The crane operator was in the process of moving a marine sanitary waste unit from the platform to the boat when a valve on the unit struck a handrail.  The damage to the handrail is very minor, less than $2,000.  No injuries occurred during this incident._x000D_

While pulling the IRS, a roustabout was working in the moon-pool removing umbilical clamps from the riser.  As he went to take a break he took a step down from the sliding platform he injured himself.  The IP was flown to shore for further evaluation.

A roughneck was assisting Subsea with work on the BOP removing bolts with a pneumatic impact wrench complete with a no DROPS socket. The socket was additionally wrapped with duct tape to assist the pin on the socket from coming out. While removing the bolt the pin worked loose and protruded through the tape and cut the IP.

An employee was using a hydraulic wrench to remove MUX cable clamps while pulling riser.  The employee used the wrench and the hydraulic hose became hung up so he pulled harder on the wrench in an attempt to free it. The hose was freed allowing the wrench to swing toward the riser, however the IP was injured in the process. The IP was transported to shore for further evaluation.

On November 8, 2016 at approximately 1421 hours, an incident occurred during a well workover operation involving the crane and wireline unit. Prior to the incident, the Wireline Operator utilized the tool string by positioning it into the the wireline and lubricator. Then the lead operator went down to the well bay to close in the well. Soon after, the Assistant Wireline Operator bled down the pressure on the tool string and lubricator. When that was completed, the Assistant Wireline Operator signaled to the Crane Operator to begin hoisting the tool string and lubricator. During the hoisting of the lubricator, the wireline parted resulting in the tool string dropping approximately 10 feet to the deck. There were no injuries reported as result of the incident.

The Aux Line Plate (2 piece) for anti-two block system on west crane fell off during unloading operations. Pieces fell into an empty basket that was just put on boat. The plate is located above the ball. The load had just been put on the boat by the CBI Crane Operator. The plate was held together with two 5/16" bolts and center hole where cable runs through was worn making plate able to move during loads. When the incident occurred, the crane operations were suspended until all rigging and equipment were inspected and deemed safe and functional. The damage amount was less than $25,000 _x000D_
_x000D_

During Personnel transfer, the M/V Chad Michael contacted the South boat landing causing damage to the landing.  The cost of this repair is unknown at this time. Estimated cost to remove the landing is $176,100.00.

In the preparation for hot work a crew set up tarps to isolate the area over the heater treater when they realized they needed to add more scaffolding. The construction crew rolled half of the 20'x 20' tarp back to allow for the scaffold builders to add what was needed. The crew thought everything was secured and broke for lunch. At approximately 11:45am the heater treater fire detector alarm sounded. Everyone reported to the muster area. The Foreman and 2 A-Operators went to assess the situation. On the way to the treater they noticed smoke rising through the grating. One of the A-Operators activated the ESD. The operators utilized the fire water system to extinguish the fire.

An employee for Burner Fire Control was in the NE column performing surface preparation (wire brush and bronze tip needle gun) for corrosion mitigation when a temporary blower fan fell from its location.  The fan fell when it was bumped by an air hose. The fan (approximately 25 pounds in weight and two feet in diameter) fell approximately 18 inches hitting a steel I-beam and came to rest between two girders. The blower's housing failed due to the fall causing the fan guard to fail.  The cast metal fan blades shattered and turned to shrapnel.  The IP was sent to shore for further evaluation and treatment.  Value of the fan is less than $500. There was no damage to the structure or process equipment._x000D_
_x000D_
While installing a head on the platform generator the Island Operator got caught. The IP was transported to shore for further evaluation.

A wireline helper was attempting to break down a three foot weight bar stem on toolstring after cutting paraffin with slickline.  IP was using two pipe wrenches when he was injured.  The IP was sent in for medical evaluation.

A flash fire was generated from the TSE being installed very close to the hatch of the dry oil tank within one inch. Closing the hatch rubbed the TSE and tubing causing a spark which ignited gas vapors from open hatch. Hatch was closed within seconds of personnel realizing gas vapors were coming from open tank hatch. Upon closing hatch the friction of TSE rubbing on tank hatch was the ignition source, igniting vapors that impinged on bottom of heater treater pan exiting out from under pan to the location of the RIO 2000 control panel due to wind direction and speed. The fire was quickly extinguished with one 30 lb. hand held unit and a little dry chemical from a wheel unit to completely exhaust heat and smoldering from equipment that may have been still hot or smoldering from the fire. Three individuals were injured and sent to shore for further evaluation and treatement. The damage is assessed at less than $25,000.

The ACO picked up the 12th joint of riser from the port riser bay, hoisted up to trolley position approximately 30ft. ACO then traveled with the joint of riser and centered it over the riser skate. ACO then slacked off the riser and landed it on the skate. After the weight of the riser was transferred to the bucket, (Landed) the ACO heard a noise and noticed the aft guide tube slide down hitting the end stops and shearing the bolts, causing the end stops to fall. An all stop was then called. No personnel were within the immediate area at the time of the incident. The ACO was the only person that observed the incident, all other personnel were in their safe zones. _x000D_Estimated cost for the sheered bolts $60.00. _x000D_

After lowering a lift the boat, the crane operator noticed that the load line cable had jumped the sheave and had been damaged. The crane was immediately taken out of service.The load involved was a 3'X 6' cargo basket with a small generator inside the basket. The load weighed 1500 pounds.The lift was being lowered from the facility to the boat.

IP reached out with their left hand, grabbed the nearest rope and attempted to pull themselves in that direction when he was injured. IP was flown in for further evaluation.  _x000D_
While off loading the boat with the blocks a 1/2" x 18" pin which holds the sheave guard on the blocks fell approximately 30 feet to the boat.

While circulating out a kick, 25-30% of LEL was detected by the ships hydrocarbon gas detection system in the mud pit room exhaust extraction ducting. The alarm was sounded and personnel were mustered. The space was ventilated and the operation resumed after 17 minutes.

The alpha booster gas compressor had low LEL levels on a gas detector (10%) inside the enclosure. As a result, the compressor was shut down and a blowdown of the compressor was initiated.  The leak was identified as a split on the 2nd stage discharge pipe, just upstream of the silencer. Personnel gathered in a safe haven.

The IP was in the process of removing a clamp from the well head and while sizing up the bolt with a socket the socket came free and fell.  The IP tried to catch the socket and pinched himself between the socket and clamp below.

At approximately 1406 hours on November 26, 2016, an incident occurred on the Floating Production, Storage, and Offloading (FPSO) vessel Turritella. The FPSO is located at Walker Ridge (WR) Block 551-A, lease OCS-G 21861 (Stones development). The operator of record is Shell Offshore, Inc. A high pressure gas release occurred around the gas export metering skid, resulting in an automatic shutdown and blowdown of the production system. Alarms sounded, and personnel went to their assigned muster stations. No evacuation was necessary. During normal operations on the day of the incident, the production superintendant instructed the production supervisor and the lab technician to prepare to collect gas samples at the gas export sample board located on Module 16. Upon realizing that the sample point had been seal-locked by the pipeline company, the lab technician felt uncomfortable with the operation. At that time, the production supervisor contacted an engineer to assist him in locating an alternate gas sample point on the skid. When both employees returned to the skid, they found what they believed to be a possible collection point at a double block and bleed valve. While the production supervisor was looking inside the panel, the engineer mistakenly pulled a half-inch plug from the side of the valve without bleeding down the line. (It should be noted that both employees saw that there were up to 2500 pounds per square inch of pressure on the system in that area at the time.) The plug was not isolated from the system pressure, and once the plug was removed, the gas escape occurred, slightly injuring the engineer. The escaping gas was detected by the gas detection system, causing a process shutdown. The engineer proceeded to close several valves to stop the escaping gas; then both men went to their assigned muster area. After production resumed, the engineer received treatment and a tetanus shot from the onboard medic and was released back to work.

An operator while making rounds saw a flash fire coming from the compressor around the turbo charger. The fire was announced over the PA system and shut down compressor. The Fire was self extinguished when compressor was shutdown, duration of the fire approximately 30 seconds. No damage to equipment or injuries to personnel. A 3/8inch SS tubing oil supply line to the Turbo charger developed leak and sprayed oil onto hot surfaces.  This resulted in vibration, the tubing rubbed against another piece of tubing and developed a leak.

The crew was in the process of starting Fuel Gas Compressor #1 on the facility when the combustible gas alarm was activated. The control room operators shut down both Fuel Gas Compressors #1 and #2. Full muster of 56 personnel on board was obtained within 5 minutes. Investigation revealed that the leak originated from the Fuel Gas Compressor #2 package seal gas supply shutdown valve. The control room was notified that a leak was detected and instructed to close the seal gas supply to Fuel Gas Compressor #2 (SDV-8252). Lock out tag out was performed and the valve was replaced.

The rig floor was attempting to install flush mounted slips into the forward rotary.  The rig floor air tugger was being used to move the slips into place rigged up to a 4-part sling and the swivel lifting eyes on the slips.  The slips needed to be moved sideways so a chain fall was rigged up to one of the swivel lifting eyes.  This attachment side loaded the D ring of the swivel eye causing it to fail. The 3 other lifting points of the sling remained in place supporting the slips.  There were no dropped objects or injuries as a result of the event and no personnel in the immediate area during the operation._x000D_ Damage occurred to the swivel lifting eye.  Replacement cost is approximately $300.

While in the process of lifting a nitrogen rack from the MV GIS Linda onto WD 109A with the platform crane, the deck hand on the MV GIS Linda lost his balance while rigging up a stinger to the nitrogen rack.  After the deckhand had secured the stinger on the rack, the wave action caused the stinger on the nitrogen rack to tense up and shift, which caused him to lose his balance.  He fell on the deck of the boat.  The deck hand was not injured in the fall._x000D_ The nitrogen rack being lifted was 32" x 42" x 72" tall.  The deck hand had to stand on his toes, off balance, to reach the lifting eye in the top center of the rack.
While performing routine testing, the IP pulled the handle of a valve on the Flare/Vent Scrubber injuring himself.  The IP was transported to shore for further evaluation.

A platform operator witnessed smoke coming from gas generator enclosure and shut unit down.  When the enclosure doors were open on the generator end, sparks and a flame were seen and a hand held extinguisher was used to extinguish. Total time from smoke visual to extinguished was less than 5 min The generator was damage and estimated costs are $18,000. 

_x000D_

The IP was doing rig maintenance work (H&P 406 on Auger is warm stacked). IP was using a vise on a work bench to stabilize a section of pipe with valve attached in preparation to replace valve. While tightening the vise, the pipe began to align itself with the vise jaws which in turn caused the end with the valve to be pulled off of the work bench resulting in an injury._x000D_ The IP was sent to shore for further evaluation.

A flash fire occurred inside of the waste oil incinerator service tank which caused a pressure rise. The resulting rise in pressure caused the side walls of the service tank to balloon out and deform the integrity of the tank causing a crack in a weld on the mill pump suction line.
